#8277. We Tested the Viral ‘Slither Rig’ So You Don’t Have To

Published Nov 5, 2026 3:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

When it comes to bass fishing baits, the Slither Rig is the latest craze on social media. Half flipping bait, half saltwater spoon, this setup certainly raises an eyebrow at first glance. But when an urchin is the most effective lure for catching a bass, who’s to say a saltwater spoon couldn’t work, too? So I set out to try this new contraption, and here’s what I found.

The Slither Rig consists of three parts: a saltwater jigging spoon, a flipping hook, and a flipping bait. Any saltwater jigging spoon will do; I picked up a pack of five for about 12 bucks on Amazon. You’ll want the spoon to weigh at least an ounce, because you’ll essentially be using it as a flipping weight. Remove the hooks from the spoon and replace the back one with a 4/0 flipping hook. Then slide your soft-plastic bait onto the hook, rig it weedless, and you’re ready to go.

The idea behind the Slither Rig is that you replace the traditional bullet-style weight with a spoon and use the weight of that spoon to plunge your bait through thick vegetation. For this style of fishing, you’ll need an extra-heavy/fast flipping/punching rod that’s at least 7 feet, 8 inches long. Pair that rod with a reel with a 7:1 or higher gear ratio, and spool the combo with 65-pound or stronger braid.

I fished the Slither Rig intermittently over the course of three trips, totaling six or seven hours with it. Toward the end of my testing, I finally got a couple of bites flipping thick gator grass and hyacinth mats. But up until that point, I found the Slither Rig to be more trouble than it was worth.

My biggest frustration with the Slither Rig was its inability to punch cleanly through the mat. Granted, I was only using a 1-ounce spoon in areas where I would typically use a 1 1/2-ounce tungsten weight. But this chunk of metal was already as long as my bait, so I didn’t want to go any bigger for fear of increasing the risk of a fish hitting the spoon and missing the bait carrying the hook. And I’m not sure it would have mattered anyway. The issue had less to do with the weight of the setup and more to do with the way it hinged in the middle.

Nine times out of ten, when I flipped the Slither Rig out, it would land flat on the cover and then bend in the middle, causing both the bait and the spoon to catch on the cover. It was like trying to push an already-sprung drywall anchor into a hole in the wall. The physics just didn’t work.

I found that I could flip the bait higher and get it to go through a little better, but the kerplunk of it smacking the mat was off-putting to me and no doubt disturbing to any bass sitting in the foot or two of water beneath the mats. So I was left with no option but to flip the bait onto the mat and then gently jiggle it until it fell through, which worked about a third of the time.

Personally, I don’t see a situation in which the Slither Rig would ever be a better choice than a traditional punching setup. Yes, the spoon adds flash that could have some appeal in stained water, perhaps. But silver tungsten weights can do the same thing, and they punch through cover far more cleanly.

While I did manage to get a couple of bites on the Slither Rig, I have zero doubt that I could have caught more fish had I flipped a traditional pegged punching rig or Texas rig through all of the same areas, simply because I would have been able to present my bait to the bass better.

Is the Slither Rig legit? Practically speaking, no. You may see someone on facespace talking about how it’s the next big thing, but don’t let them fool you. While I did prove to myself that I could get bit on it, the mechanics of the setup just aren’t conducive to heavy cover. Consider this one debunked.

#8276. How Two Bored Belgians Broke the Backyard Ultra World Record

Trail Runner contributing photographer Jacob Zocherman drove 15 hours from his home in Sweden to document the Belgian team at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship in Retie, Belgium. Unlike a typical race with a predetermined finish and a predictable narrative arc within it, backyard ultras only end when there is one runner left. Zocherman spent the five days and four hours of what ended up being a world-record-breaking run on the course, sleeping in a camper van when he could. He spoke with managing editor Abby Levene during and shortly after the race.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts had been running for 98 hours at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, and they were bored. Never mind they had each run over 400 miles on the same 4.167-mile course. Never mind they hadn’t gotten more than a few minutes of sleep at once in over four days. They looked fresh, the nights were long, and blah blah blah, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports. But with the 100th lap on the horizon, something clicked.

“You could see something happen to them, like a spring flower waiting through winter,” Zocherman tells Trail Runner. “Suddenly the sun comes and nothing happens, nothing happens, and then in a specific moment everything happens and the flower comes out in bloom. That’s what I saw in them—suddenly they were happy to be there, cheering with the audience, laughing with each other and joking.”

It was like colleagues going out to the bar on a Friday afternoon: They’ve found their happy place, Zocherman says. Except in this case, their happy place was a park in Retie, Belgium, aka the middle of nowhere.

“It’s very touching to see, because they are so humble and so easy to like,” Zocherman says. “At that point, I felt like the race would go on forever. But it also feels very fragile—when there are only two runners left, there is no room for error.”

Per backyard ultra rules, runners must run the 4.167-mile lap on the hour, every hour, until only one runner remains and is declared the winner. In case that isn’t nutty enough, the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is an even nuttier spinoff of this format: Each participating country (of which this year there were 67) simultaneously conducts its own backyard race with 15 participants, and the country with the most cumulative laps wins. This backyard team world championship now alternates every other year with the individual championship, held on the original backyard ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Team USA would go on to win the team world title, with Mark Dowdle leading the stars and stripes to a collective 1,120 laps, also known as “yards,” for its second world title in six years. Australia took second, 51 yards behind, and Belgium took third, 11 yards off of them. While the team competition inherently shaped the dynamic of the race, with runners sacrificing their own best interests to slow down and pull teammates along, Steyaert and Geerts had several additional goals on their minds.

They’d each run over 100 laps multiple times—four times for Steyaert and six for Geerts. But neither had ever run through a fifth night. Belgium’s fourth-place runner Kenneth Vanthuyne was long gone after hallucinating that he was at work when Steyaert and Geerts put on their headlamps for the fifth time.

“That was the critical moment,” Zocherman says. “It was the one thing they had always wanted to do.”

As the sun rose over the dewy fields surrounding the dirt road of the race course, they both looked unscathed.

“I was like, ‘OK, nothing can stop them,” Zocherman says. They turned their attention to the Belgium national backyard ultra record of 115 laps, held by Jan Vandekerckhove. They checked that off and reset the goal to the world record of 119 laps, set by Australia’s Phil Gore at Dead Cow Gully in Queensland last year. That, too, proved to be seemingly no problem.

At 5:00 p.m. on Thursday, October 22—over five days after they started running—Zocherman heard rumors that Steyaert and Geerts were setting out on their final lap.

“I think they could have continued. They looked fresh, they looked really good,” Zocherman says. “But I also know they wanted to finish together. And the longer you go, the smaller the margins are that something will happen and one will finish over the other. And they wanted to avoid that. But they wanted to finish together.”

Sure enough, when the pair returned to the start/finish arch at 5:57 p.m., they did not go back out when the clock reached the top of the hour. Instead, the two friends, standing side-by-side in matching red shirts, grinned to the crowd of cheering onlookers, each raising a hand and joining them together over their heads in the shape of a heart.

Together, they had accomplished what no one had done before: Run 124 laps of a 4.167-mile course every hour, on the hour, for a total of 516.7 miles and a new backyard ultra individual world record.

“They are like brothers and have run many times as the two remaining runners,” Zochermans says. “So to them, it is not a competition that late in the race. They are doing it together. And they want it to remain like that. It’s kind of beautiful. It’s poetry.”

From the start at 2 p.m. local time on Saturday, October 17, until Steyaert and Geerts concluded their record-breaking run five days and four hours later, Zocherman was on the ground to document it all. It’s a stroke of good fortune that of the 67 backyard ultra team competitions happening around the world, Zocherman—who lives in his native Sweden—chose to go to Belgium. It’s also not a coincidence.

In fact, Zocherman almost didn’t make the 15 hour drive to Retie after his mother was unexpectedly diagnosed with an aggressive form of cancer two weeks before the race. The only reason he did go, Zocherman tells Trail Runner, is because that random campground in a foreign country is like home. Zocherman had been at the same course in April for the Legends Backyard Ultra, and the mini-universe environment of these events bring people together in a special way that’s hard to describe.

“It was an emotional rollercoaster and a logistical battle,” Zocherman says. “I wouldn’t have gone if it wasn’t this backyard ultra. It was a personal reason to be among people I know and like. I didn’t think it would be the crazy result that it was.”

Zocherman made the trek with his dog Balou, who he says keeps him grounded at these events with no predetermined end, or even rhythm. (She’s now witnessed three world records and could not be less impressed.) They did two laps of the course every day and got a decent amount of sleep for the first few nights before squeezing in 20 minutes at a time between loops by the end.

“I also know it will be a very long race and I have to drive home for 15 hours after so I can’t be crazy wasted,” he says. “Although you become crazy wasted anyway.”

Here’s how this world-record-setting run unfolded, through Zocherman’s eyes and words.

The first out of 372 whistles marks the start for the team world championships, by whistler Eilis Lanclus.

Matthias Pelgrims, one of the top runners the Belgian team is preserving his energy during the first loops of the competition.

Never a dull moment for the crews in between the loops. Always something to worry about.

The hula skirt. Once in a while there is a loop with someone wearing a hula skirt in order to break the monotony.

Resting runners in-between the loops with the watcher waiting to collect.

The puzzle. Whatever brings joy to the table and something to do during the early days is welcomed.

Approaching camp on day three. It’s a misty and cool morning after a very wet and challenging second night of the race.

The runners don’t fear the rain so much during the race, they say. It’s the wind ripping over the exposed night loop that they worry about.

Willem De Troyer is suffering from pain in his legs and is screaming out in pain at every step during what would be his last loop before timing out.

The emotions are rising as the race continues.

Jelle Tielemans is having a hard time during day three, moments before he quits. After 45 hours of racing, only 13 runners of the 990 who started in 67 countries remain.

As the race goes on, usually runners move closer to the start area in order to save time in between the loops.

Bert Verbist on his way back to the camp after yet another successful loop.

Common duties by different hands. Although the race is repetitive, the things that need to be done are endless and carried out by volunteers throughout all the hours of the day and night.

The remains of a celebration for Merijn Geerts, who turned 52 during the race.

Evariest Callens gets a massage on his throbbing legs after 69 hours of running.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

The intersection of the two loops. The night loop is more open and exposed, while the day loop is more sheltered but also a bit more technical in the forest.

Merijn Geerts takes a micro-nap in between loops.

Tanja Steyaert crews her husband Ivo throughout the race.

The control center with the camera feeds from different parts of the loops, as well as the race broadcast and other tracking sites.

A tense wait for the remaining runners to finish their loops and go out for another.

Sleep is grabbed when you can and where you can. Nothing is certain in a backyard ultra, other than knowing you will get little sleep.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts run through the fifth night. They are the only remaining runners of the 15 who started for Team Belgium.

The party is getting real in the Belgian countryside.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert’s backyard ultra world record is celebrated with the power cutting out (and the start/finish arch falling down) after heavy rain broke the electric circuits. But nothing, seemingly, can stop their progress.

The remains of the previous days. A lot of food, drinks, and beer.

Ultimately, Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert ran 124 loops—and set a new world record—before stopping.

#8275. The 3 Best Ways to Cook a Venison Backstrap

Published Nov 5, 2026 4:00 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I ate a lot of venison when I was a kid. Any recipe that could be made with beef, my mother made with deer meat — hamburgers, spaghetti sauce, pot roast, and more. However, she didn’t ever get too creative with venison backstraps. Although she realized they were a prized piece of meat, she mostly over-cooked them in a frying pan and then smothered them with gravy.

When I started harvesting my own deer, it felt like preparing a delicious meal was the best way to honor the animal. WIth a little culinary research and some experimentation in the kitchen, I learned that there are far tastier venison backstrap recipes for turning this prime cut into a meal. Here are some of my favorite ways to prepare a venison backstrap. These recipes were refined with whitetail meat, but they also work well for any big game animal.

The backstrap is a super lean and tender strip of meat that runs along a deer’s spine, stretching from the shoulder blades to the last vertebra. There are two backstraps, one on each side of the spine. Each one will weigh 1 to 3 pounds depending on the size of the deer.

The backstrap of a deer is equivalent to ribeye and filet mignon cuts from cattle. However, venison backstraps are much leaner than beef ribeye. It is a coveted cut of meat best served medium rare (between 130 and 135 degrees Fahrenheit). When cooked to a higher temp than that, the meat quickly turns from tender and juicy to dry and chewy.

When it comes off the deer, the backstrap is covered in a layer of connective tissue often referred to as “silver skin.” When exposed to heat, the silver skin becomes very tough. Remove the silver skin before cooking. Here’s how:

Because backstrap is such an inherently delicious and tender cut of meat, it doesn’t really need any elaborate preparations. Sometimes simple is better. It lets the natural taste really shine through. You could even serve just the steaks alone without the mushrooms and onions.

You can really fancy-fy your venison backstrap recipe with this twist on traditional Wellington. The process is long, but the rewards are well worth the effort. Serve with roasted potatoes and winter veggies.This recipe is relatively complicated and has lots of steps. If it seems confusing, check out this step-by-step guide to beef Wellington by Gordon Ramsey. We’re essentially doing the same thing—but with venison and without the accent.

The key to any delicious venison backstrap recipe is to not overcook. Although the loin is naturally tender and juicy, it can turn tough and dry in a hurry with too much exposure to heat. The best venison backstrap will still be plenty pink in the middle.

Alice Jones Webb is a contributor for Outdoor Life, covering everything from breaking news to in-depth gear reviews. She lives in rural North Carolina with her non-hunting husband, a codependent dog, and a well-stocked chest freezer.

In Spain’s emptying countryside, nature is moving back in.

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

#8273. Plant These 7 Flower Seeds in November for Gorgeous Early Blooms Next Year

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

November can feel like the end of things, but if you put these cottage garden and prairie favorites in the ground this month, you can enjoy beautiful early flowering displays

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November often feels like the end of the growing season in many backyards. Annual and perennial borders have likely died back for the year, and deciduous trees and shrubs stand have lost their leaves. Yet while the air is getting fresher, you can still work a little magic in your cooling soil. Because as it turns out, this month is a prime time for sowing some classic hardy flower seeds.

Many pretty cottage garden favorites, native prairie wildflowers, and pollinator staples actually need a winter chill to thrive. In nature, wild flower seeds drop from seed heads in late fall, settle into the cool earth, and take part in a natural winter cycle known as cold stratification. Exposure to freezing and thawing breaks down the tough seed jackets of key annual and perennial flower types, prompting the embryo to awaken as soon as spring conditions become favorable.

Sowing these flower seeds in November gives them a big head start. Seeds planted now establish strong roots. This means healthier conditions in spring, with sturdier stems, superior drought resistance, and prolific displays that can bloom a month ahead of spring-sown counterparts. By taking advantage of these planting conditions now, you lay the groundwork for an effortless explosion of color next season.

Keep in mind your USDA hardiness zone, your local climate, and weather conditions before deciding on specific plants and a sowing strategy. Successfully sowing flowers in November comes down to matching your plant variety with the right late-season sowing technique. There are a few primary approaches you can try with these flowers, depending on your region and weather. In mild winter climates (zones 7-10), you can try fall sowing (directly outdoors) so seeds germinate before winter, overwintering as frost-hardy rosettes that bloom in April.

In colder northern climates (zones 3-6), there is also dormant sowing. This is where seeds are sown directly into garden beds once the ground is cold enough to prevent immediate germination. Soil temperatures consistently below 45°F (7°C) allow seeds to sit dormant until early spring. For native perennial flowers or regions with erratic thaws, the best approach is winter sowing. This means sowing in outdoor containers and placing in a protected area, like an unheated cold frame, to shield seeds from rodents and heavy downpours while still providing natural chilling.

Before sowing, ground preparation is vital. Check soil temperatures before you start sowing with a good soil probe. Budget-friendly Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter, available from Amazon gives a reliable read on current moisture and temperature levels. Then clear away thick, suffocating leaves, remove weeds, and lightly rake the top inch (2.5cm) of soil into a fine, crumbly tilth. Pay attention to seed packet instructions regarding sowing depth, as this can have a big effect on germination. Some larger seeds may require burying an inch deep, while fine wildflower seeds need light to germinate and need to be surface-sown with just a whisper of sand or light compost.

Water the seedbed gently with a fine mist to settle the soil without dislodging the seeds, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Mark each row clearly with durable weatherproof tags, and cover vulnerable beds with breathable floating row covers, mesh, or clean straw to deter birds. Whether sowing directly in the soil or indoors, these gorgeous flowering picks are all good to go this month…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Sweet peas (Lathyrus odoratus) are the quintessential cottage border bloomers. They are celebrated for their intoxicating scents and ruffled hues, which can cascade across trellises from late spring through early summer. These vintage darlings thrive in cool weather. Sowing sweet peas in November allows the seeds to develop deep roots while temperatures are low. This leads to more prolific flowering displays, with longer, sturdier stems. If you fancy a floriferous blend of lavender, violet and maroon blooms, buy Sweet Pea Burgundy Mix Sweet Peas from Eden Brothers.

In milder climates (zones 7-10), you can direct-sow sweet peas along sunny, well-draining trellises. In colder zones (3–6), sow seeds indoors in deep root-trainer tubes or biodegradable pots, and keep in an unheated greenhouse, sheltered porch, or cold frame. Sweet pea seeds have hard shells, so nick these with a nail file (or soak in room-temperature water for 12 hours prior to planting) to speed up moisture absorption. Plant seeds an inch (2.5cm) deep in rich, organic-rich soil, and pinch the central tips once seedlings develop 3 sets of true leaves for bushier plants.

With their luminous, silky petals, California poppies (Eschscholzia californica) bring effortless cheer to borders, gravel gardens, and sunny slopes. These tough-as-nails wildflowers thrive in sandy or rocky soils, making them ideal for challenging areas where other ornamentals struggle. However, because they have brittle taproots that resent disturbance, they should be direct-sown where they are intended to bloom. Buy Marde Ross & Co California Dreaming California Poppy Seed Mix from Amazon for a near-neon flush of tangerine, melon and magenta blooms.

You can sow seeds now in regions with milder winters (zones 7-10). In these areas, fall rains will trigger late-fall germination, establishing fern-like foliage that bursts into bloom by April. To sow California poppies, scatter them over the soil in an area that drains well and has full sun. Lightly rake the seeds into the soil so they are barely covered, as poppy seeds require light to germinate. If you have colder or very wet winters, it’s best to wait until spring to sow these seeds.

Offering the vertical grandeur of delphiniums without the fussy growing requirements, annual larkspur (Consolida ajacis) produces epic flowering spires in shades of royal purple, lavender, rose, and white. This cottage garden classic is a cool-season annual that is ideal for November sowing. In fact, waiting until spring often results in poor, erratic germination, as seeds need a period of stratification to break dormancy. For a shock of saturated purple-blue spires, buy QIS Dark Blue Larkspur Seeds from Eden Brothers.

Direct-sow in a rich, sunny, well-drained bed. Cover very lightly with an eighth of an inch of fine compost or sand. Winter rain and freezing nights should satisfy the seed's chilling requirements, triggering early emergence in spring. Fall-sown larkspur often blooms up to a month earlier than spring-sown seeds, beating the summer heatwaves that can cause these cool-season annuals to fade. If your winters are very cold, try winter sowing in containers.

Also known as cornflowers, bachelor’s buttons (Centaurea cyanus) are cherished vintage annuals. Their blue ruffled blooms erupt in late spring and summer to create a dazzling contrast with cottage perennials and ornamental grasses (though you can get varieties in shades of pink, purple and white). Also cold tolerant, they are naturally adapted to late-season sowing. Sowing in November helps it to grow strong roots that can withstand hotter summer days far longer than spring-started plants.

Sow in a bright, sunny border with average to poor, well-draining garden soil. Sow at roughly a quarter-inch (0.6cm) deep, firming the soil gently. For the best results, ensure the area with seeds doesn’t erode or get waterlogged over winter. In mild winter regions, seeds will sprout within a few weeks; in northern climates, they will sleep until early March, flowering from late spring all the way to July. Buy SVI Store’s Bachelor Button Mix Seeds from Amazon for a lively mixture of floral heirloom tones.

Black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia hirta) are prairie icons that light up borders from early summer well into fall. With their sunny yellow petals and chocolate-brown cones, these pollinator-friendly perennials and biennials are often bought as transplants. Hardy in zones 3-9, they are super tough. However, their seeds possess dormancy inhibitors that can lead to patchy germination in spring soil. November sowing solves this problem naturally. By scattering now, you allow the rhythm of winter rains, snow cover, and sub-freezing nights to break dormancy smoothly.

Clear away heavy mulch and scatter seeds thinly over the surface. They require light to germinate, so press them into the soil without burying them. While fall-sown plants spend their first spring developing roots and crowns, many will reward you with late-summer blooms in the first year. Buy Harris Seeds’ Rudbeckia Goldilocks Seeds from Walmart for a ruffled twist on the dazzling classic. Just keep in mind that many varieties benefit from cold exposure, but not all, so know your type before you sow.

With their delicate, two-toned blooms and graceful spurs, columbines (Aquilegia spp.) bring woodland romance and grace to borders, cottage beds, and rockeries. Native across North America and Europe, Aquilegia species are hardy down to zone 3. Seeds require 4-6 weeks of cold, damp stratification, making November sowing the easiest, most reliable way to propagate them. Buy Blue Star Columbine Seeds from Eden Brothers for a vivid bounty of iconic violet-blue and white blooms.

Select a site that receives gentle morning sun and dappled afternoon shade with rich, well-draining soil. Some varieties require sunlight to trigger germination, so check the seed packet. Scatter seeds onto the soil surface and press lightly into the earth, but don’t cover with soil. If you live in an area with winter gales or heavy rains, you can winter-sow columbines into ventilated plastic jugs in a shaded outdoor spot. Seedlings will emerge in spring, providing pretty nectar for returning hummingbirds.

Purple coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) is a perennial staple in the sustainable, pollinator-friendly yard. Featuring daisy-like blooms and spiky cones, echinacea feeds native bees and butterflies in summer, while offering seed cones for goldfinches in fall. Seeds have evolved to weather harsh winters before germinating, making November a great time for sowing. Buy Purple Coneflower Heirloom Seeds by the Kviter Store from Amazon for a generous supply of purple drifts.

Broadcast seeds in a sunny spot with well-drained, average soil. Echinacea seeds need minimal light filtering through to sprout, so rake them into the earth no more than an eighth of an inch deep, firming the soil. Winter's freeze-thaw cycles settle the seeds, softening their husks so that strong roots push down early in spring. While coneflowers focus heavily on root establishment in the first year, November-sown echinacea tend to bloom reliably by the second season.

Your gardening season doesn’t have to be over in November. Taking a little time this month to start off some pretty cottage garden and pollinator favorites is such a rewarding investment in future backyard bloomers. By partnering with winter’s cold cycles rather than fighting them, you give these key annuals and perennials a real head start on early spring beauty. Using seeds is also a cost-effective way to get more flowers. If some don’t germinate or establish, you haven’t lost a lot of money. So grab a few seed packets, prep your beds, and get planting. It’s time to start looking forward to an effortless run of blooms well ahead of the neighbors.

#8272. Bowhunter Tags Massive 191-Inch Buck That’s Somehow Still in Velvet

Published Nov 6, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Jackson Berner was at work when one of his remote trail cameras captured a photo of a giant velvet buck the morning of October 20. The 21-year-old commercial insulator was on the job in southwest Ohio when he got the early morning picture of the deer near his hunting treestand.

“I said ‘Holy Smoke’ when I saw the size of the deer and its velvet,” Berner tells Outdoor Life. “The buck came by my camera at 7:50 a.m., and I’d never seen it before.”

Berner wanted to be in his treestand the following morning in case the buck happened to walk by the spot again.

“I asked my boss if I could have the next day off to hunt,” Berner says. “I showed him photos of the buck, and he said to go and get that deer.”

The following morning on Oct. 21, Berner was 22 feet up a tree sitting in a lock-on stand near where his trail camera had gotten photos of the velvet buck the previous morning.

“My brother-in-law told me he believed I was gonna shoot that buck,” explains Berner, of Springfield, Ohio. “I just had a feeling I’d get that deer, too.”

He climbed into his treestand just as it was nearing legal shooting light, a bit after 7 a.m.

“Legal shooting time was 7:22 a.m., and the velvet buck showed up at 7:30, like the previous day,” he says. “The velvet buck had been with a smaller buck on camera the first day I had photos of him. I first saw the little 4-point buck on the trail that morning, and not far behind him was the big buck.”

When the big deer got closer it stopped and looked up directly at the hunter.

“I froze, and when he dropped his head and walked a few steps, I drew my bow and took the shot at 15 yards.”

His 62-pound Darton bow sent an arrow tipped with a G5 Megameat 3-blade expandable broadhead. The arrow hit home and passed through.

“My adrenaline was on fire, as I watched him run out of sight about 60 yards away,” Berner says. “I decided to leave the woods and come back in an hour with some help to track my deer.”

Berner returned with his father Jason, cousin and brother-in-law. It was an easy-to-follow blood trail, and the party found the deer dead only 50 yards beyond from where Berner had lost sight of it that morning.

They loaded the deer into a Polaris side-by-side and then started field dressing the deer.

“We got to looking at him for gutting and thought perhaps it had no testicles, which is common for late-season velvet bucks,” Berner says. “But he had his man parts. The only thing we could figure is his testes had been injured somehow, and that resulted in him keeping his velvet so late in the year.”

Read Next: Here’s Why This Giant Missouri Buck Was Still in Velvet in Late September

Berner took his velvet buck to Toby Hughes, a popular Buckmasters scorer who measured the 16-pointer rack at 191 inches. Hughes says it’s one of the biggest velvet bucks ever taken in Ohio.

Berner delivered his deer to a meat processor, and the butcher told him he found a bullet in the deer’s hindquarters. Berner says the deer showed no signs of having been shot previously, and its hide was completely healed over.

“One other thing about that buck, is when I spotted it first on my trail camera, it was near where my fiance and I are planning to get married,” Berner says. “That’s pretty amazing.”

It is in fact a geologic formation, a remarkably friable gray-blue-brown mudstone deposited in the Late Cretaceous, some ninety million years before present, when much of what we today call the American West was inundated by a vast inland sea. #8270. Here’s Why the Classic Buck Knife Is the Only Deer Gutting Blade I’ll Ever Need

Published Nov 6, 2026 11:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

A few weeks ago, I broke out my sharpener and got my Buck knife ready for another long season. This is an annual ritual, and each year I take a moment to admire the wear and tear the blade and handle have seen. Each little blemish tells its own story, and for this knife, it holds every story of my hunting career.

I received this knife when I began hunting which, here in Pennsylvania, kicked off when I was 12 years old. Back then, the knife was new, shiny, and sharper than I could ever get it to be now. But more important than the aesthetics of the knife was its potential. I had no idea what it would help me accomplish in the next 17 hunting seasons.

I know that large, fixed blade knives like this one are not trendy in the hunting world. Everyone seems to be moving to smaller blades with fancier steels or ultra-light and ultra-sharp replaceable-blade knives. But the truth is, you don’t need an expensive precision instrument to gut a deer. For me, it’s a lot more meaningful to use a knife that has so many good memories scratched into it than a new high-end blade.

And that, among a few other reasons, is why I believe the Buck knife will live forever.

In 1902 Hoyt Buck, a 13-year-old blacksmith’s apprentice in Kansas, was experimenting with ways to temper steel so it would keep an edge for longer. He was, of course, successful in his experiment, although the Buck knife didn’t show up in the market for years after Buck’s discovery.

In 1947, Hoyt and his son Alfred set up a shop called H.H. Buck & Son behind their home. The father and son duo continued to make high-quality hand made knives and their business took off. In fact, Hoyt Buck made approximately 25 knives by hand each week until his death in 1949.

Alfred Buck then took over where his father left off. In the early 50s, he expanded advertising of Buck knives to mail order catalogs. In 1961, Buck was incorporated and in 1964, the company introduced the Model 110 Folding Hunter knife, which became one of the most popular knives ever made. In 1992, Buck debuted the Nighthawk, a fixed-blade knife that was 6.5 inches and had a black handle made of Zytel for an ergonomic grip. This knife was submitted to the U.S. Navy for evaluation for use by Navy Seals.

With over 100 years of blacksmithing and knife work under the Buck name’s belt, it’s no wonder why they’re still one of the most popular knife producers to this day.

While my Buck knife isn’t the original Model 110 Folding Hunter, it still carries a traditional feel to it. My Buck 119 Special fixed blade knife has some quality components, and admittedly does leave some room for improvements too.

The 6-inch blade is made from 420HC steel and is clipped into a phenolic handle. In total, the knife weighs 7.5 ounces. It’s heavy, bulky, and not always easy to maneuver, but it sure does work. It’s great for that first cut while field dressing a deer because the tip curves, allowing my hand to drop down lower than the tip to avoid puncturing the stomach or other intestines during the process.

Where it seems to fall short in comparison to newer, fancier knives are the close-quarters work above the diaphragm when removing the heart and lungs. The large blade is often difficult to twist and turn in the tight space, leading to a few accidental knicks to my fingers from time to time.

When I compared it with a new Montana Knife Company Whitetail knife, I was able to see just how much more convenient it is to have a smaller, 4” blade for maneuverability in the body cavity. I’ll be doing a full side-by-side comparison between the two knives in the coming weeks, so more on that later.

I’m not sure if it’s because I’m getting older or what, but recalling all of the memories this knife and I have shared really hit home this year. We’ve come a long way together. This knife has been there for all of the “firsts” in my hunting career: My first deer, first buck, first turkey, and even my first bear. It’s been on out-of-state hunts, out-of-country hunts, and even got lost in the prairie of South Dakota for a day or two after it gutted my first mule deer.

Sometimes it’s so dull from running into bone that it couldn’t cut a piece of paper, while other times, I’ve kept the edge so keen it’s like running a knife through butter. It hasn’t lived a glamorous life, but it’s been there for each of the moments I truly live for.

After chatting with OL’s executive gear editor Scott Einsmann and realizing that many hunters don’t have the same knife they started with, I called my Dad to tell him we might just be a tad weird. You see, I can’t claim that I’m the one who started this “same knife forever” trend. My Dad has been running the same gutting knife in his deer hunting pack for over 43 years.

After running my Buck knife through the WorkSharp a few times, I felt the edge to make sure it was ready for another year being lugged around the deer woods with me. There are, admittedly, a few burrs that I need to address if I want it to be perfect, but it’s good enough for me. The knife may not be perfect, but it’s perfect for me.

I packed it away in its black sheath and tucked it into my hunting pack, hoping it would see the light of day in a few short weeks. As luck would have it, opening week was quite successful, and the knife gutted a doe for me, and a first archery buck for a close friend. After a quick rinse and another few rounds in the WorkSharp, it’s right back where it belongs, in my pack, ready for our next adventure.

Derek Horner is the manager of audience development for Outdoor Life where he manages OL’s social accounts and email campaigns, and shares our stories with the world. He was born and raised in central Pennsylvania where his father and grandfather taught him to hunt and fish. He graduated from Pennsylvania State University in 2018 and still lives in central Pennsylvania.

#8269. 10 Best Winter Hiking Boots

Today’s winter hiking boots are waterproof, insulated, and compatible with traction aids such as microspikes and snowshoes. While 200-gram insulated mids are fine for commuting and half-day hikes down to about 10-20 degrees (F), we recommend buying boots with higher calf coverage and 400-gram insulation for all-day hikes and mountain climbs in colder temperatures. We are experienced winter hikers with hundreds of successful mountain summits, and we understand what it takes to stay safe and comfortable on long, challenging winter hikes.

Here are our top 10 winter hiking boot recommendations:

You can’t use your regular 3-season boots or shoes for winter hiking because they lack waterproofing and insulation. Most insulated winter hiking boots are guaranteed waterproof out of the box. Many have rubber or waterproof synthetic soles, so you don’t have to worry about water soaking into the fabric. If moisture does get into your boots, insulated winter boots will still keep your feet warm. The same isn’t true of leather hiking boots, even when treated with waterproofing creams and sprays. If your regular hiking boots absorb water in winter, they can freeze and cause frostbite.

Winter boots should be waterproof and insulated to keep your feet dry and warm, have laces for a secure fit, be comfortable enough to wear all day, and be compatible with traction aids like microspikes and snowshoes. While the insulation you need varies, winter boots with non-removable synthetic insulation are the lightest and therefore the easiest to hike in. Synthetic boots are also lighter and more waterproof than leather boots.

Some boot manufacturers provide temperature ratings, but there’s no standard way to measure how warm winter boots are. Understand that these ratings are estimates at best and that users will have varying experiences based on their activity level, health, weight, sex, metabolism, and other factors.

Most 400 g insulated winter hiking boots suit all-day winter hikes and snowshoeing in subzero temperatures. They have calf-high uppers, which makes them warmer than mids because more of your lower leg is covered by insulation. Many manufacturers claim they’ll keep your feet warm down to -40F, but that assumes you’re actively hiking, not sitting around doing nothing. Realistically, they work best in temperatures from 30F down to -15F.  If you plan to climb 4000-footers in winter in New Hampshire’s White Mountains, the Adirondacks, Maine, or Vermont, we recommend using 400 g boots.

Most 200 g winter hiking boots are ankle-high mids and retain less heat on the lower leg than calf-height 400g boots. On the other hand, they’re a little easier to hike in because they’re lighter and feel more like regular hiking boots. 200 g boots suit temperatures from 30°F to 10°F and are ideal for milder winter conditions and shorter hikes, where you’re less likely to get caught out after dark when temperatures drop.

Mountaineering boots have rigid soles that work with crampons that lack flexible center bars, for rugged mountains with steeper slopes or thick ice. You can hike in them, but it feels very different from a soft-soled 400g or 200g insulated winter hiking boot. Most insulated mountaineering boot manufacturers don’t rate their boots’ temperature ranges, so you have to rely on anecdotal word-of-mouth about how warm they are. If you hike across glaciers or go on trips led by mountaineering guides, it’s usually best to ask them which boots to bring. They may even rent you boots.

While you should take the manufacturer’s temperature ratings with a grain of salt, they are a good indicator of a boot’s relative warmth. It’s difficult to compare warmth between boots with different insulation, but knowing how much insulation a boot has can help you compare models from the same manufacturer.

This is like a regular boot tongue, except the sides are closed and sewn to the boot sides to prevent water from leaking in when you step in puddles.

In addition to providing more protection, a beefy toe cap won’t collapse when you wear microspikes or crampons.

Your boots’ soles should provide good traction on loose or packed snow. Look for boots with a deep tread, like a Vibram sole, though you’ll likely augment your boot with microspikes.

Look for boots with a soft cuff that closes off the gap between your leg and boot.

A gaiter ring is a small ring attached to the top of the boot that you can hook your gaiters onto. It’s not the end of the world if your boots don’t have one since you can still hook the gaiter to your boot laces.

#8268. Forest Troop

Lessons in primate behavior on my first women’s surf trip.

Baboons are assholes. After leaving his birth troop at around age seven, a male will find a new one and spend his prime years trying to fang his way up the hierarchy. Once he’s gained a modicum of status, he devotes his days to terrorizing lower-ranking males and females, who only grow to half his size. Gashes, puncture wounds, and missing ears are not uncommon among baboons.

In the mid-1980s, Dr. Robert M. Sapolsky, a primatologist living in Kenya, documented an unprecedented cultural shift when he noticed that the alpha males of a baboon population suddenly vanished. The alphas had come upon a garbage dump near a tourist lodge, and they defended their spoils furiously from low-ranking males and females, who were relegated to leaves, seeds, and insects on the forest floor. One day, in the East African heat, the alphas were exposed to tainted meat at the dump, infecting them with bovine tuberculosis. They died soon after. Left behind were sixty-two baboons. The

#8267. Feds Unveil Plan to Overhaul National Wildlife Refuges, Get More ‘Boots on the Ground’

Published Nov 6, 2026 1:06 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Following a 6-month review of the operation, purpose, and function of America’s National Wildlife Refuges, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service today announced an initiative to improve habitat, expand refuge access, and redirect resources to field operations.

Results of the internal refuge review were greeted with relief by wildlife organizations, some of which worried that the Trump administration intended to divest some refuges or to weaken their role as America’s top-tier wildlife properties.

In comments this morning at the Audubon NWR in North Dakota, both Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum and USFWS Director Brian Nesvik outlined 29 recommendations that generally support refuge field operations, improve both public access and administrative efficiency, and boost law enforcement resources.

However, with a 20 percent cut in funding and the loss of nearly a third of its workforce, it’s unclear how the Service will implement some of today’s directives.

The recommendations announced today are compiled in a program called Rooted In Purpose that generally increases the Department of Interior’s investments in the National Wildlife Refuge System that includes 573 refuges across 95 million acres of land. Nesvik announced the initiative in December 2025 and tapped fellow Wyomingite and senior advisor Joshua Coursey to conduct the 6-month review. Nesvik further detailed the background and sideboards of the refuge review in a wide-ranging interview with Outdoor Life in January 2026.

“Our purpose is simply to confirm that [each] refuges’ original purpose still aligns with the Service’s current mission,” Nesvik told Outdoor Life in January. “People have assumed that means we’re looking for ways to sell land. That is not the intent. The intent is to make sure we’re still doing those things that were intended when the refuge was created but also to make sure that things aren’t completely askew from our current mission.”

Today’s announcement, which is also detailed in a Secretarial Order entitled “Making America’s National Wildlife Refuges Great Again” issued by Burgum, distilled the 6-month review into four main areas of focus that the Service will apply over the next two years.

Nesvik noted today that his Director’s Order 230 resulted in 41 in-person refuge visits, 118 virtual visits, and four regional office visits along with internal surveys that solicited more than 1,000 responses from USFWS staff, and an external survey that received more than 2,000 responses.

“Refuge employees know what the land needs and what it takes to get the work done,” Nesvik said today in remarks delivered at the North Dakota refuge. “Their experience shaped this review, and their input will help us put its recommendations into action. We are focused on giving them practical tools and clear guidance to manage habitat, protect wildlife and provide Americans with quality hunting, fishing and other outdoor opportunities.”

Today’s news was generally welcomed by wildlife organizations.

“The USFWS refuge system has been an important part of the conservation successes in North America,” said Corey Mason, CEO and executive vice president of conservation for the Wild Sheep Foundation. “We applaud Secretary Burgum and Director Nesvik’s efforts to refocus the refuge system on the field work necessary to ensure quality habitat for wildlife and opportunity for Americans to benefit from that work and access these unique places.”

Ariel Weigard, vice president for government affairs for Pheasants Forever and Quail Forever commended Burgum and Nesvik “for their efforts to strengthen the National Wildlife Refuge System and its ability to deliver conservation on the ground.”

Today’s announcement didn’t detail how the Rooted in Purpose initiative will be funded and implemented. The USFWS budget has been cut by about 20 percent, or some $323 million in the Trump administration’s 2027 budget. Programs that have been either cut or eliminated next year include state and tribal wildlife grants, migratory bird conservation funds, and the entire National Wildlife Refuge Fund.

The Rooted in Purpose program provides some insights in how funding might be redirected to achieve the goals of refuge reform. The document details the Service intends to eliminate the Urban Wildlife Conservation Program Policy and “redirect all discretionary program funding to activities that directly support the conservation mission.”

The directive also prioritizes what it calls “boots on the ground.”

Read Next: The Rush to Build Data Centers on Public Land Is Worse Than You Thought

“Reduce headquarters and regional office staffing and reallocate positions to refuge operations, prioritizing the people needed to manage habitat, maintain facilities, support public access and protect resources.”

Lastly, the Service intends to stretch limited resources by using “technology and Super Intelligence to improve efficiency” and to promote contracting and reducing barriers for “for qualified local businesses competing for federal work.”

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8266. The Clever Secret to Speed Fall Leaves into Free Compost by Spring

Trying to make compost from fallen leaves takes forever, right? Not if you know this gardeners’ trick to get it ready to use in your yard in time for spring.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Making free compost from fall leaves is such an easy win, and with these smart hacks you’ll have a nutritious mix ready to enrich your garden soil by spring. While creating traditional leaf mold compost can take up to two years, this quick and easy method speeds up decomposition to bring garden-ready compost in 4-5 months. What’s more, it’s mess-free!

Want to know the secret? Any compost pile relies on tiny organisms, way too small for us to see without a microscope, to break plant matter down. These microbes are responsible for around 80-90% of the chemical decomposition process when making compost, and this method simply creates the ideal conditions for the speediest members of this recycling workforce to flourish.

It’s cheap, too, as you’re going to make compost in a black trash bag. Heavy-duty contractor bags such as Brute Super Tuff Bags, available from Walmart, are best as they’re much stronger than those designed for residential use. Your reward will be a rich and crumbly, well-structured compost that will feed plants as well as help soil hold moisture. Spread it as a mulch onto perennial borders and around shrubs to lock moisture in and deliver nutrients to roots. Dig it into veggie beds to fuel healthy crops, or mix with coco coir to make your own potting mix. You can even steep a scoop in a bucket of water for a couple of days to make a compost tea that’ll help protect your plants from disease.

Ready? Part of the Weekend Wins series, making a quick compost from fall leaves is one of those easy garden jobs that brings a big reward. Here's what to do.

Not all leaves break down at the same speed, and many species have evolved strong defences against microbes. Oak, beech, sycamore, horse chestnut, holly, laurel and magnolia leaves are all high in a compound called lignin that acts as a protective armor against microbes. They’re also rich in tannins, a compound that effectively halts the digestive action of microbes, so they're slow to decompose.

Instead, use foliage that’s thin, flexible and soft to make compost from autumn leaves. Maple, ash, elderberry, willow and fruit tree foliage are all far lower in lignin and tannin so they’ll break down in a fraction of the time. It doesn't matter if a few high-lignin, high-tannin leaves get mixed in, but keep them to a minimum. And don't worry if you're not sure about tree identification: just avoid using thick, leathery or glossy leaves.

Cutting the leaves up into smaller sections also speeds up the process by increasing the surface area and exposing the less protected innards of the foliage for the microbial feasting. Shredding leaves before composting is the equivalent of chopping a log into kindling: you give the microbes plenty of vulnerable material that quickly gets the process going.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The chopped-up material won’t mat together like whole leaves do, and it'll absorb water rather than repelling it, both also speeding decomposition.

Shredding leaves is easy to do, even if you don’t have a leaf shredder. Simply run your lawnmower over the leaves multiple times or tip the foliage into an old trash can and shred with a string trimmer or weed whacker.

In any compost pile you need to mix carbon – the ‘browns’ – with nitrogen – the ‘greens’ – for microbes to work efficiently. And this applies when you make compost from fall leaves, too. Leaves are very high in carbon so, to get a good balance of browns and greens to keep those microbes happy, you need to add some nitrogen.

Grass clippings are super-high in nitrogen: use a lawnmower to shred leaves on your lawn and the job’s done for you. Coffee grounds are also nitrogen-rich so toss those in, and if you have access to free chicken manure, that works a treat, too. Aim for one part greens to three parts brown.

To kickstart the decomposition process, toss a shovelful or two of garden soil – or homemade compost if you have it – into the mix. This will be packed full of microbes that will immediately get to work.

Microbes work best in damp conditions so pour water over the leaf mix, unless of course it's recently rained and the leaves are already wet. Aim for moist not wet, as you don’t want the leaves sitting in water.

Making compost this way requires oxygen so when you tie the sack closed (using a zip tie is easiest) don’t squash all the air out of the sack first. So this air can be replaced, delivering a fresh supply of oxygen, use a sharp knife to punch air holes into the sack. Around 15 holes in a regular contractor sack is about right, and try to distribute them well around the sides and base of the sack.

Those microbes are going to generate plenty of heat as they get to work, and you can help retain that warmth by storing the bag in a sunny, sheltered spot so the black plastic absorbs lots of solar heat. Tucking the bag against a south-facing wall or shed-side is ideal as here it'll enjoy plenty of sunshine and be shielded from cold northerly winds.

When you make traditional leaf mold compost, you rely on the battalion of slow-working fungi among the microbial army to do the hard work. But in this accelerated composting method, you want to encourage the fast-working bacteria contingent to head up the recycling force. To do this, you need to regularly aerate the compost and add fresh oxygen, and the easiest way to do this is to give the bag a shake, flip it over or simply kick it along the ground every few days.

Do all these steps and your homemade compost will be ready to use in 4-5 months, right on time for when your garden wakes up in spring. You’ll know when it’s ready, even without opening the bag. While the microbes are busy breaking down the leaf mix, the contents will feel warmer to the touch; once they’re done, the temperature of the bag with match the ambient air temperature.

When you do open the bag, the compost should smell earthy, like a fresh forest floor. If you notice a slightly sour note, simply leave the sack open for a week or so to allow the compost to air.

Then you’re all ready to use your free compost to give your garden plants a nutritious boost for healthy growth, abundant blooms and bumper crops. Making a quick compost is one of the best ways to use fallen leaves in your garden so put this easy task on your list of garden jobs to do in fall.

This feature is part of the Weekend Wins series, packed with quick and easy gardening tasks that bring a big reward.

Waterlogged soil is the prime reason potted plants fail in fall and winter, and this speedy solution couldn't be simpler.

This great-value gardening tool transforms lawns in fall, fast, if you want lush grass next year for next-to-no effort.

Christmas cactus blooms are a delightful part of holiday decor when you trick plants into flowering on time.

Tuck cold-hardy pansies into pots and hanging baskets for months of easy-breezy fall-to-winter blooms.

Plant fast-growing bulbs in your lawn and enjoy drifts of lavender-hued blooms in a few weeks.

Remove suckers that are stealing energy from your rose shrubs and enjoy bigger blooms next summer.

#8265. Scarpa Golden Gate LT Review: Moderate Stack Is So Back

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail shoes with a moderate stack are becoming harder to find. New trail models either have inches of soft, bouncy foam underfoot (sometimes with a carbon plate), or they are minimalist models that let your feet feel every pebble. Fortunately, a few that balance protection and ground feel still exist. I’ve just discovered one: the Scarpa Golden Gate LT.

Scarpa is an Italian mountain brand based in the Dolomites. Specializing in mountain climbing footwear, elite mountaineers historically wore the brand’s lightweight mountain shoes to cross rugged terrain. Scarpa’s trail running shoes reflect that heritage; they’re known for their rugged protection and firm, surefooted ride. But many trail runners who don’t live in places like the Alps or the White Mountains don’t need an indestructible mountain running boot. Enter Scarpa’s new trail shoe line-up.

The Golden Gate LT is Scarpa’s lightweight “door-to-trail” shoe meant for a broader trail running audience who want a single functional trainer on runs that bridge varied terrain, from asphalt to gravel to rocky singletrack. I put the shoe’s prowess to the test across Los Angeles’s urban streets, steep horse trails, and sandy beaches.

Weight: 10.5oz (men’s 9, women’s 10) Stack Height: 30 – 24 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm

+ Handles road-to-trail transitions smoothly + Stable base + Excellent traction – Fit too narrow for wide feet – Slightly sluggish on quick turnover

The Golden Gate LT may be a departure from Scarpa’s roots in many ways, but not in style: I received a hot orange-white colorway that immediately reminded me of the Orange Crush soda can and blends right in with Scarpa’s line up of mountain running shoes and ski boots. Though the flashy look isn’t entirely my style, I’m just glad it’s not a monster truck of a trail shoe.

Most of my test runs were on the hilly, paved roads of my neighborhood. Cruising through the familiar streets, I was happy to find that while cushioned, my landings weren’t squishy at all. Instead, I noticed a small bounciness in the midsole — like I was running on a shallow trampoline. That’s likely because Scarpa blended 20% PEBAX into the EVA compound midsole to provide extra responsiveness for what I call the “road” side of the hybrid shoe’s performance.

Taking the shoes uphill, the rebound was still there but didn’t do the heavy lifting for me. That changed, however, when I picked up the pace. With some downhill momentum, my stride lengthened, and any feeling of a firm trail shoe was completely gone. At quicker paces, the bounce takes over and helps maintain speed, feeling like an uptempo road shoe. Normally I don’t like shoes with much cushioning, but the upper’s gentle TPU-reinforced support wrapped my feet so nicely that I felt confident running faster and farther.

Later, I took them out for a long run mostly on trails, connected by some roads, to see how they held up on different surfaces. On the trails, the midsole bounce was less noticeable, which I appreciated, as bouncing over unstable surfaces doesn’t make sense to me.

Compared to other trail models I’ve worn, the lugs are far more flexible, providing amazing traction across sand, dirt, and rocks. The flexibility of the outsole kept my stride smooth and stable on uneven trails and helped the shoe maintain its beginning-of-the-run feeling late into a 14-mile long run. Overall, the outsole’s efficiency felt more alive on the trails than on paved surfaces.

If you’re crazy, like me, and sprint down steep trails, you’ll appreciate the moderate, 24 mm stack under the forefoot, making toe-offs effortless, helping short, quick strides remain stable, and ensuring that tight cornering is no problem. The 30 mm heel stack, however, which contributed to the smooth cushioning on the road, could sometimes feel a bit sluggish on steep trail descents. I prefer 4 mm-drop shoes to keep my steps quick and agile and maximize the thrill of heading downhill with my hair on fire. But if you’re more sensible and take it easy on descents, then the 6 mm drop shouldn’t be a problem at all.

Back on the roads toward the end of my long run, I felt the same road-shoe ride I get on my neighborhood runs. Though my legs were more tired after battling the dusty, hilly terrain, the flexibility of the upper and the outsole encouraged me to keep my pace until the end of the run.

Durability seems mixed so far: After testing the shoe for a month of road and trail runs, the outsole has progressively felt more flexible under my feet and can take on rocks and tough objects on the trails. The edges of the lugs have retained their sharp definition from when it was new, while the upper and overall cushioning still feel just as comfortable. The midsole bounce, however, is much gentler than when it was new (for better or worse), and the bright Orange Crush splash has since faded.

Quality moderate-stack trail shoes are becoming harder to find. If your favorite model lost its way in the “space-age arms race of trail super shoes,” as our editor Cade Michael aptly put it, and you don’t like feeling every rock beneath your feet through a thin minimalist sole, this one’s for you.

Runners with narrow or medium-narrow feet who prefer a tight fit should appreciate this shoe. The heel and midfoot’s gentle padding hug my narrow feet quite tightly, and the toe box has some room for toe splay, though it’s not wide — it’s right in the middle. This close-fitting shape is useful for tight cornering and platform stability, but if you have wide feet and need breathing space for your toes, the M2C H1, an Altra, or a Topo trail shoe might be a better fit.

So, is this the lower-stacked hybrid shoe that we’ve been waiting for? With its dual personality, the Golden Gate LT certainly handles roads and trails like it’s built for both. You can also totally wear this exclusively as a trail shoe for runs of any length. Though difficult trails with demanding terrain may not be its greatest strength, this shoe provides a comfortable, energetic ride on all other terrain, achieving exactly what it’s designed for.

#8263. The Best Gifts for Hunters: Get Them What They Actually Want

Published Nov 6, 2026 1:22 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Hunters can present a challenge when it comes to gift buying. They already have one of these or two of those. They don’t particularly care for Model A or Brand B. There’s always the $100 Gift Card, but you really don’t want to be that impersonal, now do you?

Fortunately, there’s an almost endless array of “I’d love one of those” gift ideas whether the hunter on your list chases waterfowl, big game, upland birds, or small game. This year, the following gift ideas will help you put the right hunting gear beneath the tree.

Missing a target means lost or broken arrows. Not only does that get expensive, it’s downright discouraging. The BlackOut LongShot 36 is a big target that allows bowhunters to confidently practice shooting their bows at extended ranges without worrying about missing the target. Best of all, it’s affordable. In my testing, I’ve found arrow removal is easy, even though I’m shooting small-diameter arrows over 290 fps.

Even if you’re shopping for a bowhunter who already owns a backyard target, they’ll still want and need this one. It’s a can’t-miss gift for anyone who loves flinging arrows.

Thermal monoculars are handy devices to have around the house and in the field. They can help you locate coyotes in the pitch dark, blood trail a deer (where legal) and make home repairs, such as finding heat leaking out of a window. The key to choosing a thermal as a gift is understanding that the more you spend, the better the image gets. But not all use cases require top-end performance. If someone is going to use their thermal to scan fields, recover game, and use around the property, a lower-resolution sensor works well. If they need to view and identify animals at longer ranges (beyond 100 yards), they’ll need a top-of-the-line unit.

The ATN BlazeSeeker 6 is a compact thermal that slips easily into a pocket and can record photos and videos. It costs only $429 to $489 and is ideal for everyday use around the property and in the field. If you’re buying for someone who needs more capability, I recommend the BlazeTrek 6. The BlazeTrek 6 has a better image and costs $795 to $1,499. Both monoculars are easy to use, and the ATN app has a handy AI assistant to guide you through any snags the recipient might encounter. Any hunter will be thrilled to receive an ATN monocular, and it’s another fantastic gift to consider.

Good gifts are practical, but the best gifts help people have fun. One of the keys to having fun in the outdoors is being comfortable no matter the conditions. The Uncompahgre Foundry Jacket is a highly versatile, packable layer that’s ideal for staying outside when the weather turns cold. From fishing to late-season hunting, this is an outer shell that will get a ton of use. We’ve tested and recommended the Foundry Jacket. You can read our full review to learn more.

Soft cases are the practical way to carry a shotgun to the range or to your hunting spot. They’re something that every bird hunter needs and will use regularly. They’re also relatively affordable, which makes them a great gift. The Evolution Outdoor Rawhide Classic Camo Shotgun Case is a stylish and practical case that’s made from waxed canvas. It will carry shotguns up to 50 inches in overall length, so it will accommodate most semi-automatics with 28-inch or shorter barrels and double guns with up to 30-inch barrels.

It’s tough buying the right knife for an outdoorsman, but you can’t go wrong with the iconic Victorinox Huntsman made by the folks who produced the original Swiss Army Knife™. The Huntsman has 15 functions, including blades, corkscrew, reamer, punch and sewing awl, scissors, wood saw, wire stripper, screwdrivers, and more. It’s available in 7 different color patterns. You can be sure that the outdoorsman on your list will find unlimited uses for this versatile Swiss-made tool through the many seasons that it will serve them.

Built to handle rough roads, bad weather, and air travel, this is a gift that tells someone you understand their passion and want to protect the tools that make it possible. It’s designed to hold two scoped rifles, with thick protective foam inside and six sturdy latches that keep everything sealed tight. Whether you’re shopping for a hunter that drives to the deer camp or flies out west for elk season, this case gives them peace of mind that their firearms will arrive zeroed and ready to hunt.— Scott Einsmann

You can get a turkey hunter a new call, a knife, or this piece of turkey hunting culture. The Tenth Legion is a book that captures the heart of what it is to be a diehard turkey hunter and is guaranteed to be enjoyed by anyone that chases gobbles throughout the spring. It was written by the legendary Colonel Tom Kelly, who recently passed on. I keep a copy of the Tenth Legion in my vest and read through it when the birds aren’t feeling talkative, and I highly recommend it as a gift for the turkey obsessed. — Scott Einsmann

Securely packaging your hard-won wild game, be it fresh venison, wild turkey, or mallard duck breasts has never been as easy as it is now, thanks to Cabela’s Deluxe 12 (D12) vacuum sealer. Weighing just four pounds, the D12 features a heavy-duty commercial vacuum pump designed for years of service. User-friendly, easy-to-clean, and programmable, the D12 takes up little counter space, while offering multiple modes of operation including manual seal, pulse, Auto/Vac, Standard, and Extended, as well as ‘Canister’ option great for preserving tough-to-seal foodstuffs.

This chest pack is designed to hold a hunter’s binoculars, and much much more. For backcountry hunters, a chest pack is a critical piece of gear and there are few out there that offer more features than the Kuiu Pro. It includes: magnetic closure for maximum quietness, adjustable main pouch for proper bino fit, rail-lock system for bottom accessory, rail-lock mount for ammo holder, plus a variety of extra pockets. It comes in five different camo/solid color options (I don’t think you can go wrong with solid Ash). This is an ideal gift for a big game hunter or even a turkey hunter, who needs quick access to optics and other critical gear.

A cellular trail camera is a perfect gift for any deer or turkey hunter. If the hunter already has a cell cam, they’ll be happy to have another (you can never have too many cameras out there). And if they don’t have camera yet, then your gift will get them in the game. And there’s not a trail camera out there that’s more effective and easy to use than the Tactacam 4.0. The Outdoor Life crew thoroughly tests trail cams every year, and the Tactacam 4.0 won the editor’s choice award, hands down, in 2026. Features include: Up to 4K photo definition, up to 96 feet of flash range, Low-glow or no-glow flash settings, 16 gb of internal storage, powered by 12 AA batteries, live video, on-demand photos, GPS enabled.

Sure, the description says ‘Waterfowl Backpack,’ and all duck hunters should have one of these, but don’t let the name fool you. This well-built large capacity pack has 101 uses in the field, e.g. camera bag, lunch box, blind bag, and dry clothes storage to name just a handful. With over 1,550 cubic inches of interior space, the Northern Flight backpack is crafted of rugged 600D polyester with a water-resistant polyurethane coating to help keep what’s inside nice and dry. There’s plenty of pockets, glove-friendly zippers, a huge main compartment, hydration pouch, and MOLLE attachment points for additional capacity. In other words this is an excellent hunting pack for a variety of scenarios.

How many times have you wished for some warmth while waiting out that trophy whitetail from inside the chilly confines of that late January ground blind? Thanks to the innovative minds at TideWe and their heated hunting chair, turning up the thermostat just became possible. At first glance, the chair seems ordinary enough – adjustable height; swiveling through 360 degrees; armrests; and a detachable gear pouch. But this chair adds a little spice in the form of battery-powered heat. Three heat levels (100 through 130 degrees), long 10-hour  battery life at the lowest setting, and a fast three-hour charge time make this ‘hot seat’ a Must-Have this winter.

Hunters constantly need to keep knives and broadheads sharp. This folding field sharpener is a versatile and handy way to maintain everything from pocketknives to axes. It’s only $13, and I’ve been testing it while sharpening broadheads and honing knives. It works great, and I recommend it.

*I noticed this product has only a three-star rating from customer reviews. But the reviews are all for a fishing reel. This appears to be a glitch on the Bass Pro Shops/Cabela’s website.

There’s nothing worse than slipping your feet into cold wet boots. Fortunately, the folks at PEET Dryer have the answer in their original boot dryer. The PEET dryer uses convection to push warm air upwards through specially designed chambers and ports to dry shoes and boots of all shapes, sizes, and material types. Safe enough to operate 24/7, this makes the perfect gift for anyone who goes outside, but especially hunters who are prone to get their boots wet.

Hunters often like to forage while they’re in the field. But wild mushrooms are nothing to be guessed at when it comes to their edibility. Some make wonderful meals, while others can make a person terribly sick, or worse. This makes a good mushroom identification book an absolute necessity for the forestland forager. And few are as comprehensive as David Arora’s All That The Rain Promises, and More. An educator in the field of mycology, Arora’s easy to understand descriptive prose, along with his excellent photographs, takes much of the mystery out of separating the ‘good’ from the ‘not so good’ when it comes to fungi.

Virtually indestructible. That’s the best way to describe YETI’s latest introduction, the Loadout Gobox 1 Gear Case. Built out of what the company refers to as ‘Defender II Material,’ the Gobox 1 is the perfect hard case if you’re looking to safely store items such as a wallet, passport, keys, portable power, or anything else. The Gobox 1 seals out Mother Nature, while providing roughly 56 cubic inches of interior space, yet only weighing 1.7 pounds. The Gobox 1 is ideal for kayakers, rafting enthusiasts, off-roaders, mountain bikers, and of course, hunters. And it’s available in five different colors.

There are about 101 different ways to repel mosquitoes but few are as effective and easy to use as a ThermaCELL. The lightweight MR300 uses a cylindrical fuel canister to gently warm a small metal plate, which in turn activates the material infused into the unit’s repellent mat. This repellent diffuses into a 15 square-foot zone of protection around the unit, keeping mosquitoes at bay within 15 minutes and (under optimal conditions) for as long as four hours. No batteries. No DEET sprays. And it’s safe to use around pets.

Firearm maintenance should be a concern of all hunters. Fortunately, the Allen Company’s Breakthrough Clean Technologies Universal Cleaning Kit helps make the job much easier. Included in the tough ammo can container are a variety of nylon brushes, brass patch jags, two multi-section cleaning rods, patches, swabs, a silicone gun cloth, solvent, and a bottle of ‘Battle Born’ high purity gun oil. It’s everything you need to clean a gun in one place.

Even in these modern times of precision air rifles, there’s still something to be said about Old School stuff — like Crosman’s 760 Pumpmaster air rifle. Now here’s a tool developed specifically to introduce young or new shooters to the shooting sports. The 760 handles both .177 caliber pellets and BBs, sending them downrange at 615/700 and 645 feet-per-second, respectively. A crossbolt safety, synthetic stock/fore-end, grooved receiver to accommodate a 4x scope, and traditional front/rear blade sights make this the perfect gift for all ages.

#8262. Winter Hiking Gift Guide (2026)

Winter is a great time to gear up and head out for cold-weather hiking, mountaineering, or snowshoeing. The bugs are gone, and so are the crowds, leaving the mountains and the hills to those who can’t live without their weekly dose of sun and snow. Here are 20 expert gift recommendations for the winter hiker and backpacker in your life.

Drinking water will freeze in winter unless you do something to prevent it. The best way to carry water in winter is to fill wide-mouth Nalgene bottles with boiling water and carry them upside down (so the caps don’t freeze) in an external insulated water bottle pocket, like the Hyperlite Mountain Gear Insulator, so they stay warm longer.

Glove leashes keep your winter gloves or mittens safely attached to your wrists. When you take them off to use your camera, check your GPS app, or adjust gear, the gloves dangle by the strap instead of falling into the snow or getting lost.

The Black Diamond Alpine Start Hoody is a highly breathable, lightweight softshell jacket that works well as a wind shirt and protects against light precipitation. Ideal for cold-weather pursuits, it offers excellent breathability without the weight of a heavier technical shell. Made with Schoeller stretch-woven fabric, it’s ideal for dynamic activities like winter hiking, mountaineering, ice climbing, or XC skiing. You want a highly breathable wind layer with an adjustable helmet-compatible hood, stretch cuffs, and a zippered chest pocket. Available for men and women.

You can wear the Polar Buff as a helmet liner, balaclava, mask, scarf, hood, or hat for warmth where you need it. One side features an original Buff, while the other adds a layer of Polartec fleece to help reduce heat loss. Super warm and comfortable, this item’s value comes from its versatility in winter conditions.

IF A FREIGHTER STEAMING out of Okinawa takes a big typhoon swell starboard and dumps a container full of Hot Wheels into the Pacific, there are about eleventy billion beaches where those packages of little cars might wash ashore.
