#8187. The Blue Ridge Mountains Are Where You Want to Be This Winter

Beech Mountain in the North Carolina High Country. (Photo: Sam Dean)

Everyone who loves the outdoors has heard of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Many have been there, likely during a magical Appalachian summer or to catch one of the world’s most magnificent fall foliage shows. But few know that the Blue Ridge Mountains are also a winter wonderland. Discover why for yourself on a trip to the North Carolina High Country.

The biggest surprise here is the skiing. There are three major ski areas in the High Country, all with some of the best trails, conditions, and vibes in the East. Here’s how they stack up.

Sugar Mountain Resort is the largest ski area in North Carolina, with 125 skiable acres, six chairlifts, and terrain for all levels. It also has the most vertical of the three Boone Area resorts, with 1,200 feet from summit to base. Bonus: A 700-foot-long tubing park adds another great option for family-friendly downhill fun.

With a peak elevation just over a mile high, Beech Mountain Resort is the highest resort in the Boone area—which makes sense, since it’s located in the highest municipality in the eastern United States. With 17 trails, a tubing park, cozy slopeside firepits, and even an on-site brewery, there’s a way for everyone to enjoy this winter hub.

First opened in 1962, Appalachian Ski Mountain is the region’s oldest ski resort and has grown into a local institution. The mountain hosts community events and ski/snowboard competitions throughout the year and is loved by first-timers and seasoned vets alike. Like a little variety in your winter sports vacation? There’s also an outdoor ice rink that offers skate rentals and private lessons.

It’s always a good snow year in the Boone Area, thanks to the area’s reliable snowmaking capabilities. You can expect 100 percent slope coverage at Beech Mountain and Sugar Mountain and the greatest snowmaking pumping capacity per acre of any resort in the Southeast at Appalachian Ski Mountain. All this is to say you can ski and ride in consistent conditions from opening to closing day. Another perk for squeezing the most out of a winter getaway? Night skiing. All three resorts are open until 10 p.m. most days. Appalachian Ski Mountain is even open for “Midnight Blast” on the weekend.

And, of course, no ski day is complete without a quality après scene. There’s plenty to eat and drink in and around downtown Boone. Just a 20-minute drive from Appalachian Ski Mountain, Boone has everything from High Country wine to craft brews to farm-to-table restaurants with seasonally rotating menus.

You can also experience winter’s peace and quiet in the Blue Ridge backcountry on a hiking or snowshoeing adventure. Explore the trail network at Moses Cone Memorial Park, close to Boone, or enjoy sweeping views of the Appalachian Range at Elk Knob State Park, which has fun and challenging routes that will make you remember why the Blue Ridge Mountains are great in any season.

Explore Boone is the Boone and Watauga County Tourism Development Authority responsible for promoting travel, tourism, and corporate travel, sponsoring tourist-related events and activities, and financing tourism-related capital projects. As a popular outdoor recreation, dining, and shopping destination, Boone is known as “the Heart of the High Country.”

#8186. The Best Ice Climbing Gear of 2027: Boots, Tools, Crampons, and More

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The author, Anthony Walsh, heads up 'Nightmare on Wolfstreet' (WI6 M7+) on B.C.'s famed Stanley Headwall. (Photo: Sebastian Pelletti)

Overview: The best ice climbing gear of 2027 includes Petzl Dart crampons, La Sportiva Olympus Mons Pro boots, Black Diamond Viper ice tool, the Blue Ice Choucas Pro harness, and the Mountain Equipment Xenith jacket, plus proven picks like the La Sportiva G-Summit boots. Our testers climbed up to WI5+ and M7 from the Canadian Rockies to the Patagonian Andes, in temperatures down to -30°F.

Ice climbing is a high-stakes sport. Do it right, and you’re in for a meditative cruise with just the right level of spice. Do it wrong, and you’ll be left spooked, shivering—or worse. The difference often boils down to your experience level. But right after that comes your ice climbing gear. When you’re 100 feet off the ground, pinned to a silvery ribbon of ice by nothing but four blades of steel, you need absolute trust in your equipment. But how can you tell which products to rely on? That’s our job.

This season, our team of testers tried out 15 pieces of ice climbing gear that are either new for 2026-’27 or came out partway through last winter. Some turned out to be overengineered, overpriced, or poorly built. Others proved thoughtfully designed and dependable in a range of winter conditions. Over thousands of vertical feet of testing everywhere from the Patagonian Andes to the Canadian Rockies, we sorted out the bad from the good. Below: nothing but the best ice climbing gear available this season.

Weight: 11.3 oz (men’s medium) / 9.9 oz (women’s medium)

Pros and Cons + Novel and effective baffle design + Two-way zipper with bottom hem snap + Low-profile, elasticated cuffs + Impressive warmth-to-weight ratio – No way to tighten hood – Gimmicky and impractical hexagonal stuff sack

Mountain Equipment’s all-new Xenith is the big experiment in winter insulation this year. After a research paper suggested hexagons might be the most thermally efficient shape, the brand built the jacket with hexagonal baffles. (These weirdly shaped baffles also seem to limit down migration.)

Our testers found it extremely warm for 11.3 ounces (with 4.3 ounces of 800-fill hydrophobic goose down)—making it the ideal midlayer on -30°F days and nearly unnoticeable clipped to a harness on warmer ones. The Xenith’s low weight comes from its spare design. It has two hand-warming pockets, elasticated cuffs, a two-way zipper, internal drop pockets, a hem-cinch cord, and a hood. Downside: The hood can’t be cinched at all. Without a helmet to fill it, you’ll feel like a kid wearing your parent’s oversized clothes.

Weight: 8.5 oz Sizes: men’s XXS-XXL (the women’s counterpart is the M10 Storm Bib)

Pros and Cons + Surprising stretch and durability + Superior range of motion – No women’s-specific version

The M10 Storm Hardshell offers hands-down the best range of motion we’ve ever experienced in an alpine climbing pant. Thanks to a roomy fit, gusseted crotch, and slightly stretchy fabric—a mix of ripstop nylon, proprietary waterproof laminate, and a slick jersey backer—we were able to step high and wide without feeling constricted—a refreshing departure from the Euro-style, slim-fit trousers that have taken over the market in recent years.

“While transitioning from a panel of limestone to a hanging ice dagger, I stemmed my legs as far as I could between the two mediums and felt zero resistance,” reported Climbing senior editor Anthony Walsh. Some testers reported doing a full split just to test out the mobility. No torn crotches yet.

The rest of the layout is smart but simple. The thigh pocket, big enough to fit a smartphone, and fly are both positioned to remain accessible even with a harness on. “The zipper is on a diagonal rather than vertically-oriented like most other pants, so you can relieve yourself without a harness’s tie-in points or belay loop getting in the way,” Walsh reports. Elasticized cuffs keep moisture out—something we appreciated when spring conditions left our ice pitches streaming with water.

We loved how waterproof the M10s were, too. “I tested the M10s on some of the wettest pitches of my entire season,” said Walsh. “My ‘waterproof’ gloves soon wetted out, and my face had a steady drip of water coming off my nose, but under the M10 pants, I stayed 100 percent dry.” Credit goes to a lightweight, breathable, proprietary membrane and a PFCs-free DWR (durable water repellent) that boasted best-in-test longevity. After eight straight days of fighting up scrappy mixed lines in the Canadian Rockies, both the waterproofing and the fabric remained intact.

Pros and Cons + Legitimately waterproof + Decently breathable + Cuff closure keeps out loose snow – Not very warm

These insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

The Temres is not exceedingly warm, but for temps hovering around freezing (or those with excellent circulation) these are a fantastic, cheap option. Otherwise, buy a larger size and add a thin liner glove for deep-winter leads. A note on sizing: Showa gloves run small, so size one up from your typical ice glove.

Pros and Cons + Warmest technical mountaineering boot made + Easy adjustment with BOA system + Surprisingly nimble and lightweight – Expensive – Unnecessarily tall gaiter

Knee-height mountain boots are no longer just for guided Himalayan climbers. La Sportiva’s new Olympus Mons Pro—a 4-pound-4-ounce pair of “8,000-meter boots”—is a game changer for ice and mixed climbers who need serious warmth without sacrificing performance.

Our tester wore them on Field of Dreams (WI5; 250ft), Mixed Master (WI4 M5; 1,000ft), and M7 cragging. “I have generally cold feet yet I was sweating standing around in -5°F in these boots,” he said. “Despite all the insulation, these are plenty nimble for WI5 and M5.” The Olympus Mons Pro might be a couple ounces heavier than La Sportiva’s G-Summit boot, but it is drastically warmer and just as comfortable. Unbelievably, it’s also 7 ounces lighter per pair than the brand’s flagship leather single boot, the Nepal EVO, thanks to Primaloft Gold Aerogel insulation.

The one gripe: an unnecessarily tall gaiter. “With such a long zipper to get in and out of the boot, I’m less likely to adjust the Velcro power strap when I need to,” said one tester. Thankfully the external BOA allows a climber to adjust some of the fit on the fly.

Weight: 1 lb 13 oz (per boot) Sizes: 37-48 (half sizes)

Pros and Cons + Easy to adjust with gloves on + Highly versatile + Ideal fit for small and low-volume feet – Not as durable as they should be for the price

The G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. The insulated foam liner—combined with the wrap-around inner shell and external gaiter—creates an envelope that’s warm enough for high-altitude mountaineering, and yet low-profile and precise enough for hard technical climbing up to WI6 and M7. The rubber rand was sticky enough to provide purchase in foot jams on B.C.’s Stanley Headwall, and the Vibram sole gave testers enough grip to cross boulder fields and icy scruff in Norway, Patagonia, and beyond.

“I loved the BOA system for quick tightening mid-pitch and for equally quick loosening when I arrived at the next belay and needed blood to rush into my feet,” said Climbing Senior Editor Anthony Walsh, who was able to operate the dial easily with gloves on. The system eliminated heel-lift, both on-route and off. “I’ve front-pointed 10,000 feet in these boots and walked many horizontal miles. I haven’t received one blister, and yet I can still climb WI6 and M7 in them,” Walsh said.

Our female testers raved about the fit, calling it a serious game-changer in a world dominated by men’s boots. “Not only does this accommodate lower-volume feet, but the BOA ratchets tight enough to keep my heel down,” said one woman. “That allows me to climb a lot harder, for a lot longer.”

The boot isn’t totally waterproof, but its TPU coating, weather-resistant zipper, and water-repellant finishes kept our feet dry after dozens of days on ice and snow. “Lots of approaches in the Rockies have semi-frozen rivers at the base,” said one tester. “I punched through multiple, and never felt humidity or wetness.”

But while the weather resistance easily survives hard use, some of the plastic parts may not. One tester noted a sticky zipper and a peeling toe cap. Another reported that the toe welt quickly shows signs of wear and had to order a replacement after just a few weeks of testing. The toe welts on her second pair have held up fine. Still, if you’re hoping for a boot that will last you for years, you might want to get some reassurances from La Sportiva’s warranty department first.

Pros and Cons + Top-tier durability + Technical aptitude + Out-of-the-box comfort – Not quite warm enough for extreme-altitude objectives

Scarpa’s fan-favorite Phantom Tech HD offers the same climbing precision as the old Phantom Tech, with more warmth, durability, and comfort at just a 2.5-ounce penalty. Body-mapped insulation—micropile, aerogel, and PrimaLoft Gold Eco—kept our feet frostbite-free at -22°F (with vapor barrier socks) near Field, British Columbia, but we wouldn’t quite trust it on Denali. “The rockered outsole has a trail-runner-like feel,” said one tester. “I’ve hiked and skied many miles in ice climbing boots over the years, and the Phantom Tech HD is without a doubt the most comfortable I’ve used.” After a full season, our pair shows no wear or delamination.

Pros and Cons + Packable + Superlight + Five gear loops – Uncomfortable to hang in – Ice clipper locations reduce usability of gear loops

For multi-pitch ice, where hanging belays are rare, our testers gravitate to a minimalist harness like the updated Blue Ice Choucas Pro. Its UHMWPE construction is surprisingly durable for 5.1 ounces, and it’s fully featured: gear loops, a haul loop, four ice clipper slots, and leg loops that open for skis or crampons.

Unfortunately, Blue Ice sewed the clipper slots over the gear loops, so loop real estate feels a bit scarce. Nevertheless, it easily held a full rack of screws on Murchison Falls (WI4+; 600ft), but our tester noticed the unpadded leg loops on the free-hanging 100-foot rappel.

Skip it for cragging or steep terrain; it thrives on big days in the alpine—where a harness’s weight and packability make a real difference.

Pros and Cons + IP56 water resistance + Low operating limit (-20°F) + Invaluable for anchors and belay-station communication – Expensive

An IP56 water-resistance rating and a -20°F lower operating limit make the Rocky Talkies as well suited to ice as to the mountains they’re named for. We found them invaluable for setting up anchors in Ouray Ice Park and for communicating between multi-pitch belay stations. The only knock is the price, though most testers found the durability worth it.

Pros and Cons + Long-lasting dry treatment + Easy handling – No middle mark

If you’re the kind of person who prefers the safety and flexibility of a half/twin rope setup, you’d be hard-pressed to do better than the DYAD 7.7. Our testers used these ropes on everything from Bridal Veil Falls to ice park laps over a full season in Ouray, Colorado, and not even the wettest pitches iced them up or wetted them out. Cons: There’s no middle mark, and the ropes are pricey.

Pros and Cons + Many accessories for specific customization + High-performance ice pick – Shaft shape and handle is not suited for sustained vertical or overhanging pitches

Gently curved ice tools have fallen out of favor for the flashier, radically shaped Black Diamond Hydra, but the updated Viper still has a home in our quiver. Its 2.5-millimeter pick is incredible in ice, but the tool’s standout feature is its customization: it comes with modular headweights, a long alpine spike for snow plunging, a micro spike, a full-size alpine hammer, a micro hammer, and an adze. One tester, an ACMG apprentice alpine guide, found the mellow shape natural for sniffing out thin hooks on slabby, traddy mixed up to M7, versus an aggressive tool like the C.A.M.P. X-Dream. The knuckle-bashing shape isn’t ideal for overhanging mixed or WI5, but it’s a great option for moderate and big-mountain routes.

Weight: 1 lb 9 oz (per pair, with monopoint setup) Sizes: 34-44; 38-49 with extension bar (sold separately)

+ Extremely light + Solid climbing performance + Surprisingly durable + Wide range of adjustability – Aluminum heel doesn’t penetrate dense ice well

With razor-sharp points and a modular design, the Petzl Dart has been our favorite technical crampon for years. Its new aluminum rear section and linking bar save 4 ounces per pair and eliminate the need to jerry-rig fit with Petzl’s Cord-Tec Kit.

Testers climbed up to WI5+ and M7 with zero flex or shifting. Like the all-steel Dart, it’s simple to switch between mono- and dual-point layouts, and interchangeable toe bails customize the Dart for any boot, welts or not. Testers used these ‘pons on everything from Bridalveil Falls (WI5+) in Telluride and hard mixed cragging to big Canadian Rockies north faces, including Mount Robson and Mount Temple.

The geometry of the front point is just downturned enough to hook securely into ice, but not so aggressive that you have to adjust your technique to get a solid stick. In fact, most testers found they hardly had to double-kick at all to get a quick, reliable bite.

“The secondary points are far enough back that they don’t get in your way when you just want to use your front point, but forward enough to engage when you want them to,” said one tester, who wore them on more than 100 pitches this winter. He also found them blessedly intuitive to walk in: “Even when hiking up and down the Ouray Ice Park trails or navigating a mixture of rocks and ice between backcountry pitches, the Darts kept me secure and balanced.”

Cons: Honestly, not many. One climber found the newly slimmed-down heel lever tough to operate with thick gloves on. Another found the metal buckle fussy—though Petzl’s sold-separately Elastic Strap ($26) fixes that issue with a surprisingly durable plastic buckle.

Pros and Cons + Triple-grip handle + Flexibility and reach in steep terrain – Too aggressive for pure ice – Handle isn’t as ergonomically contoured as other triple-grip models

One climbing coach and U.S. Ice Climbing Team member used the X-Dream Total Dry on hard mixed routes in Ouray and D14 king lines in the Italian Dolomites. The first widely available commercial tool with a triple-grip handle, it gives you tons of flexibility and reach in steep terrain. But it’s too aggressive for pure ice, and the handle isn’t as ergonomically contoured as on other triple-grip models. Thankfully, the X-Dream’s all-around handle is available separately.

Pros and Cons + Modular head weights + Ultra-sharp picks + Adjustable handle size – Geometry isn’t aggressive enough for seriously overhung terrain

An impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. “I certainly appreciated being able to adjust the handle size to accommodate the difference,” said one tester, who swapped between thin dry-tooling gloves and thick, three-finger mitts. The geometry isn’t aggressive enough for overhung mixed, though, like the crux ice-dagger transfer on Dark Nature (WI5+ M5/6).

Pros and Cons + Lightweight + Durable steel + Seamless rotation + Easy to place – Spring-loaded crank knobs are sometimes overeager

We occasionally steer clear of aluminum screws because we find they bind up in plasticky ice. But the featherweight, all-steel Blue Ice Aeros are easily the next best thing. The lightest steel screw on the market, the Aeros are easy to start, easy to clean, and rack neatly on a harness. The three-tooth design seems to bite more reliably than four-toothed models, and we found the Aeros never bound up, even in warm, snowy conditions in Colorado’s Ouray Ice Park.

Ease of racking was another fan-favorite perk. You can fit six screws on a single clipper as opposed to Black Diamond or Petzl’s four to five. Credit goes to the low-profile aluminum hangers, which Blue Ice managed to trim down without sacrificing the size of the crank knob or the length of the hanger.

“The hangers are long enough to provide plenty of torque to easily turn the screw, and they’re simple to manipulate with gloves,” said one Colorado-based tester after a season of backcountry ascents in the San Juans.

The Aeros also offer a larger barrel diameter than any other screw we’ve tried, which means you can thread them into old screw holes in a pinch and still get a tight, reliable placement. The larger diameter also came in handy while setting up rappels.

“V-threading was a breeze with the Aero, providing a wide window of ice to thread the rope and get it back out with my V-thread tool,” reported one tester.

The only thing we didn’t like was the spring-loaded crank knobs. While some testers loved that they snap back into the screw automatically, others found that the snapping sometimes occurred prematurely, pinching their fingers or gloves in the process.

Buy in this order: boots, layers, gloves, then a big belay parka. Crampons, ice tools, and screws are easy to rent or borrow while you’re learning. Boots and apparel aren’t, and they matter most to your comfort on the ice.

Start with boots, because fit is everything.

You can find used boots for $200 to $300, but buy new if that’s what it takes to get a perfect fit. Visit a local climbing shop, tell the sales associate about your objectives and experience level, and let them guide you.

Layer for the conditions, and keep your insulation adjustable.

Carry two to three pairs. Wet hands are cold hands, so the number-one tip for staying comfortable is keeping your mitts dry. You’ll need:

As with boots, buy your gloves new if that’s what it takes to get the fit right.

Yes, eventually. Make it the last piece of your kit. A two-way zipper and interior drop pockets are nice, but warmth matters most. Standing around belaying in the snow can be downright frigid, and the bigger and warmer your belay puffy, the happier you’ll be.

Rent or borrow these until you know what you like:

Yes, but upgrade as you get more into the sport.

Buy safety essentials new. That means ropes, harnesses, and helmets. It’s hard to tell if used gear has been compromised, and trustworthy safety gear is the cheapest insurance policy you’ll ever buy.

For most other items, shopping secondhand can help you figure out what you like before you shell out for a spendy new kit. Try MountainProject.com, GearTrade.com, and eBay, or Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace if you live in an outdoorsy town.

Gear reviews are highly subjective, but we do our best to combat that by taking a slightly more scientific approach to testing ice climbing gear. At the beginning of each season, we wade through sheaves of PR requests, consider the specs and promise of each one, and then carefully select the gear we deem fit to test. Then, we do our utmost to get each piece in the hands of as many testers as we can—and in as varied conditions as the team can manage.

This year, testers picked and kicked their way up everything from steep ice in Colorado’s San Juans to long mixed lines on Mount Robson. Samples traveled from Denali to the Italian Dolomites to the Patagonian Andes and back again. We belayed through blizzards, swung into bullet-hard ice, whooped over perfect sticks, and cursed through some of the wettest pitches of our lives. At the end of the year, we compared notes and selected only the best ice climbing gear to review. Those are the products you’ll see here.

Anthony Walsh is a senior editor at Climbing. Based in the Canadian Rockies, he does it all—from steep ice to long alpine routes to rowdy mixed climbs. All those pitches have helped him hone two unmatched talents: suffering honorably in Arctic conditions, and complaining about poorly constructed gear in the most eloquent way possible.

Corey Buhay is a freelance writer and editor based in Boulder, Colorado. She is a current member of the U.S. Ice Climbing Team and has redpointed up to WI5, M12-, and D14 around the Colorado Rockies and beyond. She is a coach and board member at The Ice Coop, Colorado’s only dedicated ice-climbing gym.

Emilie Grenier is a regular contributor to Climbing who actually prefers climbing ice to rock. As a result, Emilie is hunting for frozen smears come September each year, and you can’t drag her out of crampons until at least May.

If it feels too early to start thinking about holiday shopping, well, I agree. Halloween is just behind us, Thanksgiving is still weeks away, and yet every store has already decked their halls with fairy lights, Christmas trees, and giant faux candy canes. But, setting aside my Scroogey (and maybe slightly Boomer) complaints for a minute, there are some real advantages to getting your holiday shopping early. While not all brands have officially started their Black Friday or winter sales yet—REI’s doesn’t begin until the 13th—eager bargain hunters can find heavy discounts on everything from tents to boots already. These 11 Backpacker-tested and -approved shelters, bags, trail runners, and other assorted goodies are on sale for 25 percent or more off right now.

For beginners and anyone who prefers to linger in camp, a tent’s weight matters less than its durability and livability. The Marmot Limelight has both in spades: With 34.4 square feet of floor space for the 2 (42.5 for the 3), double doors and vestibules, and additional gear storage space in the included wings, the tents have enough room for even tall backpackers to spread out comfortably.

A legit backpacking tent for less than $200 is a steal in this economy. Like the Limelights, the Tungsten is a solid option for anyone who prefers to live a little larger in the backcountry. The freestanding tent features an 8.72-square-foot vestibule and a 38.2-inch peak height, making it comfortable for long nights or waiting out a storm. Bonus: The color-coded clips make setup easy.

Swapping to a trekking pole tent is an easy upgrade for anyone who wants to cut their pack weight. While the REI Co-op Flash Air 2 lost out to models from Durston, Zpacks, and Six Moon in this year’s ultralight tent test, at this price, it’s still a legit option for anyone searching for an upgrade. The 2 lb, 6.5 oz tent pitches with a pair of adjustable trekking poles, while two additional small poles at the feet and crossbar create extra room.

The Copper Spur line is a perennial favorite of our testers; we’ve tested it in almost every kind of conditions, from South American rainstorms to clear desert nights. The HV UL1 Bikepack features 20 square feet of floor space; at 2 lb, 5 oz, it’s light for a freestanding tent, too.

From thin sleeping pads to inconveniently-placed zippers, we side sleepers have a lot stacked against us in the backcountry. The Sidewinder is specifically made for those of us who prefer to curl up, with a center zip that you won’t end up laying on when you toss and turn.

The REI Co-op Magma 30 doesn’t have any gimmicks: It’s just a down-the-middle, well-made sleeping bag suitable for 3 season use. The 850-fill-power down lets it compress handily, with a long taking up just slightly more room than two 2-liter Nalgenes.

The Aspire was our testers’ favorite women’s rain jacket of 2026 (the Foray is the men’s version), so at half off it’s an easy buy. Our testers praised the breathability of the 3-layer Ascentshell construction, while the 40D, 100-percent recycled nylon face fabric shrugged off close encounters with trailside foliage.

We named Black Diamond’s Fineline the best-value rainshell for women in our 2026 test. But value isn’t all this lightweight shell has going for it. The 2.5-layer shell’s light stretch made it comfortable to wear on everything from high-tempo hikes to mountain bike rides, and we appreciated the helmet-compatible hood and hand pockets.

With their wide, splay-friendly toebox and zero-drop design, Altra’s shoes are popular enough on hiking trails that they need no introduction. With its 33mm stack height, the Olympus 6 is an excellent pick for backpackers who want a little more cushion than the popular Lone Peak provides.

I’m personally a big fan of Adidas’ Terrex Free series, which I’ve taken everywhere from the Panamanian jungle to the Appalachian Trail. Testers who tried this speedy shoe out agreed. A Gore-Tex bootie shuts out slop, while the DreamStrike+ EVA midsole kept them feeling bouncy underfoot.

Don’t be fooled by the space-age looks: Our testers reported that these kicks from Merrell were at home on the trail, with a “ridiculously thick” EVA foam midsole that absorbed shock on rough treadpath without ever feeling unstable.

#8182. 7 Foolproof Plants Anyone Can Propagate From Cuttings in November – Grow More of Your Favorite Shrubs for Free

There is no easier way to make new plants for free than by taking hardwood cuttings from deciduous shrubs in late fall. Try it yourself and see!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November doesn't have to mean the end of the gardening season, as late fall is the perfect time to multiply your backyard shrubs for free. Taking hardwood cuttings sounds complicated but it’s as simple as poking sticks into pots of soil and waiting for them to grow. Yes, really! November is the very best time for this propagation method as stems of deciduous shrubs are full of stored energy ready to go into winter so you'll get great results, even if you're a beginner gardener or it's your first time trying.

Many of our favorite garden shrubs can be multiplied by taking cuttings in late fall, from roses to butterfly bush, dogwood to mock orange, so add this enjoyable task to your fall gardening checklist. Whether you’ve got a new garden to fill on a budget or you’re planting up a fresh area, or you want to propagate some plants to sell at a yard sale next year, you'll get free shrubs without spending a dime at the garden center. Or perhaps you’ve been eyeing up a pretty shrub in a friend’s garden and want it growing in your yard, too!

Clone these deciduous shrubs now and they’ll root over winter, ready to be planted in spring. Ready to have a go? Here’s exactly how to take hardwood cuttings, step by step.

Timing is everything when you propagate plants, and late fall is peak time for growing free shrubs from hardwood cuttings. In November, deciduous shrubs will be about to enter dormancy so they’ll have stored up plenty of energy in their stems and the bare outer bark is tough and weather-resistant. To catch the optimum moment, wait until your shrub has just dropped its leaves or, in a mild autumn, lost a good three quarters of its foliage.

Look for stems that grew this year, as these are going to be far keener to throw out fresh roots than older growth. Choose stems from the outer, sunniest side of the shrub, too, as these will have stored more energy. Stems that are about the width of a standard pencil are ideal, and remember these are hardwood cuttings: you need stems that are mature enough to snap rather than softly bend if you tried to fold them in half.

You’re going to need straight-ish stem sections, and cut plenty as not even expert gardeners get a 100% success rate from hardwood cuttings.

Make the base cut just below a bud or leaf node, straight across the stem. Make this cut close to the node – ⅛ inch below is perfect – as there's a high concentration of rooting cells and hormones in the stem here. Make the top cut about ¼ inch above a bud or leaf node, at a 45° angle. This little bit of extra room allows the stem to heal over without damaging the node. Ideally, you want 2-3 nodes in between the top and bottom nodes (so 5 in total). For most shrubs, that means your stem sections will be 6-12 inches long.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

While the top cut is angled to encourage rain to run off rather than pool on the step tip, the base cut is horizontal simply so it’s easy to tell which end of your cutting is which. Use your pruners to trim off any remaining foliage (don’t tear leaves off as this can damage the stem).

Rooting your cuttings in deep containers rather than the ground makes it easy to provide the sharp drainage and shelter needed for stems to root rather than rot. You can either use one pot per cutting or put multiple cuttings into a bigger container.

Use an all-purpose potting soil without any added fertilizer or synthetic moisture retainers such as Organic Mechanics Premium Blend Potting Soil, available from Amazon, and mix in a similar volume of horticultural grit, sand or perlite such as this from Walmart to open up that soil some more.

Water the mix and leave the pots to sit for 15 minutes to drain.

Use a stick or pencil to poke holes into the potting mix, making them deep enough to swallow two-thirds of the stem length. If you're using a larger container to hold multiple cuttings, space the holes about 2 inches apart. Then pop the stems, base cut downwards, into the holes and use your fingers to gently close the soil around them. There’s no need to water.

Some shrubs have a high-enough concentration of natural auxins – the hormones that foster rooting – that they'll root just fine, all by themselves. Twig dogwood, forsythia, butterfly bush and spirea all fall into this category. Some shrubs need a little help, however. Roses are still reliable rooters, but encouraging them with a rooting powder that stimulates their natural hormones brings a higher success rate. Simply dip the base of the stem into a rooting hormone like Garden Safe Take Root, available from Amazon, and tap off any excess before popping it into the hole.

A few, like mock orange and viburnum, need an even bigger nudge, and that’s easy to deliver by slicing off a narrow inch-long strip of bark at the stem's base before dipping it into the rooting powder, and popping it into the hole. This ‘scoring’ cuts through the tough outer bark to expose the green cambium layer beneath, which is where the cells that will become roots are concentrated. Scoring also triggers auxins to be sent straight to the damaged area.

Stand your pots of cuttings in a sheltered spot where they’re shielded from the worst of the winter rain and cold. Position them up against a south-facing wall of your house and they’ll be protected from cold northerly winds and benefit from the heat escaping your home. An unheated greenhouse, conservatory or sunroom is another good option, as is a bright porch. You could also cover your cuttings with lightweight horticultural fleece such as this AgFabric Plant Blanket from The Home Depot to keep them cozy, pushing canes around the pot so the fabric doesn’t sit directly on the stems.

The stems will use very little water so only irrigate occasionally when the top inch or two of the soil is dry, which will only be once a month or so. By spring, you’ll see fresh green leaves on the cuttings that have rooted. If you're growing multiple cuttings in one big pot, move them into their own container at this point.

Shrub dogwoods or twig dogwoods are super-easy to propagate from hardwood cuttings in late fall, and grow fast for quick results. Why not raise enough to create a wildlife-friendly hedge with a flurry of fragrant spring-summer flowers followed by fall berries? Or create a vibrant display of winter stems for you to enjoy? Cornus has a high concentration of natural rooting compounds so you’ll enjoy a near 100% success rate from hardwood cuttings.

This bulletproof shrub is one of the earliest to bloom in spring, bursting into a cheery show of bright yellow flowers in March. Once mature, Forsythia is drought-tolerant, cold-hardy and incredibly low maintenance, and even copes with urban pollution, making it a welcome gift for beginner gardeners or new home owners. Forsythia's easy-going nature also makes this one of the easiest shrubs to propagate from hardwood cuttings.

Buddleia earned its common name for good reason, putting on a bountiful summer buffet for pollinators from July to October. Butterfly bush is an enthusiastic, fast grower so it’s a useful shrub to quickly make a new garden look more mature, or fill an empty yard corner. Do check that the Buddleia you’re taking cuttings from is a newer, non-invasive butterfly bush variety first though. There is no easier shrub to take hardwood cuttings from as this is a plant that’s naturally programmed to grow, grow, grow!

Spirea is a low-maintenance must-have, bringing fabulous flowers and fall foliage colors in a size to suit every garden. This deciduous shrub responds really well to clipping so you can use it to create a stylish low hedge for free by taking November cuttings. Spirea is a foolproof shrub to start with if you're propagating this way for the first time.

You can never have too many roses in a garden and these shrubs are expensive to buy, so propagating from cuttings will fill your yard with scented flowers for free. The ‘backyard rule’ means you can propagate even named, patented Rosa for your own use, but restrictions apply if you’re planning on selling the resulting plants. While your new rose plant will probably try to flower in its first summer, pinch off any flower buds to focus its energy on growing roots and stems.

Philadelphus brings an aromatic blend of jasmine and citrus to your garden from May to June, so adding a few more mock orange shrubs to your yard will boost its perfume as well as flower power. Mock orange shrubs have tough bark so carefully scrape an inch-long strip off both sides of the stem base and dip into rooting powder to stimulate root growth, and don't worry if cuttings take their time to show spring growth.

The viburnum family includes so many garden-worthy deciduous shrubs such as snowball bush (Viburnum opulus) and the Arrowwood viburnum (Viburnum dentatum) that are straightforward to propagate from hardwood cuttings. Viburnum go into deep winter dormancy however, so also need a boost to root. Score by removing an inch-long strip of bark from the base (one side is plenty) and dip into rooting powder to trigger the stem into action.

Clean cuts made with sharp pruner blades significantly increase your chances of success as crushing stems with blunt pruners damages the plant tissue and creates jagged surfaces where fungal spores can settle.

Wipe isopropyl alcohol over pruner blades to disinfect before cutting stems or scoring, to make sure you’re not transferring any fungal spores or bacteria that might cause rotting rather than rooting.

Winter stems can look identical so be sure to label those sticks clearly so you know what your plants are in spring. These hook-ring tags are useful if you’re rooting cuttings of different varieties in one big pot.

You see, you really are growing free plants by sticking stems into soil, so add this to your list of November gardening jobs. You can put a heap of cuttings into the same pot to propagate plenty of plants without spending a fortune on compost, too. Looking after hardwood cuttings takes minimal time over winter, and it’s so satisfying to spot bare stems bursting into leaf in spring. And just wait till you discover how much more you love a favorite plant when you’ve propagated it yourself!

If you want to propagate plants that are growing outside of your garden, do be aware of the legalities of taking plant cuttings from public spaces and get permission from the landowner.

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

#8180. A Skier Broke Both Legs in an Avalanche, Then Survived More Than 36 Hours in a Crevasse

Members of France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue team search a snow-covered slope near Pointe Sommeiller in the French Alps after a skier was swept into a crevasse by an avalanche on November 8, 2026. (Photo: CRS Savoie)

A backcountry skier in France is lucky to be alive after an avalanche left him trapped in a crevasse for more than 36 hours with both legs broken.

The avalanche, which occurred in the French Alps, swept the skier into the crevasse on November 8, according to a Facebook statement from the French national police’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue team. The skier crawled the length of a football field along a passage inside the crevasse, searching for a way out, before rescuers found him alive on November 9.

The 39-year-old, whose name has not been released, was on a solo backcountry ski trip near the French-Italian border. He was headed for the summit of Pointe Sommeiller, a 10,932-foot peak known for its steep, technical terrain, according to the French Alpine Club, when the avalanche hit.

The peak is located on the France-Italy border, 100 miles east of Grenoble.

Details of the rescue were shared in the official Facebook post, and also in a news story published by French newspaper Le Dauphiné Libére.

According to these reports, the skier left the Alpine village of Bramans on November 7 and spent the night at a backcountry mountain hut before setting out the following morning to climb Pointe Sommeiller.

At the base of a steep, snow-filled chute, he strapped his skis to his pack and began booting up the slope in crampons. His weight triggered a slab avalanche that swept him into a crevasse, fracturing his femur and breaking his other lower leg. Stranded without cell service, he ditched his gear and began crawling down a sloping passage inside the crevasse, hunting for an exit to the surface.

He eventually reached a chamber roughly 50 feet beneath the snow, but the slope leading out was too steep to climb with broken legs, Major Yoann Haberey of the CRS Alpes mountain-rescue unit told Le Dauphiné Libéré.

A concerned relative reported the skier missing late on November 8, prompting a search that continued until approximately 2 A.M., after the risk of another avalanche forced rescuers to suspend operations.

Crews returned the following morning, when a helicopter spotted signs of the avalanche. Search teams began probing and digging through the snow, gradually uncovering the man’s skis and backpack.

After more than five hours of excavation, rescuers finally heard his voice coming from roughly 50 feet beneath them.

The man was conscious but suffering from hypothermia when crews reached him. They extracted him using a stretcher and winch system, lowered him roughly 650 vertical feet down the mountain, and evacuated him by helicopter to a hospital in southeastern France.

The operation involved 22 officers from France’s CRS mountain-rescue unit, six military police rescuers, and three helicopters.

“He really is a miracle survivor,” Haberey told Le Dauphiné Libéré. “They were forecasting snowfall overnight, so after that, we weren’t going to go back.”

Following the rescue, the CRS Savoie mountain-rescue team urged people heading into the mountains to adjust their plans to current conditions, prepare their routes and equipment, and know when to turn back.

“The mountain will always be there tomorrow,” the rescuers wrote.

#8178. 4 Speed Records and Free Solos That Went Down in the Last 2 Weeks

Becca Droz (left) and Kate Kelleghan (right) set a new female speed record on the classic 'Naked Edge' in Boulder's Eldorado Canyon on October 26. (Photo: Jon and Jess Glassberg / Courtesy COROS)

Maybe it’s the erratic weather pressures of El Niño, or perhaps there’s just a particularly competitive spirit in the air right now. In the past two weeks, several climbers have broken records, made improbable repeats, and soloed terrain that would make many of us squirm.

Last week, we looked into the culture of free solo speed climbing in Boulder, Colorado, speaking with several athletes about the risks and influences they carry in their high-stakes sport. On the heels of this deep dive, two of the athletes who spoke to us went on to break additional records of their own within the past few days. This includes a new FKT on Half Dome and a fresh women’s speed record on Eldorado’s most famous route.

More broadly, we’ve seen a few historic achievements in the past couple weeks by free soloists and speed athletes alike. Here are four record-breakers we’ve been watching lately, in chronological order.

Just a few weeks ago, Alex Honnold told Adrian Ballinger that he thought someone would likely repeat his free solo of El Capitan before anyone dared to repeat his insanely hard linkup of peaks and scrambles in Red Rock. Back in 2022, he dubbed that linkup the Honnold Ultimate Red Rock Traverse (aka the HURT).

Honnold will have to eat his words, because on October 19, Nevada climbing guide Nik Mirhashemi put down the world’s second HURT, with slight modifications. Friends have been calling his revised route the NURT: Nik’s Ultimate Red Rock Traverse.

For the NURT, the 36-year-old skipped four non-technical summits, including Goodman, Buffalo Wall, Sandstone North, and Limestone North. Instead he traversed from White Rock Peak to ascend the seven-pitch Frigid Air Buttress (5.9+; 800ft). He then continued to the top of Icebox Peak. “Basically, I had to choose between adding Frigid Air or sticking with the OG route, where those nontechnical peaks are,” Mirhashemi said. “I didn’t want to skip Frigid Air as it is quite classic.” He also called the section he swapped in one of the traverse’s “routefinding cruxes.”

Despite the variations, Mirhashemi doesn’t think there’s a significant difference in effort level. He said that though his traverse is slightly shorter, he added more technical terrain, making the difference essentially a wash. “Nice to add a little personal flair to these things I suppose,” Mirhashemi said.

“I wanted to try the HURT for similar reasons to Alex,” Mirhashemi told Climbing. “Super long days of soloing moderate terrain is one of my favorite things to do. I’ve been coming out to Red Rock for many years and just moved here a year ago. I’m always looking for new ways to challenge myself and it just made sense as a goal right in my backyard.”

Last spring, Mirhashemi made his first HURT attempt, then completed several “scoping missions”  to prepare for his fall go. “I was never sure if I could pull it off,” he said. “Stoked it’s not haunting me anymore!”

Kate Kelleghan has been busy breaking her own record again, shaving minutes and seconds off the female fastest known time on The Naked Edge (5.11b), a classic multi-pitch in Colorado’s Eldorado Canyon.

Kelleghan, along with her French partner Laura Pineau, already held the record for the route’s women’s speed record of 37 minutes and eight seconds, which was 32 seconds faster than Kelleghan’s previous go in 2021 with Becca Droz, a Boulder-based climbing guide.

In late October, Kelleghan began working the route again with Droz. And on October 26, the athletes set a new record of 36 minutes, 26 seconds, shaving 42 seconds off the previous record.

“Becca and I were the team that started the women’s record, so taking it back together feels full circle for our friendship and our community,” Kelleghan said. Droz added that being able to track splits, as well as time out the approach, actual climb, and descent with their COROS watches “was a game changer”; both women are COROS athletes.

The men’s record is held by John Ebers and Ben Wilbur at 24 minutes and 14 seconds.

Just a couple months after smashing the speed record on the First Flatiron in Boulder, 32-year-old American climber Michael Reese established a fastest known time on Yosemite’s Half Dome on October 28. In so doing, he broke an 11-year FKT set by the late Dean Potter. Reese climbed the 2,000-foot batholith from the Mist Trailhead to its summit in 1 hour, 12 minutes, and 58 seconds. He followed Potter’s original line up Grizzly Gully, then free soloed Snake Dike (5.7 R; 800ft). He broke Potter’s previous record set on May 3, 2015 by about six minutes.

A few days after his Half Dome lap, our reporter Holly Chen, who also reported on his Flatiron speed record, caught up with Reese.

“In 2021, one of Dean Potter’s good friends told me about this as a potential record to try. He became one of my main climbing partners,” Reese told Chen. Since then, Reese has made 16 attempts and several scouting missions before his record-breaking attempt in late October.

“Records are made to be broken. I’m not gonna be surprised if it’s broken one day,” Reese said.

In the second-hardest free solo by a woman, Aleksandra “Ola” Taistra climbed a seven-pitch, 720-foot route in Sardinia, Italy on October 29. The line in question is Margarites (7a+/5.12a) up the limestone cliffs of Monte Oddeu. Established in 1998 by Andrea Calvo and Lorenzo Nadali, the route has become one of Sardinia’s “most sought-after lines,” according to Taistra. It includes a bouldery 7a+/5.12a crux pitch high off the deck; two 7a/5.11d pitches; and four additional pitches graded 6c+/5.11c, 6b+/5.11a, 6a+/5.10c, and 5c/5.10a, in order of descending difficulty.

“Climbing Margarites for the first time I thought that climbing it without a rope was impossible for me,” Taistra shared with Climbing, “and that’s exactly how the plan was born—first get to know the route, and then properly assess my skills.” Taistra says that when she finished free soloing Margarites, she thought: “Oh, that’s it?”

Taistra already put down one of the hardest female free solos in history in May, when she climbed Alfredo Alfredo (5.11d/7a) ropeless. Now, the only known harder female free solo belongs to French legend Catherine Destivelle, who climbed an unnamed route in Mali without a rope that she said maxed out at 7b or 5.12a/b.

In May, 44-year-old Taistra told Climbing that free soloing gives her “so much peace” and feels less stressful than climbing with a rope. The 44-year-old climber rehearses her routes on toprope until she feels confident in the moves.

#8177. Three Ground Rules for Getting Outside

Getting outside is for everyone. That’s what Sierra is all about, finding top active and outdoor brands at prices that make it accessible to try a bunch of new adventures. That’s the spirit behind Sierra in the Sierras, in which Dylan Efron (Emmy-winning co-producer of Netflix’s Down to Earth with Zac Efron) hits the trail with a friend to try something completely new.

With gear and apparel from Sierra and guidance from Outside editors, in episode one Dylan explores the Sierra Nevada with Danielle Fishel, Boy Meets World icon and Dancing With the Stars co-star. Along with new adventures, they learn some fundamental principles for having fun outside. Ones you can use yourself.

Whether it’s your first hike or just your first hike today, no one likes to be uncomfortable. The right gear helps. If you’re like Danielle, a self-proclaimed “indoor person,” or simply trying a new activity, you’ll want to focus on comfort and versatility above all else. The aim is to A) feel good while enjoying your new hobby and B) have the freedom to explore further as you progress. The gear choices at Sierra make this easy, thanks to a combo of trusted brands, great prices, and an ever evolving inventory of fresh finds in-store and online.

Like most things in life, getting outside is better with friends. In the first episode of Sierra in the Sierras, Dylan recruits Outside’s Climbing Editor, Anthony Walsh, to give Danielle a lesson in bouldering. And that’s just the start. Next up is slacklining and then a highlining adventure.

If you’re nervous about trying a new sport, having a friend or guide to show you the ropes (literally or figuratively) can make a big difference. But the most important thing is trying something new—it can be just as fun to be complete beginners together.

Dylan and Danielle got the chance to explore the stunning terrain in the Sierra Nevada around Lake Tahoe, but you don’t have to wait for your next big trip to take an adventure outside. Wherever you live, there are more natural playgrounds in your area than you think. Use apps like Trailforks and Gaia GPS to plan your next outing, and discover the outdoors in your own backyard.

The world says to go harder, faster, stronger—but Sierra says, “go however you want.” From hiking up mountains to strolling down the block, Sierra loves it all. Whether you’re athletic or more athletish, Sierra has tons of active & outdoor essentials like top-brand gear, footwear, apparel & more for everything you’re into, all at unexpectedly low prices.

#8174. Plant Your Holiday Porch Pots Now – These 7 Beautiful Plants Create a Spectacular Christmas Display

Why settle for decorations that only last a few weeks? Create beautiful seasonal containers that can brighten your entrance well into winter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Holiday porch pots are a cheerful way to decorate your home's entrance for the festive season. These outdoor winter arrangements look beautiful and welcoming when placed near front doors, steps, or entryways to greet guests during the holidays.

As October ends, the holiday season approaches. Families make Thanksgiving plans, starting a season that lasts right through the new year. This is the ideal time to start putting together natural holiday decorations that bring bright colors and greenery to your home's entrance.

If you are ready to jump into a creative gardening project for winter, we’ve got the ideas to get you started. The basic idea is to combine beautiful plants and greenery to make spectacular seasonal containers. But you should plan to have some fun while you are doing it.

The best plants for DIY holiday porch pots combine appealing structure with festive cut boughs. They should be hardy enough to survive cold weather and add winter curb appeal.

Why not start with an evergreen that nobody else on your block is likely to display? This silver Korean fir cultivar is one of a kind: a curious, fascinating dwarf evergreen with twisted, curled silvery needles. The twisted needles of ‘Ice Breaker’ Korean fir (Abies koreana), available at Nature Hills, have frosted undersides, making it look as if it is perpetually snow-covered. These little beauties grow very slowly, getting to 2 feet tall after 10 years. They are hardy down to -20°F.

It’s easy to find evergreen foliage plants without red berries, but harder to find red berries without evergreen foliage. That’s exactly why winterberry holly (Ilex verticillata) in holiday porch pots is totally intriguing. You can order a best-selling Berry Poppins winterberry holly from Plant Addicts.

These native hollies – growing in eastern Canada through the southern United States – are pretty plants all year long, but they become stunningly beautiful at the dreariest time of the year. They lose their leaves in autumn, leaving only the amazing crop of bright berries to light up your winter pots. They are hardy down to USDA zone 3.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Ornamental cabbages and kales (Brassica oleracea) are cold-hardy foliage plants that provide exceptionally vivid white, pink, red, and purple winter colors for holiday pots. They are technically edible but are not grown for eating. Rather, they are cultivated for their bright, rose-like center rosettes.

Ornamental cabbage and kale plants maintain their bright structure and color well into freezing winter months. For a festive container, they can be combined with winter-hardy pansies, berried twigs, chrysanthemums, or ornamental grasses.

Pick up a four-pack of Song Bird Red Ornamental Kale Plants from Burpee.

You may know these stunning plants as hellebores (Helleborus niger), or as Christmas roses. Whatever you call them, they make fantastic additions to holiday porch pots, with their shining white flowers and strong, dark green leaves. The only issue with hellebores is that they usually don’t bloom until January – past the heart of the holiday porch pot season. But some cultivars bloom just in time for the holidays, such as ‘Christmas Carol Early’, 'Jacob', and 'Snowbells', available at Plant Delights Nursery. The Christmas rose is usually hardy to USDA zone 3.

This dense, naturally round shrub is a perfect little ball of soft green needles. Its small size and low-maintenance nature make Little Gem Norway spruce (Picea abies 'Little Gem') a popular addition to your holiday porch pot. You can order a plant from Magic Valley Gardens at Walmart.

Norway spruce grows slowly, adding only about an inch or two in size every year and topping out at about 3 feet tall and wide. Don’t worry about winter weather – ‘Little Gem’ is hardy down to -40°F. The new growth emerges soft and bright lime, but by Christmas it will be a handsome forest green.

The flowers that give Heuchera its common name of coral bells only appear in spring and summer. By the time the holiday season rolls around, you’ll appreciate this plant's incredible foliage. Coral bells offer a wide range of leaf colors beyond green, including apricot, bronze, pewter, burgundy, and deep purple. The foliage often adds even more enchantment with scalloped, wavy, or veined edges. Select ‘Caramel’ or ‘Peachberry Ice’ cultivars, both available at Plant Addicts, for foliage with rich tones and holiday warmth.

Many trailing “spiller” plants work well in holiday plant pots, but few are better than the classic evergreen trailing English ivy (Hedera helix), available in an ivy variety pack from Plant Addicts. This hardy vine softens the edges of holiday planters and offers all-weather resilience. It stays vibrant throughout the season and works well with flowers or small evergreen shrubs to create a festive feel. The cascading leaves create a rich, full look, balancing upright or mounding holiday plants.

If you’re ready to create gorgeous holiday plant pots of your own, a few practical tips will help. Let’s get down to the basics of how to put it all together.

The base of it all is the pots or containers you select. Choose pots in materials that can handle winter temperatures, like metal, wood, or even plastic. Avoid materials that will crack when the temperatures drop. Get pots that are big enough, but not too big. Generally, front door holiday plant pots should be between 12 and 30 inches in diameter and between 12 and 18 inches deep.

You’ll want to use potting soil in the containers. Leftover summer potting soil works just fine, but it’s best to buy fresh, like Miracle-Gro Organic Outdoor Potting Mix, from Amazon.

Next, you’ll want to put in the plants, and I suggest using a classic thriller, filler, spiller design. Start with the thrillers. These are the tall, eye-catching focal plants that make guests admire the pots. You can use one of the taller plants you have selected – like winterberry holly or ‘Ice Breaker’ fir – or you can use cut boughs after trimming the stems.

Get ready to layer in the fillers. This is the place for medium-height evergreens or foliage plants. Coral bells or ornamental cabbage work well in this role. Alternate textures and shades.

Last, add the spillers, plants with draping or trailing foliage. These go around the bottom edge of the container so that they cascade gracefully over the edges of the container.

Creating your plant pots is fun, but you’ll also have to put in a little effort to keep them going strong through the season.

This starts with care immediately after you set out the pots. Give each of them a deep watering, enough to saturate the entire soil. Excess water should run out of the drainage holes in the bottom of the pot. Make sure that’s the case, or your plants will die of root rot. It helps to add pot feet to elevate the containers off freezing patios.

Don’t worry too much about freezing weather. It is normal for the moisture in the patio pots to freeze. Keep checking the soil and add more water if the top inches are dry. Mist the evergreen branches during dry winter days to rehydrate the foliage. As the weather cools, cluster the containers close to the house wall to shield them from winter winds and create a microclimate.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.
