#8172. The 8 Best Beginner Snowboards of 2027

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

What to know: This guide covers the eight best snowboards for beginners, including the Editors’ Choice Salomon Lotus (women’s) and Salomon Pulse (men’s). Testers evaluated the boards based on how well they flex, carve, and hold an edge. Keep reading for our tips on choosing the best snowboard if you’re just starting out or are looking to progress.

Bunny hills might not be steep, but the snowboard learning curve definitely is. You’ve got to pay your dues and eat shit snow a couple times. But after a lesson or two and some good old-fashioned repetition, things will start to click.

One of the biggest mistakes beginners can make is riding the wrong equipment. We constantly see beginners riding boards that are too stiff, too big, or too small. That’s why we pulled together this guide: to help you find the right snowboard for you, so that the path from beginner to intermediate is a little smoother—and a little less painful.

This past spring, we put 44 snowboards to the test. We asked our crew of snowboard testers—including instructors and coaches—to identify boards that were easy to ride and approachable for beginners. Below, you’ll find the result of months of testing and countless laps in the Sierra, Wasatch, and Rockies: our favorite beginner snowboards of 2027.

Sizes: 142-163 cm (Pulse); 135-155 cm (Lotus) Genre: All-mountain

Pros and Cons + Versatile and fun + Beginner-friendly shape + Encourages learning fundamentals – Not ideal in choppy conditions – Overwhelmed by high speeds

If you’re looking for a snowboard that will help you learn solid fundamentals without encouraging bad habits, the Salomon Lotus (women’s) and Pulse (men’s) are hard to beat—and easy to ride. They’re soft-flexing and approachable, proving to be “exceptionally intuitive for any skill level,” according to a Tahoe tester.

Gentle camber underfoot supplies grip in firmer snow, and a touch of pop makes it approachable to learn how to ollie and cruise through the park. The Pulse and Lotus are also directional twins, with a bumped back stance for float in powder and stability at speed, while the nose and tail are the same width for solid switch handling.

In slush and hardpack, one tester appreciated the camber underfoot, which flows into a rockered nose and tail. “You would have to try very hard to catch an edge. This is a confidence-building board,” she reported. The Pulse is similarly predictable, stable, and easy to manipulate.

The Salomon decks showed their weaknesses at high speeds, on bumpy, icy snow, and in technical moguls—terrain and conditions most beginners will want to avoid anyway. For newer riders, though, this board is an ideal first buy.

Sizes: 146-161W cm Genre: All-mountain freestyle

Pros and Cons + Easy to turn + Buttery, playful for stepping into the terrain park + Rides switch well – Soft flex and rocker-dominant profile make it less of a long-term investment

For a solid beginner board that doesn’t break the bank, the Rossignol Ampage Vol. 2 is an easy-riding, rocker-dominant, twin shape that rides regular and switch equally well.

The Ampage is soft—way too soft for riding hard off-piste—but the flex is perfect for learning the ropes, practicing on groomers, and getting a feel for buttering, jibbing, and jumping in small terrain parks. “Both the nose and tail are flexible for buttering,” a Tahoe tester reported, speaking to the Ampage’s inherent playful nature. The rocker is designed to make turns feel smooth and catch-free, while a touch of camber adds moderate grip while carving.

Even at full retail ($400), the Ampage is a decent deal. But last year’s version is currently on sale, making it an incredible steal for boarders on a budget. Because of the core malleability and easy-riding rocker profile, progressing beginners might outgrow this board more quickly than other decks on this list.

Sizes: 150-167W cm Genre: All-mountain/Freeride

Pros and Cons + Floaty freeride shape + Playful freestyle chops – Not as reliable straightlining – Undergunned in chop

The redesigned Jones Frontier 2.0 is softer, more buoyant, and friendlier than ever, making it a solid option for powder-chasing beginners, intermediate riders learning to navigate the deep stuff, or cruisy shredders who appreciate surfy, laidback turns.

The exaggerated, elongated, rockered nose and a touch of taper (8 millimeters) help the Frontier perform well in powder, while three-dimensional contouring facilitates smooth and natural carving. Camber beneath your boots, a medium sidecut, and Jones’ serrated Traction Tech edges help the shape bite into piste on rail. “It lays sweet, soft trenches, and allows for nuanced wiggling underfoot,” applauded a hard-to-please Colorado tester who was surprised by how much he enjoyed the Frontier’s cruise control.

An approachable combo of biaxial fiberglass and a poplar and paulownia core yields a softer, predictable flex pattern. Testers had mixed feedback on the resulting ride. Some found the Frontier 2.0 “effortless and forgiving.” Multiple harder-charging riders called it a “dad cruiser,” with a 30-year-old ripper joking he’d happily buy it—in 20 years. But for beginners and intermediates especially, that flex makes for an intuitive, easy-to-direct deck that facilitates flowy turns and forgiving forays into powder.

Sizes: 151-170W cm (men’s); 139-154 cm (women’s) Genre: All-mountain freestyle

Pros and Cons + Approachable flex + Decent float in powder yet still solid riding switch + More butter than Land O’Lakes 𑂾 Overwhelmed at high speeds in variable conditions 𑂾 Not the most reliable for bigger drops

The Jones Rally Cat combines a capable, all-mountain directional twin shape (a touch of setback, zero taper, full camber, and spooned-out nose and tail) with a softer, forgiving flex pattern. The pliable feel comes from a poplar/paulownia wood core and a dual-direction, dual-layer, stitched fiberglass laminate.

A progressing, all-mountain Tahoe tester judged the flex “loose enough to be playful but stiff enough to hold an edge.” The shape inspired confidence and elevated her riding to a “more fun level,” and she recommended the board for “new riders, park riders, and playful freeriders.”

Despite its setback stance, the Rally Cat’s lack of taper made it equally adept at jibbing through the park and riding switch, according to one Mammoth snowboard coach. She also dug the tight, 6.6-meter sidecut for the 148-centimeter length we tested. Combined with the spoon-shaped nose and tail, she said the Rally Cat facilitates “effortless turn initiation and quick and efficient edge-to-edge transitions.”

However, a harder-charging North Lake Tahoe freerider and snowboard instructor warned that the buttery flex in the tail that makes the Rally Cat a blast on side hits and park laps can be overwhelmed by overhead drops and chop. This won’t be an issue for true beginners, but worth keeping in mind as you progress.

Sizes: 151-164X cm (men’s); 139-151 cm (women’s) Genre: All-mountain

Pros and Cons + Versatile twin + Most upside for progression out of any board in this guide + Durable build – Expensive – Too much for true beginners

Never Summer’s Proto Type 3 is more expensive and stiffer than the other options in this guide, but it’s also more stable and reliable, providing excellent edgehold, carving chops, and a solid backbone for handling sizeable jumps, cliff drops, and higher speeds. It’s too much for true beginners, but it can be a smart investment for late-stage beginners committed to progression and who want a board they can use for years to come.

The all-mountain twin features a classic Never Summer camber concoction, utilizing three camber bumps running from inserts to inserts, with rocker at the nose and tail. Combined with an adaptable sidecut and a medium-flexing, carbon-bolstered poplar-paulownia-birch core, the Proto Type 3 rips on edge. “Edgehold feels very locked in,” said a Tahoe tester. “Incredibly balanced and easy to shift from toe to heel,” commented a Mammoth rider who appreciated the Proto’s ability to tackle smaller to larger turns well.

The carbon reinforcements help the Proto Type 3 pop aggressively off lips like pubescent pimples. “Stable through the air even on the Palisades Gold Coast jump line,” commented a Tahoe freestyler who also praised the camber for keeping him upright on tail-heavy landings and the rubber laminates and UHMW sidewalls for dampening. The Mammoth rider agreed, saying the board smoothed out bumps that typically irritate her bad knees. Her verdict:  “After you’ve mastered making it down a green run, this board would be great for a late beginner to intermediate rider looking to perfect carving and increase confidence.”

Pros and Cons + Wide ride is perfect for riders with bigger boots + Turns confidently and floats well + Solid freestyle flavor – Can be sluggish compared to narrower boards

The Cardiff Lynx is a wide ride that’s a game-changer for boarders with bigger boots who have a penchant for powder. However, it’s more suited to progressing, late-stage beginners and aspiring intermediates than day-one newbies.

The generous width combined with rocker in the nose and tail, as well as a touch of taper, help the Lynx float extremely well in powder. A versatile, blended sidecut enables the Lynx to tackle a variety of turn sizes for true all-mountain capability, while subtle serrations along the edges help grip firm snow like the claws of the Cardiff’s namesake. “Edges lock into turns,” voiced a Tahoe snowboard instructor. “High-speed carving is fun.”

The Lynx is Cardiff’s softest offering, with a pliable cedar and aspen core that can handle rails, boxes, butters, and playful small-to-medium jumps. One Tahoe tester loved taking the board all over the mountain with a freestyle approach, noting that it handled switch riding better than expected for a tapered shape with a setback stance.

That said, the flex is stiffer and ultimately more capable in steeper all-mountain and freeride terrain than many of the other decks in this guide, although the Lynx’s build is not the most shock-absorbing in chunky moguls. Not to mention, that width can make the Lynx sluggish at slower speeds. But no one took issue with the cool graphics— testers loved the black, big cat-emblazoned topsheet.

Fit Tip: To make sure the Lynx will work for your boots, check the technical specs. In particular, look at the underfoot width at the front and rear foot. Compare that to the length of your boot sole, remembering that your boots may be turned slightly at an angle, depending on your stance preferences.

Sizes: 148-161W cm Genre: All-mountain freestyle

Pros and Cons + Approachable all-mountain cruiser + Excels hitting rails and boxes + Fun, buttery, and easy to maneuver – A bit soft for high-speed all-mountain ripping and freeriding

If you’ve already fallen in love with sliding boxes and rails, CAPiTA’s Outerspace Living might be a perfect fit. This directional twin rides switch well, with a sliver of setback for all-mountain riding en route to the park, so it can easily be your daily driver. It features gentle camber underfoot for pop and hardpack proficiency. Rocker in the nose and tail reduce common catch points while carving and facilitate easy jibbing and buttering. “It’s forgiving and light,” commented a Tahoe park regular. “You won’t catch an edge easily.”

The board’s minimal weight comes courtesy of a slender, malleable poplar and beech core. Despite carbon strips running parallel down the length of the deck, it rides on the softer side. Our testers loved that flex while hitting rails, spinning lazily off rollers, and sniffing out side hits, but our most advanced riders overpowered the Outerspace Living at high speeds in steeper terrain. It’s a great tool for playful all-mountain riders looking to develop their jib skills, or progressing riders looking for a stepping stone to more advanced boards.

Sizes: 135-162W cm Genre: All-mountain, park, powder

Pros and Cons + Great pop and landing gear for jumps + Decent jibber + Rides switch well – Too much for true beginners – Not our favorite in powder

When one of our crew test-drives a deck and instantly buys one for themselves, it’s a damn good sign. And that’s precisely what happened when one of our Mammoth testers put the Burton Good Company to use in her local terrain park. A true twin with camber underfoot and a slightly stiffer-than-advertised medium flex, this is a board that loves to snap ollies, power off lips, and stomp landings with authority.

“Handled medium-sized jumps like a dream,” reported that Mammoth rider, noting she felt confident and comfortable in the jump line. “Riding switch was a breeze,” voiced another Mammoth tester, who appreciated the Good Company’s grip on edge, which translated to boosting prowess in the mini pipe, too. She was also pleased by the board’s ability to spin on and off rails.

Because the Good Company felt a little stiffer than advertised, testers said it’s better for more advanced beginners or intermediates interested in park jumps. It’s also more capable than anticipated in all-mountain terrain, preferring medium and large radius turns to quicker, tighter ones. It doesn’t have a penchant for buttering, and it’s not our top pick for powder. But for progressing all-mountain riders, the Good Company delivers at a very fair price.

Shopping for a snowboard can be overwhelming, especially as a beginner. We’re not going to dive too deep on snowboard tech here (you can check out our additional snowboard coverage here for that), but we want to quickly help you understand a few key concepts discussed in this guide.

“Beginner” is a broad and admittedly unhelpful phrase. If you’re a true first-timer or close to it, you should focus on the first four snowboards in this guide. The best beginner snowboards are on the softer side, making them more approachable and easier to learn the basics on. They’re also generally a little cheaper than the next four boards we’ve included in this guide, which are boards we recommend for more experienced beginners, those approaching intermediate status, or riders who are hellbent on progression or excited to explore a certain style of riding.

Snowboards come in all shapes and sizes, but they can be considered true twins, directional boards, or directional twins.

True Twins, like the Rossignol Ampage, have a symmetrical nose and tail, which look the same and have the same flex. This ensures that the board feels the same whether you’re riding regular or switch. Twins are popular with park riders, as riding switch is a keystone of freestyle snowboarding. True twins are also a sweet choice for beginners, as they make learning “falling leaf” down steeper slopes a piece of cake.

Directional snowboards, like the Jones Frontier 2.0, have a purpose-built nose and tail. They’re designed to be ridden primarily in one direction, with the nose pointing downhill. They often have bigger, floatier noses and shorter, stubbier tails, a combination that can supply stability at speed, buoyancy in deep snow, and landing prowess. Directional snowboards often have taper, which means the nose is wider than the tail, and a setback stance that is bumped toward the back of the board. Both setback and taper can contribute to float and stability.

The main downside of directional boards is that they don’t ride switch nearly as well, which explains why many freeriders and all-mountain riders prefer directional boards, but freestylers stick to twins.

Directional twins combine certain elements from twin boards and others from directional boards to create hybrids that perform across a variety of conditions. For instance, the Jones Rally Cat is a directional twin in the sense that it features a nose and tail that are exactly the same width, enabling it to ride switch well, like a twin. But the nose is longer than the tail, helping the Rally Cat to float in powder and tackle steeper terrain like a directional board.

When you lay a snowboard flat on the ground and look at it from the side, you’re getting a feel for its profile. Profile dictates much of a snowboard’s riding qualities, as it influences how you weight, flex, and engage the board’s sidecut on snow.

Cambered snowboards, like the Burton Good Company Camber, look like an upside-down “U” when you lay them flat on the ground. There’s a raised central section between your feet, and two points of contact with the ground toward the nose and tail. Camber provides grip when you’re carving on firm snow, reliability and edgehold in technical terrain, and power when you’re snapping ollies. For some beginners, camber can be a touch trickier to learn on, and  can feel catchier than rocker. However, camber also helps snowboarders learn fundamentals the right way. You can’t cheat on a camber snowboard, whereas a rocker board is more forgiving and can subsequently let snowboarders develop sloppy habits. For that reason, we mostly recommend camber-dominant shapes in this guide, like our top pick, the Salomon Pulse and Lotus.

Rocker is the opposite of camber. The “U” is right side up this time, as rockered boards have one central point of contact with the ground between the feet, and the nose and tail are raised off the ground. Rocker-dominant boards, like the Rossignol Ampage Vol. 2, are less catchy than their camber counterparts, and they’re generally more playful, easier to butter, and more buoyant. However, they’re also less stable and don’t ollie as well.

Just like directional twins combine aspects from twins and directional shapes in search of a balanced ride, hybrid profiles merge attributes of camber and rocker. For instance, the CAPiTA Outerspace Living pairs grippy camber underfoot with catch-free, floaty rocker in the nose and tail.

Now that you’ve narrowed in on the board you want, you face an equally important question: What size should you get? Sizing a snowboard correctly can make or break your season, but the truth is that there’s no perfect formula. Here are a few things to consider to make the best possible choice for you.

Even as a beginner, you can learn about your preferences from snowboards you’ve already ridden. For instance, if you rented a 155 and it felt too squirrely and unstable, you might want to size up a touch. If you demoed a 160 and it felt too beefy and you weren’t able to turn it, sizing down is a smart idea. Especially as you’re progressing from a true beginner towards intermediate status, it’s important to demo lots of snowboards, as it’ll help you develop your personal taste and your snowboard vocabulary.

Always pay close attention to specs provided by manufacturers, as many brands provide helpful sizing parameters, including ranges for rider weight, boot size, and height. Use this information as a potential starting point.

Between two sizes? If you’re a beginner or riding park, gravitate toward the smaller size, which are easier to turn and spin. If you’re getting more advanced or you’re riding powder frequently, consider the bigger size, which provides more float and stability.

Some brands won’t give you a range of rider heights, but they will give you a range of rider weights, as weight influences how a rider engages flex and how much a board will float. For example, there are skinny 6’3” riders who like 158s, and squat, powerful 5’8” riders who dig 160s.

If you have average-sized feet for your height and weight, you don’t need to worry too much about boot compatibility. But if you have big feet—say, you’re 5’9” and 150 pounds, but you have a size 11.5 boot—it’s important to consider wider snowboards like the Cardiff Lynx. Wide boards help riders with big feet avoid dragging their toes in the snow, which is at best annoying and at worst can cause avoidable crashes. When you scan those manufacturer-provided specs, pay attention to the width and, if possible, ideal boot size ranges. It’s also worth noting that certain snowboards, like the Never Summer Proto Type 3, are available in standard sizes, as well as wide sizes, which Never Summer denotes with an “X.”

This past spring, we sent 44 snowboards out to testers across the Wasatch, Rockies, and Sierra. Those testers aren’t beginners—far from it. These are advanced to expert riders who live and breathe snowboarding, with a few progressing intermediates to mix things up. This crew is intimately familiar with snowboard design concepts, and many of them have been testing snowboards for a decade. A handful of testers are currently instructors or coaches, or they’ve held those jobs in the past. Needless to say, they know what beginners need under their boots to learn the ropes.

After testing snowboards at their home mountains all spring, those testers filled out detailed snowboard review forms. They scored boards quantitatively on aspects like flex, responsiveness, pop, playfulness, stability at speed, etcetera. Then they dove deep on additional qualitative questions, among them: Would you spend your hard-earned money on this board? What conditions or terrain does this board excel or struggle in?

And then, most importantly, we ask these testers to rewind the clock and think like a beginner. Will the board in question encourage a beginner to progress and step up their game? Is it easy to ride? Or is it a hard-to-command bronco that’ll buck a less experienced snowboarder?

Finally, we sifted through those reviews, compared our favorite snowboards of 2027 to old favorites from last year, and compiled the guide you just finished reading. Our hope is that this labor of love helps you enjoy your time on the slopes. Happy hunting—and happier shredding!

Drew Zieff is a Tahoe-based freelance writer and a lifelong snowboarder. He directs Outside’s snowboard test, a role he’s handled since 2016. He also directs Backcountry Magazine’s splitboard coverage and nerds out on snowboard gear and travel for Whitelines Snowboarding, The Snowboarder’s Journal, REI, Gear Junkie, among others. He spends his winters testing gear in his backyard backcountry zones or up at Palisades when he’s not chasing stories and storms around the globe.

In a word, Kordell Black is a character. An esoteric ripper and veteran gear tester based in the Wasatch, Black has traveled the world with his snowboard in pursuit of powder and off-the-beaten-track adventures. He approaches big mountain lines with creative, freestyle energy, specializes in finding powder stashes overlooked by the Utah crowds, and thrashes boots into oblivion in a matter of weeks. He will also obliterate you in a flat ground game of SKATE.

Truckee’s own Jenna Shlachter is as brilliant on the hill as she is off it—which is saying something since she’s a Doctor of Psychology, after all. When she’s not on the clock, she’s usually on her snowboard, ripping everything from park to powder. Her trophy shelf needs regular reinforcement, as every year she seems to add banked slalom awards to her already impressive collection. Lucky for us, Shlachter is also an unabashed snowboard nerd, and she’s been a key contributor to our snowboard test for the last few seasons.

#8171. New Climbing Gym in Massachusetts Plans to Give Away All Its Profits

Berkshire Boulders General Manager Austen McNulty (left) and founder Nick Friedman (right) inside the gym. (Photo: Courtesy Nick Friedman)

The United States has become known for corporate climbing gyms and nationwide chains fraught with labor issues that charge high dollar. A recent analysis by an adventure travel company, which leverages 2026 data as well as the Climbing Business Journal’s 2025 trends report, declared that “the United States is the industry’s laboratory” when it comes to mega-gyms backed by private equity. As climbing becomes more popular, and thus more profitable, one may question whether these gyms will inevitably become the norm.

But in Great Barrington, a small town of a little more than 7,000 residents in Western Massachusetts, entrepreneur Nick Friedman is moving in the opposite direction: starting a new, independent gym that gives away all its profits.

You can trace the 38-year-old’s vision for an altruistic gym back to his childhood, when his dad put his career on hold to demand that General Electric clean up the river that ran through town—and Friedman’s property. In the 1970s, General Electric dumped polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) into the Housatonic River, so Friedman’s dad fought to hold the company liable. GE settled, paying $250 million.

In the process, Friedman learned the importance of activism. The cause close to Friedman’s heart is climbing access, which is not exactly easy to come by in Great Barrington or the Berkshires—but not for a lack of rock. While he calls the climbing in Great Barrington world-class, he says that privately owned land and conservation organizations that don’t understand the value of climbing make access a problem.

“Great Barrington is this unique case study in incredible climbing that is barred from true public domain due to land access challenges,” said Friedman, who has been deeply involved in local access work. In 2023, Friedman, who also serves on the board of the Western Massachusetts Climbers’ Coalition (WMCC), purchased a 70-acre parcel in the Farley Ledges climbing area. This bought WMCC time to organize the permits and funding to purchase it from Friedman earlier this year. While Farley Ledges currently remains closed due to an access issue involving a private landowner, WMCC is raising funds to construct a new parking lot and trail to reopen climbing.

Making these land purchases and forging the agreements necessary to maintain and expand access in Western Massachusetts takes a lot of resources, Friedman explains. That’s where his new gym, Berkshire Boulders, which opens on November 6, comes in. He plans to donate 100% of his profits to community organizations, including WMCC and Access Fund.

“The WMCC is very excited about the opening of Berkshire Boulders and the potential it has to positively impact climbing access in Western Massachusetts,” said Regina Madden, a WMCC board member and chair of its communications committee. Protecting and maintaining access requires ongoing resources, so a local business committed to supporting that mission creates an excellent opportunity. In addition, Berkshire Boulders can serve to bridge the gap between indoor and outdoor climbing, helping to foster a stronger sense of stewardship and community.

While Friedman may pursue nonprofit status down the line, he says it was faster to get the gym off the ground as a business that gave away its profits, rather than a 501(c)3 nonprofit. And as someone who has specialized professionally in startups, he adds that he’s always been “intrigued” by hybrid models that blend for-profit business models with nonprofit values.

Currently, the organizations Berkshire Boulders plans to support include WMCC and Access Fund, as well as non-climbing local organizations including the Railroad Street Youth Project and Greenagers, which fosters sustainability work among youth.

“I felt that a climbing gym could play a central role in that effort and become this anchor and the starting point for a broader vision of bringing outdoor recreation more front and center in this small town,” Friedman said.

Friedman doesn’t see accessibility as a binary, “indoors or outdoors” issue; he views it holistically. This is why he’s made it the gym’s mission to improve climbing access indoors and out. He envisions a gym as a place where you can learn the sport, meet partners, and find people to help you make the gym-to-crag transition. In Friedman’s view, that gym-to-crag transition is the end game. That’s why he decorated Berkshire Boulders’ walls with photographs of Great Barrington rock, and rents out crashpads to climbers who want to try bouldering outside, but lack the gear.

But the other end game is community, which he says is hard to foster when you’re answering to private equity investors. Berkshire Boulders’ KPIs will instead revolve “around community impact.”

One way he’s doing that is by offering hardship memberships. Each month, Berkshire Boulders will award free memberships to low-income individuals through a lottery system. This addresses the known problem of affordability in the gym industry—one so notable that the American Alpine Club declared it an access issue in 2024. Friedman says he’s already approved one hardship membership application, but doesn’t have a monthly quota in mind yet. “We do expect to expand that program significantly over the next several months,” Friedman said.

A focus on community KPIs, however, will not come at the expense of a high-quality bouldering facility. Friedman insists that he is committed to a top-tier facility. He is partnering with local hold-maker Decoy and plans to change the setting across the 15-foot-high walls every two weeks. The gym also features a custom-built, “artistically created” adjustable spray wall. Using the Clift app, climbers will be able to set sequences, replicate local outdoor problems, and track leaderboards.

Currently, for Friedman, Berkshire Boulders is a passion project. His personal endgame is not to make a living off the gym—he still works full-time as the chief strategy officer at a small-batch cannabis startup. He also hired an experienced general manager to run the gym. Rather, that Friedman hopes to ultimately do is drive positive change in his local climbing community.

“Personally, I would love to see the Great Barrington climbing become a published resource for the public,” Friedman said. It’s a long game, but a worthy one, in his view, to turn the local climbing from an underground, tricky access dance to a veritable destination with routes documented on Mountain Project, a guidebook, and formal parking and approach trails.

Beyond local impact, could Berkshire Boulders, if successful, inspire a rising tide of small, mission-driven gyms in this era of indoor climbing corporatization? Friedman believes smaller gyms with a focus on community have a better shot at bringing together passionate climbers than the larger conglomerate gyms. “I would love to see an expansion of smaller independent gyms regionally,” he says.

#8169. These Will Be the Snowiest Adventure Towns This Winter, According to a Meteorologist

Colorado’s San Juan Mountains are heavily favored for atmospheric rivers to create stellar snow totals. (Photo: Getty)

Every year, America’s snowiest towns are typically located in the mountains or on the banks of the Great Lakes. With a few ski resorts already open, if you’re a powder chaser you are likely chomping at the bit for ski season to get into full swing—especially with projections of Super El Niño turbocharging snowfall.

I’m a television meteorologist with over 30 years of forecasting experience, as well as an avid skier and snowshoer. Growing up in Greenville, South Carolina, I prayed for snow days. Now, as an adventurer, I chase the powder.

A prime sign of Super El Niño’s influence is what just happened in Chile. In late August, a resort called Ski Portillo got multiple snow dumps tallying over 30 inches in a few days. Its record-breaking season hit almost 500 inches, double the  typical average.

As Super El Niño continues to strengthen, the NOAA Climate Prediction Center is still forecasting a greater-than-83-percent  chance of a strong-to-very strong El Niño, likely from January through March. But not everywhere is going to get a stellar snow season.

With the strengthened subtropical jet stream, Super El Niño means an active southern storm track and wetter-than-normal conditions for the southern tier of the United States. That favors the Southwest, the Southern Rockies, and California’s Sierra Nevada.

The kicker to the season—one that’s not getting a lot of buzz—is the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), a fluctuation of ocean temperature in the Pacific, entering a cooling phase. That was a big factor in Juneau, Alaska, getting its record-setting snowfall of 201.2 inches during the 2006-7 winter. A strong El Niño and a cool PDO are a highly unusual pairing we haven’t seen since 1972-73, a winter with a significant snowstorm that buried parts of the Southeastern U.S.

Then there is the recent weird behavior of the polar vortex, a rotating mass of cold air and low pressure. Its unusual weakening would normally send a significant Arctic blast into the United States, but there’s not enough cold air across Canada yet for this to happen.

Simply put, it looks like we’re in for supersized and wild weather this winter.

These are my picks for the adventure towns most likely to receive the snowiest winter, including a couple of spots that don’t normally top the “most snow” list.

Based on historical records during very strong or Super El Niños, and its maritime air pipeline at full throttle, Mammoth Mountain Ski Area is pretty much a lock for a big snow year. While the 2015-2016 very strong El Niño recorded a near-average season of 393 inches, the 1982-1983 Super El Niño produced a whopping 546.3 inches. In 1983, January picked up 118 inches of snow and March had 112 inches, extending Mammoth’s ski season through late July.

Off-Slopes Snow Fun: Take a thrilling ride on the mountain coaster or go snow tubing at Woolly’s Adventure Summit. You can zipline year-round too, or zoom through scenic terrain with Snowmobile Adventures. For a surreal, scenic stop, head to Mono Lake, just 30 minutes away, to see its pogonip ice fog. Because of the lake’s high salinity, it doesn’t freeze. The low-lying ice fog against the limestone tufa towers is otherworldly. Plus, it’s a prime place for wintering waterfowl, such as bald eagles.

Basecamp: The Village Lodge Mammoth puts you in the heart of The Village, whereas the historic Mammoth Mountain Inn is best for ski-in/ski-out access.

Where to après: For a next-level après, book the VIP Après Experience at Lincoln Bar at Canyon Lodge. For late-night shenanigans, join the “Night Shift” party at Outbound’s Bar Sierra. The best place to chill on a slopeside sundeck is Yodler Restaurant & Bar. For local sips, stop by Shelter Distilling, Mammoth Brewing Company, or Distant Brewing.

Yes, there’s skiing in Arizona, and it’s not far from the Grand Canyon. For a high-desert ski experience, the historic settlement of Fort Valley makes the perfect playground for the Arizona Snowbowl. This tiny unincorporated community is just northwest of Flagstaff, which averages more snow annually than Denver or Salt Lake City.

With a front-row seat to atmospheric river impulses riding the subtropical jet, Fort Valley and Arizona Snowbowl should have well-above-normal snow totals, with the heaviest snow likely in February.

Located in the San Francisco Peaks, Snowbowl historically gets spikes in snowfall during strong El Niño years. During the 2023-24 El Niño, Arizona Snowbowl recorded 281 inches of snow. Its six inches of snow October 24-25, 2026, is a good sign for Arizona’s only ski resort, and for Fort Valley. It is also interesting to note that during the 1972-73 winter of strong El Niño and cool PDO, nearby Flagstaff got a record-setting 210 inches of snow.

Off-Slopes Snow Fun: After a morning on the slopes, make a stop at the Museum of Northern Arizona. Don’t miss the “Native Peoples of the Colorado Plateau” and “Southwestern Jewelry” exhibits. Go cross-country skiing or snowshoeing at Arizona Nordic Village or the Peak View Winter Recreation and Parking Area in the Coconino National Forest. Just 20 minutes away, Flagstaff Snow Park is perfect for snow tubing and sledding fun.

Take a day trip to Grand Canyon National Park. The South Rim is just over an hour away. The bonus of a winter visit is the lack of crowds. You can easily visit three national monuments in a day: see Ancestral Puebloan dwellings in Walnut Canyon and Wupatki, and experience a moon-like landscape at Sunset Crater Volcano, where every astronaut who has set foot on the moon has trained. Bundle up for stargazing at nearby Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff for a truly out-of-this-world evening.

Basecamp:  Book a mountain cabin for a cozy stay. Basecamp at Snowbowl is a good budget-friendly and pet-friendly option. Plus, you get two complimentary lift tickets per night.

Where to après: Basecamp Restaurant is the go-to spot, as it’s less than 5 minutes from Fort Valley and on-site at Basecamp at Snowbowl, located 7 miles from the ski area. You’re also close enough to Flagstaff to devour delicious eats at favorites like Diablo Burger, The Toasted Owl Cafe, or MartAnne’s Burrito Palace.

Sitting at 9,800 feet in Dixie National Forest, Brian Head is the highest incorporated town in Utah. The rustic mountain town is named for nearby Brian Head Peak. Dubbed the “highest resort town in America,” it’s home to the small ski area of Brian Head Resort, which has the highest base elevation in Utah.

Brian Head is in a sweet spot for Super El Niño’s elevated snow amounts. Plus, its high elevation helps sustain snow quality. Multiple rounds of significant snow in October were the prelude to what should be above-average snowfall and cooler temperatures this winter.

Off-Slopes Snow Fun: Soak in the scenery of red rock hoodoos dusted with snow at nearby Cedar Breaks National Monument, where you can go cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. Explore the backcountry on a snowmobile tour with Thunder Mountain Motorsports.

Zoom down the hill while snow tubing at Giant Steps Snow Tubing Park. Bundle up to admire the night sky while enjoying some high-altitude stargazing. Brian Head also makes a great high-elevation base camp for day trips to Bryce Canyon National Park and Zion National Park.

Basecamp: Book two nights at Brian Head Lodge and get two free lift tickets with promo code FreedomToSki. There are also numerous cabins and condominiums for rent.

Where to après: Last Chair Grill and Brews on the third floor of Giant Steps Lodge is the premier slopeside spot. They boast the largest beer selection in southern Utah and have live music on Fridays and Saturdays. For more low-key options in town, head to 1st Chair Thai and Ramen or Pizanos Pizza.

Colorado’s San Juan Mountains are heavily favored for atmospheric rivers to create stellar snow totals. If you want to experience the Alps without leaving the U.S., the San Juans deliver, with their jagged peaks resembling their European counterparts.

Telluride is my number-one pick for where I want to go this winter. I love the Victorian architecture in the historic mining town paired with the ski resort experience in Mountain Village, connected by the free Telluride Gondola.

Off-Slopes Snow Fun: Whether you go to Bridal Veil Falls—Colorado’s tallest free-falling waterfall—or hike along locals’ favorite, the Jud Wiebe Trail, winter hiking and snowshoeing around Telluride are breathtakingly beautiful. Experience some of the best ice climbing in the world on a guided climb with San Juan Outdoor Adventures. For the ultimate backcountry experience, try heli-skiing or riding with Telluride Helitrax. Go with Telluride Outfitters on a snowmobile tour to Alta Ghost Town—a  unique way to experience Telluride’s mining history.

Basecamp: I prefer staying in town with the European chalet vibes of The Hotel Telluride being my personal favorite. If your preference is closer to the slopes, the Madeline Hotel and Residences in Mountain Village is excellent.

Where to après: Bellying up to the Historic Bar at the New Sheridan Hotel is an absolute must in Telluride. Dating back to 1895, it’s considered one of the most famous bars in the West. Grab pizza at Brown Dog and Pad Thai at Siam. The Butcher and The Baker is always good. On the mountain, sitting outside at Bon Vivant is delightful on a sunny day, and Alpino Vino is the highest fine-dining restaurant in North America. For the best sunset, take the gondola to Allred’s Restaurant.

Torrential downpours across the Four Corners caused devastating flooding across Southwestern Colorado. The heavy rains are likely an indicator of deep snowfall to come later in the fall.

Historically Wolf Creek gets the most snow in Colorado, with multi-day storms that drop feet of snow, such as the February 17 to 21, 2026, storm cycles that dumped almost five feet of snow (59 inches). During the El Niño winter of 1978-79, Wolf Creek got 807 inches of snow, which is Colorado’s record for a single-season total at a ski area or resort.

There are three reasons Wolf Creek gets so much snow. First is its high elevation. The base sits at 10,300 feet. Second is the funneling effect of its local topography. Located just south of the summit of Wolf Creek Pass, it sits in a unique L-shaped bowl that acts like a catchall basin for snow. Third are the storm tracks pushing up against the San Juans, which should bode well for a high snow total this season.

Off-Slopes Snow Fun: As one of the premier destinations on Colorado’s 800-mile Historic Hot Springs Loop, Pagosa Springs on the west side of Wolf Creek Pass is perfect for a ski-and-soak getaway. Hike to frozen Treasure Falls. The 105-foot plunge waterfall between Wolf Creek Ski Area and Pagosa Springs freezes into massive ice columns, attracting technical ice climbers.

Take the scenic drive, then hike the Piedra Ice Fissures Trail to see ice caves. Satisfy your need for speed by snowmobiling in the San Juan National Forest and to the Continental Divide on a guided tour with Wolf Creek Snowmobile Tours. You can also take a day trip to see the cliff dwellings in Mesa Verde National Park.

Basecamp: There is no lodging at the ski area, so plan to stay in Pagosa Springs. My favorite is The Springs Resort and Spa [Editor’s note: At the time of publishing, some of the pools at the resort are not open due to flooding. Please call ahead for the most up-to-date information.] It’s home to the Mother Spring, the deepest geothermal hot spring in the world, certified at a depth of at least 1,002 feet by Guinness World Records. If you stay there, you get 24-hour access to the soaking pools. The Clouds in My Coffee pool is my favorite for an early morning soak with coffee in hand.

If you don’t want to drive and park in one of the free on-mountain lots, Wilderness Journeys Pagosa runs a daily shuttle, but you need to make a reservation in advance.

Where to après: Sip an IPA at Riff Raff Brewing Company. Savor a craft cocktail at The Neon Mallard. Order the fish tacos at Kip’s Grill. You’ll thank me later. Relax with a latte or tea at the Root House. The founders of this cool coffeehouse and shop are the stars in HGTV’s Building Roots. The cinnamon rolls are sinfully good. Finally, grab a sandwich or quiche at Pagosa Baking Company.

Famous for its historic adobe architecture and vibrant art scene, Taos doesn’t normally rank high on the list of America’s snowiest adventure towns. But this year it could, since it’s in the favorable storm track of the active subtropical jet stream.

Less than 20 miles north of town, Taos Ski Valley has over 300 inches of snow annually. In town, snow typically peaks in December and January but continues to fall well into March at the ski resort. Angel Fire Resort is also about 45 minutes away.

Off-Slopes Snow Fun: Taos Pueblo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site that’s been inhabited for over 1,000 years. With the chill in the air and fireplaces glowing, I love visiting the pueblo in December. Grab a latte in Dawn Butterfly then stroll through the artisan shops, such as Pueblo Runner. Make sure to sample the fry bread while visiting. Taos Pueblo does close annually for six to eight weeks in late winter and early spring for traditional ceremonies.

Beyond the nearby slopes, you can also go snowshoeing, cross-country skiing, or winter hiking in the Carson National Forest. Soak in the therapeutic waters at Ojo Caliente, about an hour away from Taos. There are several museums and historic homes to tour in town, or you can simply stroll around Taos Plaza. The historic district is filled with art galleries and unique boutiques. Chocolate + Cashmere is my favorite spot to find something cozy, and the Sage Fine Art Gallery is filled with works by award-winning local artists.

Basecamp: If you want to stay where you ski or ride, The Blake is a ski-in/ski-out property at Taos Ski Valley. Just outside of the town’s busy historic district, Hotel Willa is a delightful option for an upscale boutique stay with character in a remodeled 1960s adobe motor lodge. For something completely off-grid, book a stay at Earthship Biotecture.

Where to après: The Bavarian is a fun option at the base of Taos Ski Valley. It’s famous for its German eats and draft beer. In town, the Adobe Bar is a classic après haunt next to historic Doc Martin’s Restaurant. My favorite place in town to chow down is Orlando’s New Mexican Café. Go hungry, and order the blue corn enchiladas. New Mexican enchiladas are layered, rather than rolled.

Located on the cusp of the transition zone between wet and dry, historical data shows mixed results for the northern Sierra. Strong El Niños trend toward below-normal seasons, while very strong El Niños historically produce above-normal snow averages. It’s a roll of the dice for Tahoe.

Strong El Niños typically mean warmer-than-average winter temperatures for Washington State, but Super El Niños add ample moisture-laden Pacific air that could mean localized wet storms. Glacier is the closest town to Mount Baker Ski Area, which holds the world record for the most snowfall in a single season of 1,140 inches in the 1998 to 1999 season. That was during a strong La Niña season, but I’m never ruling out Mount Baker for big snow totals. In past Super El Niño winters, Mount Baker Ski Area still recorded an average of 642 inches of snow.

Thanks to intense lake-effect snow off Lake Ontario, Redfield often tops the list of the snowiest places in the Great Lakes with 380-plus inches of snow annually. This winter looks milder and drier for the Great Lakes. But record-warm lake temperatures on the Great Lakes mean heavy lake-effect snow could pile up quickly when cold Arctic air arrives. Intense, localized lake-effect snow squalls look more likely this winter across the Great Lakes.

Stowe, Vermont With the NOAA Winter Outlook showing warmer-than-normal and wetter conditions, there’s the potential for heavy, wet snow events. Another key factor is that powerful coastal nor’easters occasionally develop during historical super El Niños. Typical timing for those is late January through February.

Boone, North Carolina While not normally one of America’s snowiest towns, the powerful subtropical jet stream pulling moisture from the Gulf of Mexico significantly increases precipitation across the Southeast. If a cold-air damming wedge sets up with ample moisture, that means a major winter storm in the Blue Ridge Mountains. The February 1973 “Great Southeastern Snowstorm” is proof that the Deep South sometimes measures snow in feet instead of only an inch or two.

#8168. How Useful Is An Alpine Climbing Award, Really?

The Ultar Sar team, of Sebastian Pelletti, Ethan Berman, and Maarten Van Haeren, accept their Piolet d'Or in Saint-Christophe-En-Oisans, France, in October 2026. (Photo: Piotr Drożdż)

When I learned I’d be attending a gala for the “Oscars of Alpinism,” I made a note to pack formal clothes. The Piolets d’Or, or Golden Ice Axes, is a big deal; a rare career-building opportunity in a professional alpinist’s life. Earning this award can transform a strong amateur into a full-fledged member of global alpinism’s elite. This year, I joined the recipients who’d been coaxed out of their humble mountain hideouts to partake in alpinism’s biggest award ceremony.

Established in 1992, the Piolets have a respectable mission: to promote difficult, alpine-style new routes on the world’s great mountains. But the award has weathered plenty of criticism over the years. After rejecting his Piolet nomination in 2006, U.K. legend Ian Parnell later wrote in Alpinist: “Is it possible to choose a winner in an inherently unquantifiable pursuit [like alpinism]?” Others decry the Piolets d’Or for awarding climbers who recently died in the mountains, as well as for holding a subjective line of what counts as good climbing style.

I’ve been critical of the Piolets at times myself, especially after hearing one well-known alpinist talk longingly of wanting to climb something worthy of the award. I winced thinking about anyone tackling runout mixed terrain at high altitude with a golden ice axe taunting them overhead.

I thought of these critics, and my own biases, during my transatlantic flight a few weeks ago to this year’s ceremony in Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans, France. The award clearly has a dark side. But it has also become increasingly important in the year 2026. Lately, I’ve watched the professional climbing landscape bend to the pressures of sponsorship and social-media engagement—physical performance is but one metric to make a modern-day alpinist’s career.

In this new landscape, we see some climbers eager to make a quick buck. Others orient ascents around appeasing future sponsors or gaining attention online. In some instances, this materializes as full-scale fraud. In others, imaginative white lies of what constitutes a “summit.”

Through this lens, the Piolets d’Or represents an institution that is slowly becoming necessary. Nearly every year for the last 34 years, a varied, rotating cast of legendary alpinists sifts through the reams of new climbing achievements. Tossing aside marketing fluff and half-baked route attempts, they present to the world the year’s genuine highpoints of alpinism.

I wanted to know: Does the good of the Piolets d’Or outweigh the bad?

The singular Piolet d’Or first launched with the aim of recognizing the greatest alpine ascent of the previous year. In true Oscars’ fashion, at the early Piolet, all of the potential candidates were invited to an in-person ceremony, where the sole winner was read out, for the first time, in front of a couple thousand people.

“It was a mess,” British alpinist Paul Ramsden, one of this year’s jury members, told me of the Piolet’s early days. He and countryman Mick Fowler had been invited to the ceremony in Paris in 2003, when their ascent of Siguniang (6,250m) in China was in the running. “We all got up onto the stage, and they read my and Mick’s names out, and a French team beside us burst into tears,” Ramsden said.

American Dean Potter was on stage too, in the running for his solo ascents of the Patagonian spires Cerro Torre and Fitz Roy. When he got snubbed, he was livid, Ramsden remembered. Potter screamed at the organizers, asking why they’d told him to fly all the way to Europe to stand on stage for an award they knew he’d never receive.

Later that evening, in a sign of the early Piolet d’Or attitude, a special party took place offsite to celebrate Ramsden and Fowler’s win. With his golden ice axe in hand, Ramsden remembered ambling over to the afterparty, only to be stopped by a bouncer. The club had a dress code, and Ramsden was wearing sneakers. “So we weren’t allowed into our own party,” Ramsden laughed.

The Piolet d’Or ran uninterrupted from 1992 to 2007, when mounting criticism came to a head. Most notable was from the Slovenian alpinist Marko Prezelj, who was invited to that year’s event after his ascent of Chomo Lhari (7,326m), on the border of Tibet. He walked slowly onto the stage, took a long pause, then refused to accept his award, explaining why he thought the Piolet was antithetical to his view of alpinism. “Comparing different climbs is not possible without some kind of personal involvement and even then it is difficult,” Prezelj later wrote. “Last year I climbed in Alaska, Patagonia, and Tibet. I cannot decide which expedition was the most… the ‘most what’ in fact?”

Prezelj and others had become increasingly uneasy with how the Piolet d’Or pitted alpinists against each other. With only one winner, everyone else, in their eyes, became a loser. Such was not the spirit of alpinism.

The organizers cancelled the ceremony in 2008 and took a beat to reimagine it. A year later, after personnel changes and plenty of disagreements, a new version of the Piolet emerged, complete with an updated charter. The now-plural Piolets rewarded a climb’s lightweight style, self-sufficiency, technical difficulty, and management of objective hazards. Most importantly, though, the Piolets adopted a more community-based attitude. Everyone who was nominated for the award was given a Piolet d’Or.

This year’s ceremony was devoid of the drama that tainted the Piolet’s past. No one walked onto the stage just to reject the award. There was no French team in tears, and—as far as I could tell—no leery feeling of one-upsmanship among the award recipients. It was a bunch of climbers, wearing sneakers and duct-taped down jackets, drinking a bit too much red wine.

Paul Ramsden, who is 57, has been to a number of these week-long parties over the years, five times as a recipient—the most of any climber—and multiple times again as a jury member. Despite the criticism it’s received over the years, and his own jarring experience in 2003, he is now a proud supporter of the Piolets d’Or.

“I see awful style from climbers in some parts of the world,” he told me, citing large teams with bolt kits and hundreds of meters of fixed ropes, all but assured to succeed with enough dogged, industrial determination. “By rewarding alpine-style climbs, we’re not really rewarding the recipients. We’re signalling to the rest of the climbing community what ‘good’ style is.” In practice, that means that if a climber doesn’t have the skill to scale an unclimbed face with the same hardware they might take to a crag, they should leave the objective for a future generation of climbers who can.

One alpinist, who wished to remain anonymous, but has been nominated for a Piolet before, emphasized how flimsy and subjective any notion of “good” climbing style is. In a phone call with me, they noted how the Piolets jury considers climbing in insulated boots and ultralight crampons with Google-Earth reconnaissance as “good” climbing style, but considered carrying a few extra ropes to fix sections of the route poor form. The jury considers climbing in a lightweight team of two an enviable expression of alpine self sufficiency, yet a team of five or six is antiquated and ungainly.

Even understated, minimalist climbing expeditions to the Himalaya these days require a cottage-industry of resources: international flights, bus rides, porters, cook tents, tens of thousands of dollars of equipment—the list goes on. Deciding what the “correct” amount of resources an expedition should use is an inexact science, and one which the Piolets jury is still figuring out.

“I think it’s cool that we have a pretty objective governing body deciding what is actually good for alpine climbing,” Australian-Argentine climber Sebastian Pelletti, a recipient of a Piolet this year, told me. Like me, Pelletti has noticed professional alpinists erroneously claiming a “new” route to their sponsors and the world.

Last year, I wrote about one of those so-called new routes on Jirishanca (6,094m), in Peru’s Cordillera Huayhuash. Three very famous European alpinists climbed about a thousand meters of new terrain to the mountain’s summit ridge. Above, a spine of unconsolidated snow—the crux of the mountain—proved too difficult for the team. They bailed. A few days later, the climbers and their sponsors plastered a topo for this new route far and wide, drawing a bright red line that stopped on Jirishanca’s “east summit.” The east summit does not exist, nor has it ever been considered a final destination on the mountain. It is a brief bump in an otherwise vertical landscape, at least six pitches below Jirishanca’s actual summit.

When I wrote that article, some people called it a hit piece; I thought I was going light on the climbers. So when the Piolets d’Or announced their “long list” of notable ascents of 2025 earlier this year, I combed through it, seeing which routes made the cut. (Not all long-listed ascents are short-listed for the Piolets d’Or. The long list aims to recognize all new alpine climbs accomplished in good style.)

The Jirishanca “east summit” team was absent in the Peru section; the jury had not even considered their effort a route. But also within Peru’s long list, in the very same Huayhuash range, was a route on a mountain I had not heard much about, by climbers far less famous than their peers down valley. It was about the same length as the Jirishanca route, and just as difficult, but it went to the summit of Yerupajá Grande (6,635 m) and down the opposite side of the mountain. The climbers called it The Essence of Commitment, and they were being awarded the highest prize in alpinism.

#8167. Six Feet of Snow Trapped 29 People in the Himalayas. Their Survival Came Down to the Details

(Photo: Screenshot via Aquaterra Adventures)

The mountains around Auden’s Col, an 18,010-foot high-altitude pass in India’s Garhwal Himalayas, looked deceptively calm. It was the afternoon of September 25, 2026; the sky was clear, and the 29-member expedition team had reached base camp at approximately 16,400 feet, preparing to cross one of the region’s most challenging passes the next morning.

But within hours, the weather began to change. A fast-moving depression from the Bay of Bengal swept across the Indian subcontinent towards the Himalayas. The Indian government issued a red alert only after the expedition had reached base camp. From the evening of September 25 through September 27, more than six feet of snow fell.

“There was no advance warning, and forecasting services failed to predict the severity of the storm,” Vaibhav Kala, the founder of Aquaterra Adventures, the Indian adventure outfitter that organized the expedition, tells Backpacker. “The team was caught in a very rare, heavy weather event.”

The group included six clients, three guides, and 20 porters. It was led by Jetendra Singh Rana, a mountaineering guide who had crossed the pass nine times over his 22-year guiding career. Aquaterra Adventures helped open this 10-day route to commercial departures nearly two decades ago.

“This is not a casual trek as the route traverses steep slopes, glacier terrain and moraine, to descend onto the heavily crevassed Khatling Glacier,” adds Kala.

Rana stepped out of his tent at midnight on the 25th and saw clouds stacking up over the col that hadn’t been there earlier.

“Something just did not feel right,” he says. At 2 a.m. on September 26, the sky still hadn’t improved, so he made the first critical decision to call off the next morning’s scheduled ascent to Auden’s Col. By 3:30 a.m., snow had started falling.

“No one questioned [Rana’s] decision, and that was the single most important moment during the entire trek that saved our lives,” Preeti and Raj Chauhan, guests from Bangalore, India, say. Had the group left on schedule, they would have been on the face of the col when the snow arrived. By the end of the day, winds had reached around 62 mph, and temperatures had dropped to about -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius).

Informed by two decades of guiding experience, Rana’s choice that morning came from a place of pragmatism: “In the mountains, confidence doesn’t mean ignoring danger. It means understanding the situation, trusting your preparation and making responsible decisions,” he says.

By the afternoon of September 26, the group’s small sleeping tents were no longer safe because of the snow that continued to fall. At around 4 p.m., Rana moved everyone into a The North Face 2-Meter Dome Tent, which served as the group’s dining tent.

Through the night, the wind rose to near-blizzard levels, and the team felt the tent’s metal poles straining. For about two hours, they all took turns pressing on the tent poles from the inside to prevent snow from accumulating.

“We are not sure it helped,” Chauhan says. “But it made us feel useful and not panic.”

Another guest, Vikram Badhwar, describes a quieter fear.

“It is tough to be cooped up in a tent for 48 hours, but no one lost their heads,” he says. “We were joking, laughing, talking and, of course, silently praying for our safe homecoming.”

Outside, porters and staff worked through the night with little equipment, shoveling snow off the tent and cutting a perimeter around the base to prevent the rising wall of snow from crushing it.

The only communication available to the team was through a satellite phone, which Aquaterra requires all its guides to carry. Rana used it to report the snow and relay his decision to cancel the ascent. By September 26, they were having pre-scheduled status-update calls every few hours.

That’s when headquarters concluded that the group could not walk back. Kala called the Uttarakhand tourism secretary, who escalated to the Uttarakhand Disaster Management Authority. The additional district magistrate and divisional forest officer also got involved, along with the Civil Aviation Department and the Indian Army. All six agencies collaborated to requisition nine helicopters to rescue 136 stranded trekkers in the valley, including the Aquaterra team.

On the morning of September 27, during an eight-minute phone call, Kala outlined a plan to airlift the entire team. Rana and his staff were instructed to clear a 10-by-10-meter area for a landing pad. The rescue was scheduled for sunrise the following morning.

On September 28, the weather cleared for a brief four-hour window. The crew dismantled their safety dome and used the flat surface underneath as a landing pad. Because of the continuing storm, Kala guided the pilots over base camp using Google Earth Imagery from his office in Delhi.

The first sortie lifted off about 8:45 a.m. with two passengers. “Departure order was set in advance with the guests so there was no scramble for the aircraft,” says Rana. Aquaterra Adventures was the only group that had given the pilots exact coordinates and a prepared landing zone, keeping them on track. By 11 a.m., all 29 hikers were safe.

The first day’s window evacuated 38 people in total from the valley before the weather closed in again. Thankfully, the remaining stranded hikers were evacuated over the next few days with no fatalities.

According to Kala and Rana, this rescue was one of the most successful mountain operations in Uttarakhand in recent years, thanks to an unprecedented coordination between state governments, regional municipalities, and private agencies.

Kala subsequently submitted a detailed report to the Uttarakhand Government documenting the actions of his team, Rana, and other guides and stakeholders, along with lessons for future expeditions. His key takeaways include focusing on small details like packing a central shelter, shovels, portable power banks, spare satellite-phone charging cables, and ensuring trekkers are always prepared to be rescued.

“Our objective was to cross Auden’s Col, but our responsibility was much bigger than reaching a mountain pass,” Rana says. “The mountains will always be there, and there will always be another opportunity to try again. But the safety of every person on an expedition comes first.”

Huddled in hedgerows and shedding trees this fall, your backyard birdies need your help. Here are the simple things you can do now to keep them healthy and happy through winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall can be deceptive: for a while, the lingering sunlight might be warm, and there might still be pops of color as late-season annuals stand in defiance. But all it takes is one big cold snap or a nibble of frost for the whole yard to change, literally overnight. The transition from late fall color to the reality of several months of winter can be a shock – and not just for us. As we huddle over morning hot drinks and contemplate the gaps in the yard, imagine how it feels for our feathered chums.

From plump northern cardinals to energetic black-capped chickadees, these shifting conditions present a challenge for bird feeding, shelter, and survival. Tree cover is starting to bleed away as fall leaves spiral to the ground, exposing branches to biting winds, cold rain, and sharp frosts. The juicy bugs of July are history, dogwood berries are being stripped, and crisping soils mean foraging birds have to work twice as hard for every meal. For birdies that only weigh a couple of nickels, getting through the night means burning nearly an entire day’s energy just to stay warm.

So for our pint-sized backyard companions, the big chill isn’t just an inconvenience; it’s a fearsome calorie crunch. This narrow window in late fall is your best opportunity to step in with kind, targeted care. These little backyard wins won’t punish your wallet and they don’t demand much time. Just a little thoughtful prep today will keep your feathered neighbors safe, spunky, and singing outside your window all winter.

Preparing your backyard for happy wintering birds is all about timing. Whatever you do, don’t be tempted to put these little fall tasks off too long. I get it: in the whirl of leaf raking, perennial cutting, and hose winterizing, it’s easy to get distracted. But waiting until the first blizzard strikes and the ground freezes is a classic birdcare blunder, and one that tends to result in a yard devoid of birdsong.

Early winter is when resident birds establish foraging routes. By taking action now with these simple steps, you set up your yard as the place to stop mid-route – before the mercury plunges. Your USDA hardiness zone and regional climate have a part to play. In colder northern areas (zones 3-5), the risk of sudden hard freezes requires an earlier focus on high-density fats and ice-free water sources. Warmer zones 7-10 may host nomadic cedar waxwings and lingering eastern bluebirds as well as year-round residents. Yet they tend to share the same priorities: fast fuel, reliable drinks, and a cozy place to ride out a gale.

Before diving into these quick fall tasks, survey your yard. Observe how morning light strikes your patio, identify sheltered spots safe from north winds, and check that feeding and water stations are 10 feet (3m) from protective shrubs and safe staging or waiting branches for timid finches to peek out. Speaking of peeking, if you can’t afford a smart feeder, keep some compact binoculars or a monocular scope on hand to monitor visiting species and track which treats disappear first. The Pankoo 16x52 High Powered Monocular Telescope, available from Amazon, is a great way to enjoy shy songbirds on a budget.

Helping your birds thrive during winter starts now. These timely acts of care require minimal effort, and the payoff for getting your yard dialed in for the season is huge. By setting up your stations for winter, you’ll be rewarded with fluttery visitors even when the snow starts to fall. Here’s how easy it is to create a sanctuary for birds to fly in the face of the big chill…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As late fall chills settle in, backyard birds undergo a dietary pivot. During summer, they could thrive on lean insects and grains. But once night temperatures flirt with freezing, survival tilts towards fats. Burning fuel just to stay warm until breakfast is serious business. Now’s the time for you to swap out cheap summer filler seeds like red milo for lipid-rich options that deliver maximum energy per beakful.

This is the time to load your feeders with black-oil sunflower seeds. Their thin, papery shells are easily cracked by finches and chickadees, and their plump hearts are packed with plant oils. For ground-foraging juncos and sparrows, sprinkle hulled sunflower chips on low platforms so they don’t have to waste energy on dehulling. And hang some rendered suet cakes laced with berries or raw peanuts to nourish blue jays, red-bellied woodpeckers, downy woodpeckers, and nuthatches. C&S Peanut Suet Treat Cakes, available from Amazon, come in great-value packs.

Toss a handful of crunchy, dried mealworms onto a shallow tray to entice visiting eastern bluebirds and hermit thrushes to the party. Just make sure your feeder is able to support these extra nibbles, as well as allowing fall rains to drain freely. An open platform feeder, like the Kingsyard Hanging Platform Bird Feeder Tray from Amazon, can house a healthy fall feast in comfort while reducing the risk of mold.

Some of the simplest (and yet oddly, easily overlooked) fall birdcare measures involve your bird bath. Yes, topping up the seed hoppers and platform feeders is critical, but what’s worse is when the trusty bath is just left to freeze over. For birds, crunching on cold snow isn’t a fun winter pastime but an energy disaster. It drains their internal body heat precisely when they need every drop of warmth to survive.

It’s frustrating, because this is such an easy problem to avoid. At this time of year a heated bird bath, such as the Allied Precision Heated Bird Bath with Mounted Bracket, from Amazon, can pay for itself in terms of bird visits. Alternatively, you can keep water in motion (and so reduce freezing) by adding a rubber duck or ping pong ball to your bird bath. Ensure that the water depth in the bird bath remains shallow, never exceeding a couple of inches (5cm), so that small visitors like American goldfinches and purple finches can drink safely.

Drop in a flat, textured stone so little feet have a non-slip surface. Finally, keep water supplies fresher for longer by adding a copper disc to your bird bath. The Mellbree Bird Bath Copper Cleaning Disc from Amazon is a brilliant way to prevent algae build-up between cleans. Easy!

Sitting on a bare branch in a sharp November breeze is an everyday winter reality for your garden birds, but it is one you can help them with. Backyards are losing their natural windbreaks as deciduous trees drop their leaves, exposing birdies to the elements and also nocturnal prowlers. But you can bolster the availability of natural cover and create layered roosting pockets before deep winter sets in.

Late fall is an ideal time for planting certain key containerized native shrubs, such as Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry, available from Nature Hills, which establishes quickly in late fall, providing dense roosting cover and juicy berries for over 40 bird species. American beautyberry is another excellent bird-friendly native that you can also plant now, as long as you can tuck them in a few weeks before the ground freezes. You can pick up containers of Green Promise Farms’ American Beautyberry Live Plants from Amazon which will establish relatively fast. Remember to mulch with a 3-inch (8cm) ring of shredded bark.

Leaving dense conifers and arborvitae unclipped provides dense inner chambers where northern cardinals, dark-eyed juncos, and mourning doves can huddle. It’s also helpful to stack any thick trimmings you might have accumulated from fall pruning in a quiet border. A loose brush pile is perfect for winter wrens and ground-dwelling sparrows. Finally, you can convert unused wooden nest boxes into roosting cabins by sealing ventilation holes, flipping the front panel so the entrance hole sits at the bottom to trap rising heat, and layering the base with pine shavings.

At this time of year, it only takes a couple of heavy showers or sharp gusts to knock our bird-feeding routines into disarray. Even with the best intentions, we might put off bird feeder or bird bath cleaning, promising we’ll do it at the weekend, only to wind up catching up on box sets in our pyjamas (no judgments). But leaving a greasy ring of wet kernels or hulls stuck to the bottom of a feeder is a recipe for disaster, creating a breeding ground for killers such as Salmonellosis and Aspergillosis. Left unchecked, these can spread through the feathered community in a matter of days.

Establishing a rigorous weekly cleaning rhythm is your best line of disease defense. This can be as simple as a quick Sunday scrub routine (these can be surprisingly therapeutic!). It helps to have feeders that are easy to dismantle and clean in the first place. A good bird feeder option for weekly cleaning is the Woodlink Seed Tube Bird Feeder from Home Depot, with removable base ports that detach in seconds.

Once you have disassembled your seed tubes, hopper troughs, and platform trays, discard damp or caked seed remnants. Scrub tight nooks with an extra-long bottle brush, like the Songbird Essentials Extra Long Bottle Brush, available from Amazon. Then soak the parts for 10-15 minutes. Using a ratio of nine parts to one, dip in warm water laced with distilled white vinegar. Rinse thoroughly and ensure every component is dry before refilling. Sweep away soggy fallen hulls while you’re at it, to help out ground-foragers like juncos and mourning doves.

In the fall yard, pristine neatness can often be the enemy of wildlife survival. Many of the forager’s final treasures of the season may be tucked beneath curling leaf fall or wedged in that forlorn dangling seed head. Stripping away key perennial skeletons and scooping up fallen foliage deprive backyard birds of vital natural gifts. Such backyard litter costs you nothing to leave, and they keep your birds stocked up in other sleeping nibbles, such as dormant spiders and protein-packed pupae.

So leave perennial seed heads standing, kick a mound of leaves under your hedges, and let nature do the catering. Place a low, wire-mesh ground tray nearby, filled with a sprinkling of sunflower chips and crunchy protein-rich mealworms such as Kaytee Dried Mealworms from Walmart to reward their hard work. If you need a good ground tray feeder, the Mizxxidea Mesh Ground Bird Feeder from Amazon has an ultra-fine mesh base allowing fall rains to drain through cleanly. Blending handy extra feeding stations alongside natural foraging options creates the ideal birdie hangout.

These quick fall tasks are a lovely way of supporting your local birdlife as temperatures plummet, transforming your yard into a safe, high-energy refuge. While some of these fall extras are inexpensive, it’s worth investing in a few key features to help stay one step ahead of biting winds and winter chills. These curated staples will help you protect and nurture your resident songbirds from fall through winter.

Made of solid wood with a steep-pitched roof, this charming shelter offers visitors essential insulation against freezing drafts and rain. The side door makes cleaning simple, creating an ideal roosting cabin for chickadees, titmice, and wrens looking to huddle away from the worst of the winter weather.

This pretty jewel-toned basin is made from durable embossed glass and the textured presentation is kinder on birdie feet. It looks like high-end art, but is durable and rock-steady, although it's more likely to be filled with songbirds than hummers. Very easy to keep clean, and a real talking point for friends.

Crafted with vibrant stained-glass mosaic tiling, this fly-through feeder is great for shielding birds against winds and protecting seeds from drizzle. This pretty feeder's tunnel design also provides 360-degree visibility for skittish finches, chickadees, and nuthatches.

This timely fall intervention is all about making subtle, thoughtful shifts in our birdcare. By swapping in dense, high-calorie foods, maintaining easy-access water, supporting roosting options, cleaning feeders weekly, and leaving some fallen leaves around, you provide vital comfort and protection for vulnerable birds just when they need it most. It’s worth it to watch a puffed-up cardinal chewing on a mealworm, or a towhee poking out of some crunchy leaf litter, knowing that you’re doing your bit to keep nature’s sweetest living colors fluttering in and out of your yard.
