#8157. How a 20-Year-Old Texas Climber Lost His Life on the Matterhorn

Kieran Liner, a 20-year-old climber based in Austin, TX, died in an accident on the Matterhorn in October. (Photo: Courtesy Precenia Newman duplicate)

A 20-year-old climber named Kieran Liner from Austin, Texas, died on October 27 after falling from the Matterhorn’s Hörnli Ridge. He was climbing with his friend Eli Hawkins.

Valais Cantonal Police said the two climbers were ascending shortly after 6 a.m. when rocks fell near them at about 11,500 feet. Hawkins lost sight of Liner and immediately called for help. An Air Zermatt helicopter responded. Rescuers found Liner below the route and pronounced him dead at the scene.

Prosecutors opened an investigation to determine the precise circumstances of the fall. The initial police statement reported rockfall nearby, but didn’t specify exactly how Liner fell or died.

Hawkins, who says he met Liner in Austin around five years ago, called him his “best bud” and his climbing partner. “It is what it is,” Hawkins told Climbing. “He died doing what he loved.”

Originally from Pensacola, Florida, Liner had lived in Austin since 2020. According to Hawkins, Liner liked Modest Mouse, IPAs, and American Spirit Blues. But what he loved most, Hawkins wrote, was climbing in the mountains.

In an obituary shared last week, Liner’s sister Precenia Newman remembered her younger brother as a skateboarder, golfer, and alpinist—someone who brought the same enthusiasm to everything he pursued. “He approached everything in life with 150% of himself,” Newman wrote.

Newman described a close circle of friends who had become family through shared adventures and everyday life. Among them was Hawkins, whose friendship and life as Liner’s roommate she singled out as especially meaningful. She also remembered the love surrounding Liner from his parents, Justine Hamel and Nick Liner, as well as his siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, and nephews. Newman has organized a fundraiser to bring him home so the family can celebrate his life in Pensacola and Austin.

While Hawkins grew up climbing as a kid with his father and uncle, Liner got into the sport later in life, but it quickly became his passion. Hawkins said the two of them had strong mentors, including Hawkins’s dad Stephen, Ben Darce, and his uncle Bryan Hawkins who owns a climbing gym in Everett, Washington. “He was fearless,” Hawkins said of Liner. “I was fearless—still am. I’m going to keep climbing for him. We just climbed hard and partied hard.”

This past July, Liner had started an Instagram account called @mountkieran dedicated primarily to climbing and mountaineering content. His first reel captured climbing Mt. Rainier. Most of his content leaned humorous, with jokes about “Conrad Anger” and poking fun at himself as an “Austin influencer” while board climbing.

But occasionally, Liner shared more serious content, like footage of ascending a steep snow pitch with a quote from Reinhold Messner: “To go on an adventure, you need difficulties, you need danger. If death were not a possibility, coming out would be nothing.”

Generally considered the most popular and easiest route by which to ascend the Matterhorn, the Hörnli Ridge rises roughly 4,000 vertical feet from the Hörnli Hut to the 14,692-foot summit. Rated AD (“fairly difficult”) on the alpine scale, the route combines sustained exposed scrambling with technical rock climbing rated around 5.4. In general, parties take four to five hours for the ascent, plus another five to six hours for the descent, which involves downclimbing and rappelling much of the same terrain.

Fixed ropes assist climbers on certain sections, but parties also bring their own ropes. Snow and ice can be encountered near the summit, requiring crampons and an ice axe. The technical grade captures only part of the challenge of navigating and descending that exposed terrain in mountaineering boots.

To learn more about the Hörnli Ridge where Liner’s accident took place, I reached out to my friend Steph Abegg, who claimed the fastest known time by a woman on the route this past summer.

In 1985, Abegg’s dad soloed the Matterhorn in a T-shirt. Twenty years later, when Abegg and her sister were in Zermatt and decided to climb it, that was the image they held in their minds. Their dad was an experienced climber, and he’d enjoyed ideal conditions on his ascent.

Accordingly, the Abegg sisters expected a casual adventure. Instead, they encountered verglas—a thin glaze of ice on the rock—and a whiteout. They turned around at the Solvay Hut, an emergency shelter at 13,133 feet. At this point, they were roughly 2,440 vertical feet above the Hörnli Hut, where the climb begins, and still about 1,560 feet below the summit.

“It could be said I underestimated the Matterhorn myself in 2005,” Abegg told me. “Had we continued, it’s entirely possible we could have gotten into trouble.”

This past summer, Abegg returned, climbing the Hörnli Ridge with a partner before completing a solo, unsupported round trip from Zermatt in 10 hours, 8 minutes, and 19 seconds—the fastest women’s time then recorded on the FKT website, supported or unsupported. A month later, Kalie McCrystal lowered the record to 6 hours, 47 minutes, and 33 seconds.

The route’s moderate technical grade, fixed ropes, and popularity can make the Hörnli Ridge seem approachable. But finding the line and staying on solid rock demands attention. Stray from the standard route and the rock can become looser. Altitude, changing weather, and fall consequences add to the difficulty.

During Abegg’s partnered ascent this past summer, a washing-machine-sized boulder was accidentally dislodged. It tumbled down a gully, triggering what she described as a significant rockslide, mostly off route. Higher up, loose rock littered the climbing line. Abegg described rocks ranging in size from marbles to baseballs, or even volleyballs, that climbers could knock onto people below. The terrain, she said, had historically remained under snow year-round.

“Had to move very carefully,” she wrote. Guides stopped taking clients up the route during her trip.

Aside from the omnipresent risk of rockfall in any alpine environment, a 2025 study found that climate change has caused an increase in rockfall on the Matterhorn as permafrost thaws. Just a couple months ago, German online magazine Lacrux published an article about the increasing hazards of rockfall on the Matterhorn, as well as on Mont Blanc.

“Having the innate mountain sense to know when to call it is a valuable quality on an objective like this,” Abegg said.

Andy Hansen, an IFMGA-certified (International Federation of Mountain Guides) guide based in Longmont, Colorado, has guided clients on the Matterhorn twice. Speaking from his own experience, he strongly recommends hiring a guide for a first attempt.

He said recreational climbers in Western Europe are generally more accustomed to hiring guides than their counterparts in the United States. One advantage of hiring a guide on the Hörnli Ridge is how closely they follow variable conditions on a route, according to Hansen.

“The local guides have an intimacy with the mountain that gives them the advantage of having the route finding dialed, understanding the conditions of the mountain from day to day, and knowing where and when to move quickly to manage the rockfall hazard,” Hansen told me.

Hansen observed an unusual amount of rockfall in the Alps this past spring and summer, calling the Hörnli Ridge noticeably more unstable. He pointed to local guides’ familiarity with the ridge and their day-to-day knowledge of its conditions. A weather forecast can tell any climber how warm it’s likely to get, but knowing the ridge helps a guide judge which sections are most prone to rockfall, where to move quickly to limit exposure, and whether to climb that day at all.

However, whether a guide would have changed the outcome for Liner is an entirely different question. “It’s virtually impossible to say with any degree of certainty that had this party been with a mountain guide, the outcome would have been any different,” Hansen said. In his view, it was the kind of misfortune that could befall a guided party, too.

Hawkins told Climbing that they were aware of the risk of rockfall and had accepted it as a possible and uncontrollable hazard that you can’t “really do anything about.” He added that he never considered hiring a guide because he has sufficient experience and wants to take on alpine objectives independently. “If you do hire a guide, you didn’t climb the mountain,” he said of his philosophy.

While a guide is not required to climb the Matterhorn, it does materially improve your chances of reaching the summit. According to Global Summit Guide, an independent, research-based mountaineering resource based in Utah, the summit rate varies considerably depending on whether climbers are traveling with a guide.

A Global Summit Guide report updated this past July states that while the overall Matterhorn success rate is 55%, guided climbers see a 72% success rate, while unguided climbers hover around a 38% success rate. Meanwhile, first-timers like Liner and Hawkins only have an 18% shot at reaching the top. Furthermore, during the popular climbing season of May through October, October has the lowest success rate of 22%.

Global Summit Guide also reinforces the Matterhorn’s reputation as Europe’s most deadly mountain, with an average of eight to 12 fatalities annually. They note that about 1 in 140 climbers perish in their attempt to summit. More than 500 people (and counting) have died on the Matterhorn to date.

Dialogue and debate over the broader trends indirectly related to Liner’s death have already  emerged in the climbing community.

After Liner died, a Reddit thread in r/Mountaineering sparked debate about the climbing-related content he and Hawkins had posted on their Instagram accounts. “Obviously, there are videos of me and him partying in Europe, but when we’re actually climbing, I take precautions and I’m not an idiot when I climb,” Hawkins told Climbing. “I take safety as a number one precaution.” He added that Liner would “probably be laughing” at what Hawkins sees as misinformed comments online.

Then, in an Instagram reel posted on November 2, Washington-based gear manufacturer High Mountain Gear turned the discussion toward a different topic: a video Norwegian climber Magnus Midtbø made about his 2025 Matterhorn solo. High Mountain Gear took particular issue with Midtbø looking up how to use crampons shortly before his climb. In the comments of High Mountain Gear’s reel, some agreed that a climber with Midtbø’s reach ought to think about the example he sets. Others asked why he was being brought into a conversation about someone else’s accident.

Hawkins explained that he and Liner had set the Matterhorn as a big goal independent of any online content. “It’s just a climb we wanted to do for a long time,” Hawkins said of the Matterhorn. “It had nothing to do with any Instagram videos.” He noted that he wasn’t very familiar with Midtbø’s Matterhorn video.

Beyond this recent incident, when Midtbø’s video came out, Swiss public broadcaster SRF reported that Midtbø talked openly about his limited preparation. He struggled with the altitude and got off route. Other climbers had to call him back to the right line. Once he got down, he admitted he had underestimated the risk and urged viewers against following his example. Air Zermatt’s rescue chief Anjan Truffer told SRF that he worried viewers might still interpret Midtbø’s climb as a success, without appreciating the gap between his climbing ability and their own.

In Midtbø’s defense, however, he could have cut the moments when he was tired, lost, or scared. But he chose to leave them in. Some viewers in the YouTube comments took the climb as a cautionary tale. Others wanted a follow-up with a guide explaining where things nearly went wrong. Ultimately, given the irrelevance of Midtbø’s video to Hawkins’s and Liner’s Matterhorn objective, as well as the full disclosures that Midtbø provided in his video, the notion that YouTube content is to blame for this or any other fatality seems besides the point.

As a guide, Hansen sees responsibility on both sides of the screen. He said creators like Midtbø have some accountability for what they put out, even when they include a disclaimer. But viewers must assess whether their own skills match the demands of any climb described in online content.

Abegg’s father came home with a story about soloing the Matterhorn in a T-shirt. Abegg and her sister came home with a story about turning around at the Solvay Hut. Midtbø came home, too. But in his video, you can see how close he came to a different outcome when he lost the route on exposed terrain.

Kieran Liner didn’t come home. He was 20 years old. The mountain doesn’t care what drew you there, whose story you heard, or how long you spent preparing. Even the most experienced climber can be in the wrong place at the wrong time, especially when it comes to escalating hazards like rockfall.

Liner’s family is planning to celebrate his life in Pensacola and Austin. In her obituary, Newman invited everyone who knew him, shared his adventures, or found inspiration in his life to join them. “Whether you knew him for a lifetime or crossed paths with him only briefly,” she wrote, “you are part of the story he leaves behind.”

Climbing Magazine reached out to Kyle Willis of High Mountain Gear and Magnus Midtbø for comment, but have not received a response.

#8156. My Favorite Spot in Denali National Park Is a Literal Pile of Trash

Old cans abound at one historic dump in Denali National Park. (Photo: Ryleigh Norgrove)

One of my favorite spots in Denali National Park’s vast wilderness isn’t some grand vista or rocky overlook. It’s much trashier than that.

Wander enough of the park’s frontcountry woods and you’ll come across all sorts of things: pioneer graves, little slate caves, mossy goshawk perches, a fantastic blueberry patch. Keep walking, and you might find a drainage as wide as a semi, full of garbage.

There are beer cans and glass bottles, coffee cans and broken gravy boats. It looks like a house disgorged its contents on a hillside and the tundra is slowly gobbling them up

The first time I encountered it, I wondered why no good Samaritan had come along with a bag or several by now, to haul this away to some other, less federally protected pit. We’re supposed to pack it out, after all.

After asking around at the local dive, I learned something else: This trash was considered historic. It felt like an oxymoron to me: How could a bunch of nasty empty beer cans tell us anything about the past other than a bunch of old-timers here liked to get drunk together, or that they were serving alcohol during prohibition?

One answer is that people don’t tend to write down what they’ve had for lunch. Or what kind of socks they wore through, or what they dropped and shattered. Discarded objects don’t mean much once they’ve hit the bin. And that’s exactly why impromptu landfills like this are one of the most significant sources of data archaeologists have.

“A lot of the stories of these individuals in the past never got written down,” says Dr. Justin Cramb, an assistant professor of archaeology at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, told me. “So the material traces are what we have.”

Archaeologists actually have a word for this historic trash: middens. They’re nasty and they’re everywhere. Depending on their age, they could contain shells, animal bones, or the last of someone’s canned dinner. They’re treasure troves of information, teaching us how people lived. Enough of them, alongside the other things people discarded, might tell you something about making a home in a place like Denali where getting groceries was considerably more complicated than driving to the store.

It’s something Cramb knows well. Throughout his work, he looks for details of daily lives: what resources people had, how they built their camps, and where they might have gathered building materials. Garbage is a part of that evidence.

“At the time, the world was kind of considered to be too vast to worry about those kind of things,” Cramb said. “And often in cases, somebody’s living at a place like Denali, they’re not going to haul their trash out, right? There was no mechanism for that to happen.”

Still, surely not every empty beer can deserves to spend eternity in a national park. But what’s the birthday on which it graduates from trash to treasured artifact?

The answer I got from the National Park Service on this was less tidy than I expected: “Age alone does not determine whether an object warrants preservation.”

It comes down to preserving cultural resources as much as natural ones. There are a few laws involved: Under the National Historic Preservation Act, historic areas generally need to be at least 50 years old and meet certain criteria for historical significance and integrity. The Archaeological Resources Protection Act also covers archaeological resources more than 100 years old that have cultural significance. Neither amounts to a blanket instruction to save every old can, but they do offer about 50 years of leeway on either end to determine if something is worth saving.

Cramb put it this way: “The house I grew up in is over 50 years old, right? But it’s not a historic property.”

Apparently, getting old and falling apart isn’t enough. The issue lies in what an object can teach us. Was it associated with a significant person or event? Could it fill in a piece of history we don’t know much about? And is enough of that evidence still there to make sense of it?

Around nearby Riley Creek, there’s quite a bit of history to make sense of. Before this was a place to order a latte or catch a bus, it was a place people lived. On Thanksgiving Day, 1921, Maurice Morino opened his Mount McKinley Park Hotel to feed and entertain miners, trappers and travelers. Just down the road, there were cabins, a trading post, and a silver fox ranch. Down below the old railroad bridge, you could visit “the Hole” for gambling, bootlegging, and other activities you won’t find on the ranger-program schedule.

Later on, in 1932, the park boundary absorbed that community. Today, cabin remains, debris, and trash dumps are among the traces of McKinley Station. Morino’s grave is still here, too. I haven’t been able to trace who exactly left behind my little trash pile, but it’s tucked into a landscape with considerably more human history than the trees let on.

Of course, I’d left an imprint getting there, too. I’d followed one of those little paths through the woods and added my footsteps to the record. Even my wandering had inherited a shape.

There’s something difficult in that. I want to know these woods well enough to return to the blueberries when they’re ripe, to recognize the perch before I look up for the bird. That kind of knowing takes effort. But each one presses a little more of a path into the ground.

“I always say that the goal is really to leave as little trace as possible,” says Erin Collier, Director of Education for Leave No Trace. “That doesn’t sound as good, you know, on the T-shirt and on the logo, but that’s really what the goal is.”

“If we were truly leaving no trace,” she says, “we wouldn’t be out there.”

We leave evidence of ourselves just by visiting. Roads, campgrounds, the little paths we wear into the woods. The trick is in paying attention to what we’re adding, and what we might accidentally take away.

Sometimes that means resisting the urge to clean up. The Park Service advises leaving potentially historic objects exactly where they are and asking staff if you’re unsure. Where something lies, among the other things people left behind, is part of its story.

But that doesn’t give the rest of us permission to start contributing.

“Today we have the infrastructure to deal with things like taking our trash out of the park,” Cramb told me. “We can do better. So we should.”

I know these woods, and knowing them means accepting that other people have known them, too. Their lives are still here, in cabin foundations and coffee cans, slowly disappearing into the hillside. My own footprints will leave something behind. I’d like to be thoughtful about what that is.

This story grew out of Ryleigh’s Certified Interpretive Guide (CIG) coursework, taught by Suzanne Miller, Interpretive Programs Manager for the Doyon/Aramark Joint Venture at Denali National Park and Preserve.

Anyone else already thinking about their holiday tablescapes? Because Catherine Zeta-Jones has just given us all the Thanksgiving inspiration we could ever need.

The actor recently shared a glimpse of her and Michael Douglas's Thanksgiving decor, and it's the kind of rustic autumnal display that makes you want to invite everyone over for dinner; think warm orange foliage, miniature pumpkins, natural branches and a gorgeous leafy garland.

It's the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, and you don't need a celebrity-sized decorating budget to recreate the look. In fact, I'd argue that some of the prettiest ingredients might already be growing in your backyard.

Catherine Zeta-Jones is one of those stars attached to countless big projects, from Wednesday to Chicago to America's Sweethearts. Still, though, she remains wonderfully down-to-earth... and even takes the time to make her own fall decor, too!

'A little DIY in anticipation of Thanksgiving,' she captioned a photo of her table on Instagram. 'I love this up coming holiday, my kids are home from college and I can’t wait!!!'

A post shared by Catherine Zeta-Jones (@catherinezetajones)

Keen to give it a go for yourself? Well, it's easy enough; all you really need to focus on is bringing the beauty of your autumnal garden indoors.

First things first, head outside and gather a selection of autumn leaves in warm shades of orange, red, bronze and gold. Maple and oak leaves are particularly lovely, but don't overlook interesting branches and seasonal greenery, either.

Make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and try using a mixture of different leaf shapes and sizes because it gives the arrangement a more natural, gathered-from-the-garden feel. Then, you can lay the foliage directly along the middle of the table, creating a loose runner that you can build the rest of your decorations around.

Something like the Oasis Forage Floral Create Kit on Amazon could help with this.

This clever little foraging kit has everything you need to get started on crafting your own fall decorations.

Whatever you do, just make sure anything you collect is clean and free from pests. And if you're gathering from outside your garden, always check that you're allowed to collect it.

You can't have a Thanksgiving centerpiece without pumpkins, can you? And Catherine Zeta-Jones's rustic look is a lovely reminder that you don't need enormous pumpkins to make an impact.

I'd choose a mixture of orange, cream and green varieties, placing them at intervals along the foliage. Try grouping a few together rather than spacing everything out too evenly. That slightly imperfect arrangement is what makes the whole thing feel so charming.

If you've grown your own ornamental gourds, even better! They're a wonderful way to give your Thanksgiving decorations a personal touch.

Now for my favorite part: the finishing touches! Honestly, a few interesting branches, seedheads or pinecones will add height and texture to the arrangement, and I particularly love the idea of incorporating dried ornamental grasses, which bring movement and a lovely natural softness to the display.

Then, make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and add small votive candles or LED tealights between the pumpkins and foliage. The warm glow will make the whole table feel wonderfully inviting once the evening draws in.

What I love about Catherine Zeta Jones's rustic decorations is that they remind us how much beauty there is to be found in the changing seasons!

#8154. “We’re Kind of Crushing It.” Why One Wyoming Mountain County Has a Life Expectancy of 94.

According to new data, residents in Wyoming’s Teton County have the highest average life expectancy in the country: 94 years.

Jackson Hole News and Guide first reported the finding on November 4, and Travis Riddell, MD, MPH, the director of the Teton County Health Department, first presented the data point at a Teton County Board of County Commissioners meeting on October 26.

After looking at mortality data over a three-year period, between 2022 and 2024, using U.S. Census population projections for the county as the denominator, Dr. Riddell and experts at the Teton County Health Department found that residents of the county have a life expectancy of 94 years. Dr. Riddell said that beyond comparisons to national averages and Wyoming state averages, they also compared Teton County data to that of 13 other comparable counties with popular mountain towns—called “peer counties”—including Vail in Eagle County, Colorado, Aspen in Pitkin County, Colorado, and Park City, Utah, in Summit County, among others. The numbers will be formally published in Teton County’s Triennial Community Health Assessment in June 2027.

To put the number in perspective, the average life expectancy across the United States is 79 years, per the most recent mortality data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released in 2024.

“My job here as the director of our health department is to encourage and promote health and the health of our community. And to see longevity like that, it almost makes me wonder if I will still have a job moving forward. We’re kind of crushing it, at least in this specific metric,” Dr. Riddell told Outside.

Longevity remains one of the biggest buzzwords in health conversations, with people trying any number of elixirs, fitness tests, or extreme biohacking measures to live longer. But what if living longer is as simple as getting outside and moving your body? And how can people emulate the lifestyle of mountain residents to live a longer, healthier life?

Here’s what Dr. Riddell and Ingrid Yang, MD, an internal medicine physician specializing in longevity and not affiliated with the Teton County Health Department, had to say.

Teton County is the 12th-largest county by total area in Wyoming and has a population of roughly 23,000 people. It’s known for its scenic mountain landscapes and is home to Grand Teton National Park, around 40 percent of Yellowstone National Park, and Jackson Hole—a premier hub for outdoor recreation and winter sports.

Teton County isn’t alone; other mountainous counties also have high life expectancies, according to 2025 data from the Demographics Atlas, which draws on data from the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics. San Miguel County, home to Telluride, Colorado, has a life expectancy of 86.5 years; Summit County, home to Park City, Utah, has a life expectancy of 84 years; and Deschutes County, home to Bend, Oregon, has a life expectancy of 80.9 years.

Life expectancy refers to how long a population in a specific place is expected to live. Because we can’t predict how long people will live, public health experts rely on statistical data to determine average lifespan.

“Life expectancy is a really common metric used to measure health and longevity of various populations. And of course it’s a broad number. It is not necessarily indicative of any one individual’s expected life duration. That all depends on many, many factors, some of which we get to choose in life and others which we do not,” Dr. Riddell said. Those factors may include geographic location, family medical history, access to healthcare and nutritious food, and disease risk, according to Cleveland Clinic.

At nearly 20 percent higher than the national average, Teton County’s 94-year life expectancy is an exceptional statistic. This recent data suggests that mountain towns may be leading the charge in longevity. Why is that?

“That is the million-dollar question for sure,” Dr. Riddell said. Again, any conversation about why a population lives or dies isn’t definitive, so while reasons why the life expectancy is as high as it is are speculative, they are still informed by scientific data.

“We know that Teton County is a really, really healthy place. I think recreation opportunities here are off the charts. We have low smoking rates, we have low obesity rates, and we have low disease rates that are associated with all of those things,” Dr. Riddell said.

But there may be a bit of a chicken-and-egg scenario happening here, too, Dr. Riddell said. Teton County is a healthy place, but its culture of outdoor recreation and healthy living might attract people who already have an affinity for that lifestyle.

There’s a caveat, though. While exercise is largely protective of joints and helps lower chronic inflammation over time, Dr. Yang told Outside, the biggest risk to longevity in the mountains is trauma.

“Ski, bike, and climbing injuries such as anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears damage joints far more than [regular] wear and tear does.” Extreme lifelong endurance training has been linked with higher rates of atrial fibrillation (an irregular heartbeat) in some athletes, Dr. Yang said. This doesn’t negate the overall benefits, though, she explained. Staying active is still a protective measure. “For almost everyone, the danger is too little activity, not too much,” she said.

Other facets of mountain town life, Dr. Yang said, like social connection, proximity to green spaces, and cleaner air, are also associated with long-term health.

Another major factor is wealth. “Teton County is the wealthiest county in the U.S., with one of those measures being per capita income. That brings resources that another county this size might not have,” Dr. Riddell said. He named health delivery services, high-end food options, and restaurants as a few of those beneficial resources.

“In the U.S., income is one of the strongest predictors of how long people live,” Dr. Yang said. “A 2016 study reported that at age 40, the richest one percent outlive the poorest one percent by 14.6 years (men) and 10.1 years (women),” she said.

Dr. Yang said that living at altitude may also play a role in longevity. “Teton County sits at an average elevation of 7,800 feet. At that height, moderate altitude is linked with lower cardiovascular mortality and better metabolic profiles,” she said. Still, Dr. Yang noted that the people who live there and their overall lifestyle outweigh any potential effect of altitude. And very high altitude—above 11,500 feet—Dr. Yang said, is linked with accelerated aging.

To reap the benefits of mountain-town living no matter where you’re based, Dr. Yang suggests keeping the following in mind:

#8153. Iran Executed a Mountaineer for Alleged Violence in Anti-Government Protests. Hundreds More Face the Same Fate.

Ali Sina Mostafavi (Photo: Courtesy of Iran Human Rights)

Ali Sina Mostafavi dreamed of climbing Everest. In 2019, he trekked to its Base Camp. Under a photo of him pointing to the summit, he wrote on Instagram in English: “Top of the world. I promise to come back to you.”

Mostafavi never fulfilled his promise. On October 14, he was executed by the Iranian authorities in Kerman Central Prison.

The 38-year-old is one of at least 39 people to have been executed in connection with Iran’s anti-government protests last winter, and one of six athletes among them.

Dr. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, an ice climber and co-founder of the Norway-based Human Rights for Sport, told Climbing, “From a human rights perspective, every single aspect of this case is an absolute violation. The state has not made any credible, independently verifiable evidence public.”

Born in 1987 in Bam County, southeastern Iran, Mostafavi was a professional mountaineer and a member of the Speeco mountaineering club in his home city of Kerman. He called mountains ‘the love of his life,’ according to Abdollahkhani.

Mostafavi climbed two of Iran’s highest peaks, Damavand (5,610m/18,410ft) and Alam-Kuh (4,850m/15,910ft). In 2016, he ascended Mount Kazbek (5,054m/16,581ft) in Georgia.

In 2019, Mostafavi traveled to Nepal and summited Island Peak (6,189m/20,305ft) and trekked to Everest Base Camp. In 2022, he attempted Ama Dablam (6,812m/22,349ft), reaching 6,600m/21,654ft.

Mostafavi was married and had a 13-year-old daughter, Respina. Alongside his climbing career, he was an accomplished musician who played the tar, a traditional Persian lute. Friends spoke of his sensitive, artistic spirit, and his deep love for mountains, music, and animals—notably, his beloved cat and dog.

On his Instagram account, @everest_coldhell, his bio reads: ‘Mount Explorer. Love the nature. Musician.’

In December 2025, Iran’s economic crisis sparked street protests that developed into nationwide demonstrations against the Islamic Republic’s repressive regime, which enforces compulsory hijab laws restricting women’s autonomy, conducts violent crackdowns on protests, issues arbitrary arrests, and employs the use of torture.

In an attempt to suppress dissent, authorities used lethal force, killing thousands and arresting tens of thousands of protesters. The human rights organization Amnesty International called this “the deadliest period of repression by the Iranian authorities” in its decades of monitoring the country.

Following the assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei by US-Israeli airstrikes on February 28, Iran’s government intensified repressive crackdowns on dissent under the pretext of “wartime conditions.”

By October, at least 106 people arrested during the January protests had received death sentences, according to documentation by human rights organization Hengaw.

Iran carries out the world’s second-highest number of executions after China. In 2025, its government executed at least 2,159 people, the highest figure recorded by Amnesty International since 1981.

On Instagram, Mostafavi expressed support for Iran’s former Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, an exiled dissident who calls for a secular, democratic, and liberal Iran, describing him as “the only saviour of the homeland.” Two sources claim that Mostafavi’s family were set to move abroad before the 2022 ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’ protests began, but he ultimately chose to remain to fight for Iran’s future.

One obituary claims that he had been arrested twice in recent years for political activism and had spent time in Kerman Prison. This January, the mountaineer joined protests alongside millions of Iranians.

IranWire, an independent pro-democracy outlet, reported that Mostafavi was arrested three months later on April 25 alongside his wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé, while his mother’s home was also raided.

Mostafavi was reportedly beaten during his arrest and was forced to sign confession papers to release his family members. It is not known whether he had access to an independent lawyer, a right frequently denied to defendants in political and national security cases in Iran.

The Iranian judiciary’s account of the case was published by state-aligned media outlets including Mizan News Agency, Tasnim News Agency, the IRIB, and Tabnak. The allegations have not been independently verified.

The Judiciary of Iran claimed that Mostafavi had participated in the widespread anti-government protests in January, and that he was a member of the “Immortal Guards,” an armed wing of exiled dissident Reza Pahlavi’s group.

The judiciary also alleged that Mostafavi had shot and injured two civilians, fired at security forces, and possessed firearms, ammunition, and Molotov cocktails. It further accused him of communicating with foreign media and sharing footage of missile strike locations during the US-Iran war.

Mostafavi was convicted of the capital offense of moharebeh, or “enmity against God,” alongside several charges relating to alleged violence, weapons possession, and communication with hostile media. The evidence against him has not been made public.

The judiciary reported that the fiancé of Mostafavi’s sister received a prison sentence of 12 years and seven months for alleged cooperation, while he, his wife, and his sister were also sentenced to seven months in prison for posting content deemed as propaganda against the regime.

An appeal against Mostafavi’s death sentence was rejected. IranWire reported that he was transferred to solitary confinement the night before his execution and that family members were summoned. The judiciary announced that he was hanged at dawn in Kerman Central Prison on October 14. According to IranWire, Mostafavi asked the prison guards to pass along a message to the judge: “I did not wage war against God, nor did I commit moharebeh that you should charge me with it; my fight was with you.”

That evening, state-aligned outlet Tabnak published footage purporting to show Mostafavi’s arrest, weapons allegedly found in his possession, and a confession to a planned attack on Kerman Airport. IranWire reported that the confession appeared to have been made under duress and spliced together with unverified footage. Amnesty International has also identified signs of forced confessions in 18 videos of Iranian prisoners arrested between February and May 2026, during the same period as Mostafavi’s arrest.

Shortly after his death, a video of Mostafavi’s young daughter crying on her father’s grave, accompanied by their cat, circulated on social media.

Human rights groups have voiced concerns about Mostafavi’s case in the context of widespread forced confessions and sham trials lacking due process in Iran.

“The complete absence of forensic evidence or transparent court records confirms that his conviction rested entirely on forced confessions extracted under coercion rather than any objective proof,” Abdollahkhani said.

She explained that the arrest of Mostafavi’s wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé fits an established pattern of authorities using family members as leverage.

“The Islamic Republic routinely arrests close relatives and uses threats of torture or sexual violence to force athletes into making false confessions in a desperate bid to save their loved ones,” she said.

According to Human Rights for Sport, at least eight other mountaineers’ lives are at risk.

Maryam Hadavand Siri, a 42-year-old mother of two, led the Mountaineering Board of Pakdasht County in Tehran Province. She was arrested during the January protests, transferred to Evin Prison, and sentenced to death in April, without access to an independent lawyer. Following an appeal, her case was referred to the Supreme Court for review.

Social media activist and mountaineer Fatemeh Jami was arrested at her home on June 30 by Cyber Police officers. She was transferred to Gorgan Prison, where she remains detained without access to a lawyer or medical assistance.

Tara (Shirin) Masoudi, a member of the Razhan Mountaineering Group in Mahabad, was arrested on August 19. She was transferred to a detention centre and later released on bail. She is awaiting a final verdict.

Mohammad Hakimpour, Mostafa Ghaderi, Mohammad Saleh Hosseini, Hossein Abdollahi, and Khaled Rahimi—all members of climbing clubs in Saqqez—were arrested on October 8. According to Human Rights for Sport, they were subjected to physical abuse in detention and have been denied access to legal counsel, family visits, and telephone calls.

Abdollahkhani urges climbers to raise awareness of Mostafavi’s execution and the status of the eight other mountaineers, and to contact national federations, sports governing bodies, the International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation (UIAA), and the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

“How is it possible that a member of the climbing community is at risk of execution on alleged political charges, while the global climbing world stays silent?” she asked.

On October 30, Human Rights for Sport published an open letter to the UIAA executive board and athlete commission. In the letter, Abdollahkhani asks the UIAA to appeal directly to Iran’s national mountaineering federation, along with its Ministry of Sport and National Olympic Committee, to stop further executions and advocate for the release of imprisoned climbers.

#8152. Colorado Trail and Continental Divide Trail ‘Extensively Damaged’ After Severe Flooding: Here’s What We Know

This article was updated on November 11, 2026, at 8:35 a.m. with additional information regarding the condition of the Colorado Trail section 28.

In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

“Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 update on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”

As many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

Junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A conditions report on the U.S. Forest Service webpage says that a “Huge rock and heavy debris” is currently blocking the trail about a half-mile from the trailhead. One video claims to show an area along Junction Creek Trail near Gudy’s Rest, where a footbridge has been washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a new “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote. “For example, we know that the Colorado Trail along Junction Creek has largely been obliterated and that the trail bridge is gone. In some sections, the trail is buried underneath riverflow that was re-routed during the flooding.”

On November 10, a Facebook user posted to the Durango Area Trail Conditions Report Facebook page with information about the trail section above Junction Creek. According to the report and accompanying photos, the Walls Gulch Bridge was destroyed, and the trail following Flagler Fork Creek sustained “major damage.”

Authorities said that recovery work would likely not begin until spring and summer 2027 due to weather, and discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

“Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” another post reads. “Don’t become a statistic — rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”

Another video posted to Instagram shows the sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

The CTF said that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 update.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate plans to avoid the area.”

On November 2, the CDTC posted another update for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it said. While the interactive map on its website shows no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”

Backpacker reached out to the CDTC for comment, but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

While the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

“While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”

Think your vegetable garden is finished for the year? Not so fast. Some crops relish cooler temperatures and can shrug off a little frost.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November doesn’t necessarily mark the end of the vegetable growing season. While warm-season crops are definitely done for the year, you may still be able to sow and grow some of your cold-hardy favorites.

Knowing how and when to plant a vegetable garden so late in the season depends on your USDA hardiness zone, climate, and local weather. If you have milder winters, you can likely sow seeds directly in outdoor beds. In colder climates, you’ll need to provide some protection against frost and snow.

Here, I offer pro tips on late veggie growing, along with eight vegetables you may be able to start now for a winter or spring harvest. If you’re unsure about whether or not you can grow any of these in November, contact your extension office for more location-specific guidance.

Planting veggies now takes more effort than simply sowing seeds. Beyond knowing your climate and hardiness zone, you need to pay attention to the weather. For example, avoid seeding when the soil is frozen or soggy.

Prepare the soil by clearing out weeds, raking out any stones or remaining summer plant debris, and mixing in fresh compost. Seed planting depth and spacing depend on the crop you are sowing, so do check the seed packet information.

Manage your expectations for this project. Less sunlight and colder temperatures mean germination and growth will be slow. Be patient.

Although these veggies are either cold-tolerant or good at overwintering, they still will not tolerate very cold weather. If you have cold winters, you’ll need to protect your efforts. An old milk jug can give seeds some protection and act as a mini greenhouse for a few seeds. If you want to start more seeds, use a cold frame, like the Giantex wooden cold frame, which has a flip top for easy access.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As plants develop, row covers will protect winter veggies from frost, snow, harsh winds, and flying pests. This Plant Covers Freeze Protection Kit on Amazon includes hoops, clips, and a roll of frost blanket.

Apply straw, shredded leaves, or other loose, organic mulch over and around new crops or overwintering veggies. Just take care not to drown delicate seedlings in mulch.

Take care with watering, as letting soil get soggy is easy to do in winter. Check the soil before watering plants.

These are some of our favorite vegetables that many gardeners can start in November, including those that could be ready in winter and others that you’ll harvest in spring or summer.

Garlic is an example of a crop that will overwinter and provide you with a harvest next summer. As long as your soil is workable and not waterlogged, garlic is a dependable crop for planting now. Plant individual garlic cloves with the pointy ends up. Use mulch to protect the cloves from winter freezes. If successful, your cloves will grow roots over winter, foliage in spring, and bulbs in the summer.

You can plant garlic from the grocery store, though it’s usually a softneck variety grown in milder climates and may struggle in colder regions. Hardneck garlic is often a better choice for those areas. Botanical Interests offers an organic garlic flavor sampler bundle featuring two hardneck varieties and elephant garlic.

Shallots can also be overwintered and will reward you with a harvest in late spring or early summer. Plant shallot sets or individual shallot bulbs with the pointy ends up, just slightly above the soil surface. French Red Shallots from Burpee are a delicious culinary variety worth trying.

You should mulch lightly to protect shallots in colder climates. However, fall planting is best suited to milder regions, and if you have very cold winters, the planting window may already have passed. Check with your local extension office for exact dates.

Spinach is remarkably cold-hardy. The seeds will be slow to germinate in the cold, though. This Sow Right Seeds Spinach Seed Collection contains three tasty varieties. Unless you have very mild winters, use cold frames or other protections. Once spinach plants get established, they should produce leaves you can pick throughout the winter. Harvest from the outside edge of the plants, leaving the center intact.

Kale is another very cold-hardy vegetable that many gardeners can grow now for winter harvests. It’s also hard to grow from seed in the cold, so unless you have mild weather in November, consider using transplants, like these Bonnie Plants Lacinato Kale Plants from Lowe's. Use cold frames or row covers as needed, especially during hard freezes. For warmer zones, Burpee sells a four-variety kale blend.

Arugula is a mildly cold-tolerant green that is best for growing in November in milder climates. If conditions are right, it will germinate and grow rapidly, giving you a winter harvest. If you want to grow arugula in colder regions, use frames or a greenhouse and be prepared for growth to be slower. You can pick up a pack of arugula seeds for less than $5 from Sow Right Seeds.

Like arugula, radishes grow rapidly, so if the weather and soil conditions are right, you can start plants now and get a quick winter harvest. Burpee's Cooks Custom Blend Radish Seeds Collection contains red, pink, purple, and white radishes. For the best results, the soil should be workable, and November temperatures should be cool or mild. For colder areas, plant the most cold-tolerant varieties and use cold frames.

Plant carrots now for a sweet treat in early spring. Carrots generally overwinter well, but choose the more cold-tolerant varieties for the best results. Scarlet Nantes, included in this Gardeners Basics 5-Variety Pack on Amazon, can be harvested through winter with protection. It’s also important to make sure the soil is loose and free of stones, so the roots can grow deep. Use a generous layer of mulch to keep the soil warmer over winter.

Peas can also generally be overwintered for a spring harvest. Peas grow best in cooler weather, but they still need some warmth to establish. Alaska peas, available from Eden Brothers, tolerate chilly conditions, but if your November is very cold, it might be too late. In milder growing regions, this can be a good time to start peas. Be sure to plant your peas near a trellis or other vertical structure so the plants can climb in spring.

November doesn’t have to mean the end of growing veggies for the year. Depending on your region and local weather, you may be able to grow or overwinter some or all of these cold-tolerant vegetables. Choose the plants most suited to your conditions and be patient. Colder weather means slower growth.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

#8150. A Woman Was Swept Off an Oregon Beach and Left Clinging to Rocks Offshore. A Lifeguard Rescued Her in the Darkness.

Rocky sea stacks rise along Oregon’s southern coast, where a woman was swept into the ocean by massive waves at Secret Beach on November 8. (Photo: Juan Pablo Jim/Getty)

A woman was rescued from the ocean after powerful waves swept her off a beach in southern Oregon on November 8, leaving her clinging to rocks offshore as darkness fell.

The woman had been walking along Secret Beach, a secluded stretch of rocky coastline roughly 20 miles north of the California border, when a swell pulled her into the ocean, according to a statement posted to Facebook by Curry County Aquatic Safety. Unable to reach her, the woman’s husband called 911 around 5:18 P.M. The report did not name the woman.

When a Curry County sheriff’s deputy arrived at the scene, the woman had been swept 200 feet down the coastline, where she was stranded on rocks roughly 50 to 70 feet offshore.

“People want to come see the waves, and we have a lot of great scenic viewpoints for them,” Luke Martinez, an aquatic safety officer and lifeguard with Curry County Aquatic Safety, told Outside. “Unfortunately, people sometimes get stuck in bad spots, and that was the case Sunday night.”

The National Weather Service had issued a high surf warning for Oregon’s southern coast that day, forecasting breaking waves of 25 to 33 feet.

Martinez told Outside that he and fellow lifeguard Shannon Ingram responded to the emergency as large waves continued crashing onto the beach.

“It was pretty unruly,” Martinez said. “There was huge surf. The tide was out, and we couldn’t see much, but there were surges occurring up and down the beach.”

Ingram reached the shoreline ahead of Martinez just after sunset. Wearing a wetsuit and a safety helmet, she determined she could safely enter the churning water and made her way to the stranded woman. She checked her for injuries, secured her with a rescue tube, and brought her back to shore.

The woman was able to walk off the beach with assistance before being taken to a hospital for further evaluation.

“It was a good ending to something that could have been pretty bad,” Martinez said.

Secret Beach sits along the Samuel H. Boardman State Scenic Corridor, a 12-mile stretch of coastline dotted with rocky cliffs, secluded beaches, and offshore rock formations. Martinez noted that the area has surged in popularity due to social media, even though its rugged geography poses serious risks.

“We live along a really rugged coastline,” Martinez said. “It’s similar to people visiting the mountains and climbing 14ers. Not everybody realizes the dangers involved.”

Curry County Aquatic Safety has just two lifeguards—Martinez and Ingram—covering roughly 100 miles of coastline and several rivers. On November 8, they spent much of the day advising beachgoers about the unusually powerful surf, emphasizing that volatile conditions can catch people off guard before help can arrive.

“Beachgoers will be watching the smaller waves, thinking they understand how far the water is reaching up the beach,” Martinez explained. “Then that longer-period swell arrives and surges much farther up the beach than the waves they’ve been watching. During these events, our beaches can become dangerous for anybody, including experienced surfers or swimmers.”

Massive waves are a recurring hazard along the Pacific coast from October through March, when winter storms generate the largest swells, according to the state of Oregon. During major storms, offshore waves can exceed 30 feet.

Also on November 8, videos captured similar scenes elsewhere along the coast. Footage from Cannon Beach showed a young girl nearly being swept into the ocean, while another video from Winchester Bay showed two people scrambling to escape incoming waves as their dog was swept into the water. The dog was later rescued.

Another round of massive surf is expected to batter the Oregon coastline in mid-November. A National Weather Service warning projects breaking waves reaching 30 to 35 feet November 13 and 14. The agency is urging visitors to stay off beaches, rocks, jetties, and piers while the high swells continue.

A few thoughtful changes will keep your garden landscape looking effortlessly stylish through the cooler seasons.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While you might be thinking that the gardening season is drawing to a close this month, there's plenty to look forward to, especially if make a few simple switches to help your yard transition from fall into winter. As the year segues into the cooler months, it's time to enjoy colorful stems, textural bark, sculptural seedheads and shrubs bejewelled with bright berries, and relish the quiet beauty of this season.

Check through our landscape designer tricks to take a fall yard into winter, and add one or two to your outside space now. An injection of structural evergreens, naturalistic ornamental grasses, a tree with fiery foliage or colorful autumn bulbs can make a huge difference at this time of year now the late-season flower show is coming to an end.

Consider, too, how to make your fall garden user-friendly so you feel inspired to spend plenty of time outside still, perhaps by including a cosy gathering area around a fire pit. Which of these easy tricks landscape designers use to carry a garden from fall into winter are right for your yard?

Adding a mix of ornamental grasses is a fundamental element of fall garden design and these low-maintenance plants will continue to look good all through winter. While many annual and perennial flowering plants will happily grow through airy grasses in summer, the blades will keep borders looking full once they've finish blooming.

Choose varieties that offer bold autumn color such as Panicum virgatum ‘Shenandoah’, available from Nature Hills. Also known as switch grass, this well-behaved clump-forming grass develops stunning red and damson tones in fall, topped by wiry stems of flowers. Reaching 3 feet high, it looks fabulous planted among taller shrubs as well as with perennial blooms.

Another option favored by landscape designers is blue-green-leaved Festuca glauca 'Elijah Blue', also available from Nature Hills. Growing to just a foot high, it's perfect for border edges and winter containers.

Landscape designers often choose trees with fiery foliage to create a stunning focal point with brilliant shades of scarlet, russet, gold or burgundy. Even if space is limited, there are plenty of smaller trees that will squeeze into a compact garden.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Some of most spectacular fall color is typically associated with Acer (maple) trees, but to carry the interest on into winter, choose a type with textural bark, too. Acer griseum, the paperbark maple and available from Plant Addicts, has peeling, papery warm-brown bark. Caught in the light of a low winter sun, its peeling curls of bark are nothing short of spectacular. The coral bark Japanese maple, available from trees.com, has bark in an intense red tone that's equally eye-catching.

Another option if you're wondering what to plant in fall is a multi-trunked tree that, once the bright foliage has fallen, brings architectural interest to your garden, like the Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry tree, available from trees.com.

Attractively planted container gardens are a landscape designer's best friend during the cooler months of the year. These portable pots of color and texture can be positioned wherever you want, adding a welcoming touch to an entrance or a bright splash to a patio table.

There are all sorts of vibrant plants that love life in a patio pot and last from fall into winter for a wonderful cool-season display. The go-to formula is to combine a thriller (height), filler (body) and spiller (edging) to create a full, textured look. Good choices for fall and winter include compact evergreens or ornamental grasses to add the height element, pansies to fill out the body of the planter, and ivy to tumble over the edges. For a modern look, squeezing a container full of a single variety is an even easier option.

Dwarf pine trees are enjoying a surge in popularity with landscape designers, and no wonder. While in spring, summer and fall they provide a green, textural foil to colorful flowers and leaves, once winter arrives they emerge as standout sculptural shapes. The beauty of slow-growing dwarf pines is that they naturally stay compact and well-shaped, so need very little looking after.

Dwarf Mugo pine (Pinus mugo var. pumilo) is a particular favorite thanks to its dense, dark needles. While it eventually grows to 3-5 feet high, its easily kept pruned into a neat mound. Dwarf Mugo pine, available from trees.com, keeps its seed cones all through winter, adding to the display. Adding one, or an odd number dotted through your outside space, is a great way to ensure your garden has character throughout the year, and helps avoid that sensation of sparseness that often happens in winter when many plants are dormant.

When summer perennials and annuals fade you will need something else to take their place. Autumn-flowering bulbs will pop up reliably year after year to add color and, if you choose the right sunny spot, will naturalise, gently spreading to reflect how comfortable they are in your landscape. This repetition will strengthen the planting design, as well as adding continuity.

Nerine bowdenii (also known as as Bowden lily) brings an explosion of color to rejuvenate tired fall borders. These beautiful bright blooms on sturdy stems grow to 24 inches, and can be added to pots as well as planted in drifts through a flowerbed. In addition to the standard pink petals, there are varieties from white through to a deep ruby red, and Dutch Grown stocks a good nerine selection. While it's too late to plant the bulbs this year, you can pre-order ready for planting in spring for floral fireworks next fall.

Another favorite is hardy cyclamen, which you'll likely find potted at your local garden center in fall. Plant a mix of the hardy ivy-leaved cyclamen (Cyclamen hederifolium), which flowers in fall and has pretty foliage that lasts through winter, and winter-flowering cyclamen (Cyclamen coum) which blooms winter into spring, for a long season of interest.

Even during the cooler months of the year, your outdoor space should be an inviting spot where you want to linger. A fire pit creates an ambient spot to gather around at dusk offers the opportunity for year-round entertaining, and is a go-to for landscape designers interested in creating an outdoor space with year-round usability.

Whether you want the crackle of real wood burning or the convenience of starting a fire with the click of a button, a fire pit will add visual as well as physical warmth to your fall and winter garden. Opt for a design that complements your overall aesthetic and add layers of textured cushions and throws in a palette of warm, earthy tones to garden furniture to build on the cozy vibe.

This fire pit is perfect for patio evenings, bringing friends and family together around a warm, inviting flame. Though it burns real wood, an airflow system facilitates efficient combustion to reduce smoke levels.

Fuelled by wood or wood pellets, this 7-inch diameter stainless steel mini fire pit brings the s'mores experience to a patio table. Efficient burning means it's smokeless and a removable ash pan makes clean-up easy.

Fuelled by propane gas, this stylish fire pit has an adjustable flame and can deliver plenty of warmth to keep your outdoor gatherings cozy. A lid lets it double as a coffee table and it's also available in black and stone-look.

Landscape designers often use a mix of materials to maximize texture and interest in garden design. These are automatically thrown into the spotlight during the cooler months of the year when plants die back and leave the hardscaping exposed. Gravel offers a softer alternative to bare paving slabs, and buff-toned pea gravel in mixed sizes and shapes like this landscaping pea gravel from Lowe's creates a particularly natural look.

Softening the edges of hard landscaping with plants is another landscape-designer trick that comes into its own as a garden moves from fall into winter. Use evergreen creeping thyme to blend the edges of a curving pathway and a functional garden element becomes an attractive winter feature. You can also use gravel as a mulch to avoid areas of bare border soil in winter, an option that's also easy on the budget.

Another way to maximise texture and help your garden transition from fall into winter without missing a beat is to add warm lighting from a low angle. In fall, a ground-stake spotlight will highlight foliage but then is easily moved to throw a glow through ornamental grass blades. Even a wash of light across a gravel path creates a play of shadows that shows off texture to the full, and allows you to appreciate your garden from indoors on dark evenings.

The easiest way to create individual pools of low light is with solar spotlights, although you'll need to shop smart when buying outdoor solar lights that will generate enough power in fall and winter. For a start, choose lights with adjustable solar panels so they can be angled to match the sun's lower position in the sky. Look for a high conversion rate and a large capacity battery of at least 1500 mAh, too, and opt for warm-toned LEDS that will create more ambiance than bright white lights. These Solar Spot Lights from Wayfair tick all three boxes.

#8148. The Horrific-Smelling Piece of Gear No Hiker Needs to Carry in 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

A solid-fuel stove burning a hexamine tablet (Photo: krblokhin / iStock via Getty)

There are smells I’ve experienced that still give me nightmares: The box of mail-order lobsters UPS once delivered to my parents two weeks late. The freezer filled with fish and ground beef that I had to clean out after someone unplugged it and left it outside in the summer sun. And, sliding into third place after those, the time that my hexamine fuel tablets got loose in my pack.

I was competing in the Grand Traverse, a roughly 40-mile ski mountaineering race from Crested Butte to Aspen, Colorado. Because of the ruggedness of the terrain, the organizers required that each team carry a full set of survival gear, including a stove. In an attempt to keep our kit as light as possible, my partner and I packed a tiny solid fuel burner and a few fuel tablets for a total of about 5 ounces—lighter than a 100-gram fuel canister. I double-bagged them and stuffed them in my beanie, which I hoped would stop them from jostling around in my pack.

If you’ve never used hexamine fuel tablets, the first thing to know about them is that they smell bad. And not bad in the way you’d expect: Instead of the petroleum twang of white gas or the skunky smell added to propane-butane mixes, the tablets have a distinct marine odor. Users have compared it to rotten shellfish or dead carp.

Halfway through the race, I started to notice hints of that smell when I opened my pack. But it wasn’t until after we crossed the finish line that I realized what had happened: At some point during the race, one of the bags had jostled open. The beanie I had packed it in was the main casualty; I put it on and gagged. It took multiple cycles in the washing machine and about a month of airing out before it stopped smelling like a Red Lobster during a power outage.

You, too, can have this experience, and you don’t need to spend much: Esbit stoves, the best-known brand of solid-fuel burners, can be had for as little as $12, fuel included. They’re cheap, simple, and at least notionally light. But whether you’re considering one for your ultralight kit or emergency winter use, I would buy literally anything else.

Solid-fuel stoves are old tech: The first hit the market in 1936, when Esbit, a German company, introduced hexamine fuel tablets and the compact burners designed to use them. Demand for them boomed during World War II, when Esbit’s burners became standard issue for the Wehrmacht; the Allies developed their own versions as well. Today, solid-fuel stoves still have more currency among European backpackers than American ones, who are less likely to have used them and, if they live somewhere where fire restrictions are common, often can’t, as land managers generally ban any stove without an on-off switch alongside campfires.

Fire hazard aside, there are concrete reasons why so few hikers nowadays are springing for solids. While the stoves are light, their fuel is not: It takes almost 2 standard tablets, or nearly an ounce, of hexamine fuel to bring a liter of water to a rolling boil, compared to about 0.3 ounces of fuel for a pressure-regulated canister stove like the Soto Windmaster. While someone using a canister stove does have to tote the weight of the metal container the fuel comes in, the difference in efficiency means that for any trip longer than a day or two, the solid-fuel stove’s advantage is questionable at best; at the very least, it means starting out with a heavier pack. They’re difficult, though not impossible, to light in the cold and glacially slow at melting snow, real disadvantages for an emergency stove that you may have to spark up with numb fingers. And then, of course, there’s that pungent smell.

If they’re inefficient and smell bad, why do solid-fuel stoves continue to hang on? I’ll give them this: They’re simple. Like anything with moving parts, a canister stove can break. Filters clog and piezo igniters burn out. There’s essentially no way to break a solid-fuel stove; step on it, and you can just bend it back into shape. Even when it comes to simplicity, though, I’m not convinced it’s the best choice: While they have their downsides, an alcohol burner is as cheap and light as a hexamine stove, smells better, and the fuel is easier to find. (Lest it seem like I’m trashing Esbit, I’ll note that they make a solid alcohol-burning model that doubles as a storage bottle for its fuel.)

I’m not a hater, or at least I try not to be: Every backpacker has their gear quirks, and if you’re an old-schooler who’s been using a solid-fuel stove since your scouting days, I think that’s great. But if you’re one of the newcomers on any given backpacking forum pondering whether you should buy that ultralight titanium solid-fuel burner, the answer is probably no. For about $5 and 12 grams more—that’s about the weight of a AAA battery—you could pick up a BRS-3000T, a canister stove that will give you far less grief. And as a bonus, it won’t make your pack smell like a mermaid with B.O.

#8147. Is an AI Data Center Coming to a National Park Near You? This New Map Shows Where.

(Photo: Courtesy of More Than Just Parks)

As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks.

Will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles.

“The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside. “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.”

“Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.”

Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware.

“The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz said. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.”

To use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site shows the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center.

“You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz said.

The map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West.

In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park.

At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park.

The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites.

Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17.

According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry.

Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a company called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage.

According to a report published by NPR, the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports.

The land is about two hours from both Arches and Canyonlands National Parks.

Located about 40 miles from Zion National Park, Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026.

Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities.

Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where big tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards.

“At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”
